name: Rhode Island Current
title: The League of RI Businesses made a play to sidestep campaign finance limits. Now, it’s game time.
description: Vanessa Lopez knew the odds were stacked against her. A first-time candidate going up against a three-term incumbent, Lopez realized she needed outside help to succeed in her Democratic primary challenge against Sen. Meghan Kallman for the District 15 seat representing Pawtucket and Providence.  “I have no one in my corner, so I was like, […]
text:
The League of RI Businesses used multiple, related PACs to donate $10,000 to Democratic Senate District 19 candidate James Metivier. Checks from each PAC are displayed during a March 30 fundraiser for Metivier at Phantom Farms Brewing in Cumberland. (Courtesy of The League of RI Businesses).Vanessa Lopez knew the odds were stacked against her.
A first-time candidate going up against a three-term incumbent, Lopez realized she needed outside help to succeed in her Democratic primary challenge against Sen. Meghan Kallman for the District 15 seat representing Pawtucket and Providence. 
“I have no one in my corner, so I was like, ‘how the heck am I going to do this,’” Lopez, 37, said in an interview. 
Enter The League of RI Businesses. The political group born out of a gun rights campaign was recruiting state legislative candidates to fill open seats and challenge incumbents whose records did not align with its “pro-business” platform. And, under an unprecedented maneuver to create 40 political action committees — one for each city and town plus a statewide organization — The League advertised up to $1 million in donations per year per endorsed candidate, circumventing state campaign finance laws that cap annual donations at $2,000 per candidate. 
No one has received a seven-figure donation from The League yet. But the execution of its multi-PAC strategy is coming into play for a handful of its chosen candidates, including Lopez.
A $10,000 cash infusion, divided into five, equal $2,000 donations from League PACs, was transferred to Lopez’ campaign account on March 18, according to campaign reports submitted to the Rhode Island Board of Elections. Lopez is also fundraising on her own — reporting $1,800 in donations in the second quarter — but the bulk of her $10,218 campaign balance as of June 30 comes from The League.
“This actually gives me a chance to play the game,” said Lopez, a self-employed videographer and graphic designer. “If I didn’t have the resources, even if I had the good ideas, I wouldn’t be able to compete.”
The loophole has already been employed by seasoned political strategists to a much lesser, and less vocal degree. Amica, Bally’s Corp., and the state teachers’ union all have two PACs apiece, according to state campaign finance data. The Providence firefighters union has four PACS. The union representing local and state government and public school workers has five PACS. 
“It’s a legitimate tool,” said David Levesque, cofounder of The League and the organizer of all 40 PACs. “If people don’t like the law, change the law.”
Which is what good government groups tried to do during the 2026 legislative session. The pair of bills backed by Common Cause Rhode Island and the Rhode Island Board of Elections sought to apply the existing, $2,000 donation limits to multiple political action committees when controlled by the same person or group — replicating the rules in place for federal elections. The bills failed to advance out of committee in both chambers. 
The League of RI Businesses is encouraging anonymous donations to its 501(c)4 and political action committees. State law lets donors who contribute less than $200 per candidate or organization remain anonymous. (Graphic courtesy of The League of RI Businesses)
Incognito mode 
The League lined up a 23-candidate roster and built its cash reserves, openly encouraging donations of up to $9,900. A $9,900 contribution split between 40 PACs, with a 20% cut for the 501(c)4, comes out to $198 per PAC — just below the $200 limit that lets donors remain anonymous in campaign finance reports, under state law.
“As soon as you say who you’re going to vote for, there’s somebody that doesn’t like that person, and then all of a sudden, you lost the contract, or your neighbor is mad,” said Levesque, a Narragansett resident who owns Brewed Awakenings coffee houses.   
The statewide PAC — one of the 40 — has raised nearly $60,000 since fundraising began in May 2025. Roughly 10% comes from under $200, anonymous donations.
Over the same time period, the organization has spent nearly $100,000. Half of that, $50,000, was funneled to five League-endorsed candidates who are running Democratic legislative primaries: Lopez; Mark Mesrobian, the Democratic challenger in Senate District 36; James Metivier, the Democratic challenger in Senate District 19; Leah Boisclair, the Democratic challenger in House District 36; and Kevin Hoyle, one of two Democrats in the primary for the open House District 32 seat. All but Hoyle are running against incumbent Democratic legislators.
“We’re looking at races we think are winnable,” Levesque explained. “If we can win these five races, that would really change the course of the state of Rhode Island.”



Quotation







This actually gives me a chance to play the game. If I didn’t have the resources, even if I had the good ideas, I wouldn’t be able to compete.


– Senate District 15 candidate Vanessa Lopez on campaign contributions from The League of RI Businesses


Kallman, the incumbent facing Lopez in Senate District 15, is a progressive Democrat whose work on restrictions on federal immigration authorities rankled Levesque.
“She spends more time out of the district than in the district, going to Minnesota to talk about ICE,” Levesque said. 
Kallman, along with two other Democratic lawmakers, spent two days in Minneapolis in January, invited to participate in a nonprofit conference meant to draw upon the lessons learned from interactions between federal immigration authorities and people in Minnesota. Three people were shot by ICE agents in and around Minneapolis in January 2025, two of whom died.
Kallman dismissed Levesque’s criticisms about her travels as “nonsense,” while defending her record on supporting protections for Rhode Islanders in interactions with immigration authorities.
“My focus on ICE is absolutely an indicator of what’s important in people’s lives right now,” Kallman, 42, a professor at the University of Massachusetts Boston, said. “Rhode Island has a really important job in protecting our neighbors. I am very proud I am a member of the General Assembly that continues to do that.”
Lopez, who is of Cape Verdean and Puerto Rican descent, did not comment on Kallman’s stance on immigration. A self-described “common-sense candidate,” her website names housing, healthcare and education as top priorities — all topics Kallman has also addressed during her time on Smith Hill. But their proposed solutions differ: Lopez denounces rent stabilization for its effect on landlords, while Kallman has championed stronger protections for renters. Lopez denounced the millionaire’s tax included in the fiscal 2027 budget which she believes will drive out employers and jobs, while Kallman advocates for an even more wide sweeping set of taxes on top earners. Lopez also opposed the assault-style weapons ban approved by lawmakers, including Kallman, in 2025, framing her stance as a matter of self-defense.
The League of RI Businesses organized a fundraiser wine tasting at Gasbarro’s Wines on Federal Hill in Providence on Wednesday, Nov. 19, 2025. From left, John Loughlin, a Republican candidate for lieutenant governor; Laura Turini, a Democratic candidate for state Senate District 35; David Levesque, co-founder of The League; Leah Boisclair, a Democratic candidate for House District 36; and Mark Mesrobian, a Democratic candidate for Senate District 36. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Democrats, divided 
Ideological differences characterize other League-backed candidates and their Democratic primary opponents.
Mesrobian, a Narragansett entrepreneur who is challenging Sen. Alana DiMario in the primary for the Senate seat spanning North Kingstown and Narragansett, espouses a business-centric platform focused on cutting taxes and red tape. Mesrobian received $10,500 from The League through six of its PACs in November and December.
Cumberland Town Councilor James Metivier, challenging Pearson in the Democratic primary for the Senate District 19 seat spanning parts of Cumberland and Lincoln, stresses the need to curtail state spending. Metivier received $10,000 from five of  The League’s PACs on March 30. 
Metivier and Mesrobian each declined to comment on criticism about The League’s campaign finance strategy because they did not know enough about it.
Metivier, 60, a retired IT manager for Amica Mutual Insurance Co., noted he has not spent any of The League’s donations, though he is likely to on campaign mailers. He raised $1,400 in donations from individuals in the second quarter of the year, and has $27,800 cash on hand.
Mesrobian, 58, general manager of members-only Bonnet Shore Beach Club, received $36,000 in donations during the the three-month period that ended June 30, He has over $107,000 cash on hand — more than double the $44,000 balance of DiMario, who raised $14,000 in the second quarter.
“Their contribution is not really that significant to me,” Mesrobian said of The League’s donations. 
It is for Kevin Hoyle. The first-time candidate for the open House District 32 seat representing North Kingstown raised $125 in the second quarter. But he has $66,000 in his account, thanks to a $10,000 series of PAC donations from The League in March, and a $50,000 personal loan. 
“You can’t bitch about $10,000,” said Hoyle. “The nice thing is, there’s no strings attached. It’s not like I am being told I have to vote this way or that to take the money.”
A retired entrepreneur who went back to school for a master’s degree in law studies after selling his software development company because he was “bored,” Hoyle, 67, is running against Robert Craven Jr. for the seat formerly held by Craven Jr.’s father. 
Neither has held elected office, but Hoyle framed himself as the underdog, challenging an incumbent name with political ties. Craven Jr., 32, who works as policy director for the Rhode Island General Treasurer’s office, sees Hoyle’s financial boost from The League as a philosophical problem rather than a practical one. He’s confident he can win on his own record and merits.
But, “As someone vying for the public trust in running for office, I think candidates should value transparency,” Craven Jr. said. “We have campaign finance laws to make sure we know where money is going in politics.”
Kallman, Pearson, DiMario expressed similar concerns with The League’s strategy.
“If their donors are embarrassed enough about what they’re up to, maybe they should reconsider,” Kallman said.
Unintended consequences 
Kallman and DiMario were among the 14 senators who voted against a 2023 bill that became law without the governor’s signature raising campaign contribution limits from $1,000 to $2,000 per year, while upping the threshold for donations to remain anonymous from $100 to $200.
“I think it should be the strength of candidates’ ideas rather than how much money they can put in to getting their name out there,” DiMario said.
Pearson, then-Senate Majority Leader, voted for the bill, but said it was never intended to be used the way The League has done.
“We need to close that loophole,” Pearson, 38, a Citizens Bank executive, said.



Quotation







As someone vying for the public trust in running for office, I think candidates should value transparency. We have campaign finance laws to make sure we know where money is going in politics.


– Robert Craven Jr., a Democrat running for the open House District 32 seat in North Kingstown


A dozen sitting state legislators, mostly Democrats, have received donations from The League’s PACs within the last year, though none were more than $2,000 per candidate per calendar year. 
Rep. Marie Hopkins, a first-term Warwick Republican, received the most: $2,000 in December plus $1,000 and a $800 in-kind donation in March. Deputy House Majority Leader Thomas Noret, a Coventry Democrat, received $400 while Senate Minority Whip David Tikoian received $250. Tikoian, a North Smithfield Democrat, also donated $1,250 to The League’s PACs and $250 to Mesrobian in 2025, according to his campaign finance reports.
John Marion, executive director for Common Cause Rhode Island, hopes The League’s unabashed application of state campaign finance rules will spur state lawmakers to restrict campaign donations by related PACs in the 2027 session. DiMario has already committed to reintroduce the bill next year.
Second-quarter campaign reports from The League PACs include the following description below each anonymous donation: “Tandem donations from individuals in RI that don’t want the Crazies to target them. :)”
“It certainly helps our case that they’re rubbing the public’s nose in it,” Marion said. “It’s immature and unprofessional and not smart politically.”
Thornton also clocked the comments on The League’s campaign reports but said there wasn’t anything he could do.
“As long as they’re complying with disclosure requirements and the limitations on contributions, we don’t have jurisdiction,” Thornton said.
But, he continued, “I do think this is an area of the law that needs to be tightened.” 
Early voting begins on Aug. 20 ahead of the Sept. 9 primary.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado history rhymes
description: Daily life in early Colorado history can seem alien to modern observers.  In 1876, the year of statehood, it could take weeks for mail to arrive in Breckenridge, then a hamlet of 250 people that was accessible by wagon road. Denver’s daily newspaper contained numerous items about who in town had gone on vacation and […]
text:
A locomotive on the Atchison, Topeka, & Santa Fe Railroad in southern Colorado is pictured in this 1880s photograph. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, MCC-3176)Daily life in early Colorado history can seem alien to modern observers. 
In 1876, the year of statehood, it could take weeks for mail to arrive in Breckenridge, then a hamlet of 250 people that was accessible by wagon road. Denver’s daily newspaper contained numerous items about who in town had gone on vacation and who had arrived to visit. Beer was 10 cents a glass. Needless to say, there was no screen time.
Click the image to see Newsline’s special reporting project on 150 years of Colorado statehood.
But in other ways, 15 decades of events affirms the adage about how history doesn’t repeat, it rhymes.
Newsline this year, as part of Colorado at 150, is publishing stories about the Colorado of 1876, and it recently completed a special reporting series, Fifty for 150, comprising 50 stories about events that helped define Colorado since the proclamation of its statehood. Part of what makes these articles fascinating is how different life used to be, but they also recount episodes that resonate hauntingly with modern times.
Colorado is the site of several infamous mass shootings, including those that occurred at Columbine High School, an Aurora movie theater, and the Club Q nightclub in Colorado Springs. Gun violence prevention is a perennial topic at the Legislature, and deadly shootings are up in Denver this year. But the state has a long history of gun violence, a report by Chase Woodruff revealed. 
“Between 1862 and 1872, research has estimated, the homicide rate in Colorado’s Central City averaged 68 per 100,000 residents per year — a higher rate of deadly violence than plagues even the most dangerous U.S. cities today,” Woodruff wrote. In the American West, he wrote, “Shootings by law enforcement officers were common, as were acts of quasi- or extrajudicial violence by sheriff’s posses or other vigilante groups.”
In 1870s Colorado, a populist movement developed against railroad corporations, which through lobbying and bribery shielded themselves from government interference and established the template of Gilded Age inequality and corruption. Swap out railroad barons for tech oligarchs and you’ve got a modern echo of that former dominance, as today’s grassroots backlash to toxic wealth, as well as timidity before it, resembles the varied response to corporate magnates of the late 19th century.
A recurring theme throughout Colorado history is the mistreatment of vulnerable people and communities. The most extreme example of this kind of abuse involves the Ute people and the government’s egregious betrayal of them. An 1868 treaty promised them “absolute and undisturbed use and occupation” of most of the Western Slope, but the U.S. government broke that promise four years later as gold and silver prospectors began to trespass in the region, which is thought to have sustained the Utes and ancestor cultures for as many as 13,000 years. Today, Ute tribes occupy two small reservations in southwestern Colorado.
An 1874 photograph taken in Washington, D.C., during a visit by a delegation of Utes from Colorado. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-19251)
In 1880, a white mob attacked Chinese residents in Denver and burned and raided most of their businesses. The police did little to stop this mass act of bigotry.
During World War II, Colorado was the site of an incarceration camp for Japanese Americans who were falsely suspected of disloyalty and forcibly removed from their homes. The camp in Granada held more than 7,000 people. 
In one of the most astonishing moments of state history, Gov. Edwin “Big Ed” Johnson in 1936, during the Great Depression, deployed National Guard troops to the border with New Mexico to turn back “indigent” people. The move came during a time when many in Colorado scapegoated Mexicans for economic stress.
Sound familiar? This and other instances of discrimination prefigured the immigration enforcement horrors unleashed by the Trump administration. Most Coloradans oppose the mass deportations carried out by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, but too many leaders in the state have behaved with the kind of complicity and cowardice that has always been necessary for government discrimination to occur and which is always condemned by subsequent generations.
As it happens, ICE’s history of harassing Coloradans goes back to its earliest years. In 2006, it launched the largest instance of workplace immigration enforcement in U.S. history. One of the sites targeted in the operation was a meatpacking plant in Greeley.  
The Fifty for 150 series also highlights people and moments in which Coloradans can take pride, such as a Boulder County clerk’s watershed actions to advance LGBTQ+ rights, a governor’s intervention on behalf of striking miners in 1894, the passage of a civil rights law in 1895, and Chicano Movement leadership in the 1960s.
In every case, the verses of history have something to say today, as we inscribe fresh lines that future Coloradans will read as new rhymes.

title: Nate Morris jumps through last hoops before confirmation as ambassador to Colombia
description: On Wednesday, Nate Morris jumped through one of the last hoops to become the next U.S. Ambassador to Colombia. Morris answered questions from the Senate Foreign Relations committee, in preparation for a committee vote that will send his nomination to the full Senate. Morris is a native Kentuckian, a successful businessman, and a popular figure […]
text:
Businessman Nate Morris takes questions from the press after a Jefferson County Republican Party debate for U.S. Senate candidates. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)On Wednesday, Nate Morris jumped through one of the last hoops to become the next U.S. Ambassador to Colombia. Morris answered questions from the Senate Foreign Relations committee, in preparation for a committee vote that will send his nomination to the full Senate. Morris is a native Kentuckian, a successful businessman, and a popular figure on the ideological right. How common is it for a person of his profile to become a United States ambassador? More common than most think, and much more common in the past two years. 
Career vs. political
Assuming he is confirmed by the full Senate, Nate Morris will become what is colloquially known as a “political ambassador,” as distinct from a career diplomatic professional from the US Foreign Service. Political ambassadors serve two main purposes.  The first is to reward major donors and political allies with what amounts to patronage.  The second is to convey to a foreign audience that the ambassador has a relationship with the President, and is thus to be taken seriously. In practice this means that political ambassadors fall into two camps; major political figures dispatched to manage extremely important diplomatic relationships, and underqualified friends of the President sent on extended vacations to safe, pleasant places. In both cases, career diplomats backstop the ambassador’s lack of experience and expertise, ensuring smooth functioning regardless of who formally heads the mission.  
Changes under Trump
Every modern President has nominated a mix of political and career ambassadors. President Trump entered office in 2017 with a hostile relationship towards the professional foreign service. Accordingly, in his first term the percentage of political ambassadors jumped from about 30% of the total to 43%, representing a significant change but not necessarily a full break from previous practice. By contrast, since resuming the Presidency in January 2025 some 90% of Trump’s ambassadorial appointees have come from the political side, representing a huge shift in diplomatic practice. 
Moreover, Colombia had historically been regarded as the sort of country that requires a professional, career ambassador. The complexities of the security relationship with Bogota, Colombia’s proximity to Venezuela, and the country’s role in the international narcotics trade have convinced most recent Presidents to appoint career Foreign Service officers to the position. The appointment of Morris thus represents a break not only with longtime staffing practice, but also with how the US government has viewed its relationship with Colombia. 
Previous ambassadors from Kentucky
Morris is hardly the first political ambassador to hail from Kentucky.  Just this century, Matthew Barzun served as Ambassador to the United Kingdom and to Sweden; William Farish served as Ambassador the UK; W.L. Lyons Brown Jr. served as Ambassador to Austria; Catherine Todd Bailey served as Ambassador to Latvia; and Kelly Craft served as Ambassador to Canada and to the United Nations. In addition, career diplomats Christine Ann Elder served as Ambassador to Liberia, and Greta Holtz to Oman. 
Indeed, Morris is not the first Kentuckian to serve in an ambassadorial role in Colombia. Three Kentuckians in the first half of the 19th century – Richard Clough Anderson Jr., Thomas P. Moore, and Robert B. McAfee – served in diplomatic roles to what would become Colombia, although of course 19th-century diplomatic practice was much different than modern diplomacy. 
The nomination process
Nate Morris was nominated for the position of Ambassador to Colombia on June 1, 2026, and was interviewed by the Senate Foreign Relations committee on Wednesday, August 5.  A vote to send his nomination to the full Senate should come soon. His nomination as ambassador came as payback from President Trump for dropping out of the 2026 GOP primary for US Senate, clearing the field for Representative Andy Barr. While the open nature of the quid pro quo raised eyebrows, it did not violate federal law and likely will not affect the course of his nomination.
There is little reason to believe that Morris will struggle in either the Foreign Relations committee or the full Senate. Whether he will excel as an ambassador in such a difficult posting is a different question.  Veterans of the Foreign Service are replete with stories of bad or inept behavior from political appointees, ambassadors who normally serve in far less critical positions than Morris. Moreover, with the Foreign Service strained by resignations and by the unusually large number of political ambassadors appointed during the Trump administration, Morris may lack some of the support that amateur diplomats normally receive. Still, Nate Morris is an important political figure in his own right, rather than a used car dealer who donated enough money to catch the President’s interest. Morris’ tenure as Ambassador to Colombia will be a key test of his future viability as a candidate for political office.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: State of the race: GOP backs Comer for Kentucky governor as Dems must choose Beshear allies
description: U.S. Rep. James Comer appears to be the favorite to win the Republican nomination in next year’s Kentucky governor race before he’s even announced he’s running. Meanwhile, Democrats must decide between Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former Democratic House leader Rocky Adkins.
text:
Supporters cheered for Republican Congressman James Comer who is up for re-election this fall, but is considering a run for governor in 2027. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)U.S. Rep. James Comer appears to be the favorite to win the Republican nomination in next year’s Kentucky governor race before he’s even announced he’s running. 
A plane flew over the Fancy Farm Picnic in West Kentucky Saturday saying, “Run, Comer, Run.” Most Republicans used their remarks at party events and the picnic to suggest Comer should seek the governorship — including Secretary of State Michael Adams, who had been considering a run himself. 
Adams told the Lantern after the picnic that he views Comer as “the best candidate we’ll have.” On the Democratic side, Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former Democratic state House leader Rocky Adkins have launched campaigns. They both have high-profile ties to Gov. Andy Beshear, who has remained popular with voters throughout his two-terms in office. 
Kentucky Sec. of State Michael Adams speaks to a Comer supporter on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)
Adams said it would be a “black eye” for Beshear with Democratic voters nationally if Beshear’s party were to lose the governorship after he leaves office and he were to run for president in 2028. Adams predicts that Beshear “will pull all the stops that he can to try to save the seat for his party.”
“My goal is to prevent a primary, and then we can run to free country,” Adams said. “But if we don’t have everyone shooting at James Comer, he can conserve his money, and the Democrats can have their primary battle. I think we’re going to have a very competitive general election.”
Comer, a 53-year-old who represents Kentucky’s 1st Congressional District and has gained national attention as the chairman of the fiery House Oversight Committee, told reporters Saturday that running for governor was something he’d “make a decision on very soon.” He’s currently seeking reelection to his House seat. 
“But it looks really good right now, especially at the prospect of having a pretty united Republican ticket, and that’s something that’s very important because the Democrats have had a lot greater success in the governor’s race than the Republicans over the last 50 years, and I think there’s a craving for new leadership in Kentucky,” Comer said.
Tres Watson, a former spokesperson for the Republican Party of Kentucky, said Comer has been working to “mend fences” and “make new inroads.” Watson said that with an open seat, another candidate will likely declare but “it’ll be a D or an F tier opponent, not anybody in the A- or B-tier.”
Contested primaries have worked for and against both parties. Comer previously ran for governor in 2015 after serving as agriculture commissioner. He lost that primary to former Gov. Matt Bevin by 83 votes. It was a heated primary between the Republicans, and Democrats went into the year backing former Attorney General Jack Conway, who Bevin defeated. 
In the last governor’s race, the 2023 GOP primary was crowded and former Attorney General Daniel Cameron won the nomination after besting Republican mega-donor Kelly Craft and Agriculture Commissioner Ryan Quarles. Cameron, however, lost to Beshear that fall. 
“I think there’s a lot of appetite to avoid that and be able to pool our money and sit back and wait to see which Democrat we have to face,” Watson said. 
Watson noted that Cameron had to speak a lot about opposing abortion in the primary to win over hard-right conservatives, but then later attempted to soften his stance after Beshear’s campaign ran ads targeting those views. 
“Comer doesn’t have to be as overreactive to those groups if he doesn’t have a strong primary challenge,” Watson said.
US Rep. James Comer shakes hands with a supporter on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)
How will Dems decide? 
Watson said that he anticipates that the Democrats in the race — Adkins and Coleman — “won’t be contentious publicly,” but it will be “very contentious behind closed doors.”
Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman speaks on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)
Coleman ran with Beshear in both of his elections. She’s touted her past as an assistant principal and basketball coach to make education a focus of her campaign. Meanwhile, Adkins, who left his role as Beshear’s senior adviser before launching his campaign, has said he’s the best “fighter” to take on Republicans. Adkins previously ran for governor in 2019, losing that primary to Beshear by about six points. 
Friday before the Fancy Farm Picnic, Coleman told the Lantern she plans to focus on accomplishments she’s had while working with Beshear throughout the last two terms, but also “I also think it’s important to differentiate myself as someone who is looking to the future.”
“We have to be focused on what we need to get done, not what we’ve already done,” she said. 
Former Lt. Gov. Crit Luallen, who served under former Gov. Steve Beshear, said Coleman would be Democrats’ best chance against Comer because it would be “a sharp contrast” on major policy issues, like education. Plus, education is “not a partisan issue nor a progressive versus conservative issue,” which could help Coleman reach out to moderate and independent voters in a general election, Luallen added. 
“It’s difficult for a woman candidate to walk that fine line between being really not too abrasive, not too aggressive, but also being strong enough for people to recognize her leadership strengths, and I think that’s that’s the key for Jacqueline. She has to have that balance,” Luallen said. 
Meanwhile, Adkins told reporters Friday he plans to focus on his experience in both the legislative and executive branch. He said under Beshear he’s been “in the room when decisions have been made” and travelled with and for him across the state. 
“I don’t need a class. I don’t need any special training,” he said. “I am battle-tested. I am ready to be governor, and I’m ready to be governor on day one.” 
Erin Petrey, a progressive who recently ran for the U.S. House in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, said Adkins has “the best crossover appeal” and views him as someone who could bring voters who have left the Democratic Party in recent years back into the fold. Kentucky Republicans gained the majority of registered voters in July 2022. 
Democrat Rocky Adkins speaks to a supporter on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)
Adkins’ connection to Eastern Kentucky may also be a key factor for him. From Elliot County, Adkins represented the 99th House District  from 1987 to 2019.
“Kentucky Democrats — we used to be the working class. It used to be a lot of folks in Eastern Kentucky, like where part of my family is from, and now the party has really just become identified with Louisville and Lexington,” Petrey said. “And Rocky is someone who I think every Kentuckian can see some of themselves in him.”
Both Luallen and Petrey agreed that a competitive primary is good for the Democrats. 
Luallen said that as Democrats nationally are “struggling with its identity” — a mix of progressives, moderates and conservatives — Kentucky’s primary between Coleman and Adkins will “get people interested and focused on the governor’s race.”
“I think having a healthy primary will get people focused on the governor’s race and paying attention to the candidates and the issues in ways that will help drive up the vote and turnout,” she added. 
Petrey said it’s “fascinating that the Republicans are essentially going to pull a Democrat move from 2015” to clear the field for Comer as Democrats did for Conway. She noted that “is what yielded Bevin.” 
Contested primaries “are incredibly healthy for not just democracy but for our party,” Petrey said. 
“It gets people having important conversations. It gets people thinking critically. It gets people maybe challenging some of their preconceived notions, and I think it’s very healthy for a party,” she added. “And it also makes people pay more attention to Democrats in a state where we’re still struggling.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Ideology and attendance record in question in Cumberland’s Senate District 19
description: Editor’s note: This is the fourth in a six-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on expected competitiveness between candidates and relevant issues to the district. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 22 have primaries in September. Once poised to preside over […]
text:
Sen. Ryan Pearson, left, has represented Senate District 19 in Cumberland and Lincoln since 2012. He is facing a Democratic primary challenge from  Cumberland Town Councilor James Metivier (right). (Courtesy photos)
Editor’s note: This is the fourth in a six-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on expected competitiveness between candidates and relevant issues to the district. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 22 have primaries in September.
Once poised to preside over the upper chamber Sen. Ryan Pearson’s public feud and falling out with Senate leaders — past and present — appeared to relegate the seven-term Cumberland Democrat to legislative Siberia.


About Senate District 19
Represented by Sen. Ryan Pearson since 2012
Geography: parts of Cumberland and Lincoln
Population: 30,462 residents, 19,774 registered voters 
Partisan breakdown: 54% independent, 31% Democrat, 15% Republican
Demographics: 43.9 median age, 85% white, $108,661 median household income (2024)


Cumberland Town Councilor James Metivier didn’t expect Pearson to seek reelection when Metivier filed to run for the Senate District 19 seat. 
“He hasn’t really been showing up this year,” said Metivier, 60, a retired IT manager for Amica Mutual Insurance Co. 
Pearson tells it differently.
“I’ve always seen my role in the district focused on two things: being focused on bringing back returns for my district, and being a leader on statewide issues,” Pearson, 38, said. “I have a really strong record on both of those things, and I hope to continue doing that.”
And despite his failed challenges of Senate President Valarie Lawson and before her, the late President Dominick Ruggerio, during leadership elections, Pearson says he has still been able to pass bills and shape policy — even with missing 13 of the chamber’s 43 floor sessions this year.
“No one has ever criticized me for not doing the work,” Pearson said, chalking up his absences to work obligations, health issues or, in one case, a legislative calendar that featured no actual policy votes. Pearson works as a senior vice president for Citizens Bank.



Quotation







No one has ever criticized me for not doing the work.


– Sen. Ryan Pearson, a Cumberland Democrat


Metivier acknowledged he was not clued in to the details of Pearson’s personal disagreements with legislative leaders. He believed he offered a more independent-minded option for district voters. Literally. 
During his eight years on the nonpartisan Cumberland Town Council, Metivier was unaffiliated. He opted to run for the Senate seat as a Democrat in order to “get better results” for the district encompassing parts of Cumberland and Lincoln, he said.
Backed by the conservative leaning League of RI Businesses, Metivier’s platform espouses some viewpoints traditionally associated with the Republican party: fiscal conservatism, deregulation and gun rights. He expressed skepticism over the state’s climate change mandates, which some critics, including Democratic Gov. Dan McKee, have blamed for raising energy costs.
“We’ve put in a lot of mandates but we need to make sure it’s not just a virtue signal,” Metivier said of the state’s 2021 Act on Climate Law. 
Eyeing the state’s record $15.2 billion budget, Metivier called for curtailing spending, although he could not name specific areas for cuts when asked. He was certain in his conviction that the series of state housing laws that supersede municipal planning and zoning restrictions were too broad and far-reaching. So too was the recently approved millionaire’s tax and the three-year charter school moratorium, he said.



Quotation







We've put in a lot of mandates but we need to make sure it’s not just a virtue signal.


– James Metivier, a Democratic challenger for the Senate District 19 seat


Pearson, who supported all of these Democratic-led initiatives in the chamber, helping craft many of them during his former role as majority leader, accused Metivier of masquerading as a Democrat while tying himself to a “MAGA conservative group” in the League of RI Businesses. The League’s founder, Dave Levesque, was a featured speaker at a Rhode Island First rally in May that also featured Roger Stone, a conservative consultant who worked on campaigns for former President George W. Bush and President Donald Trump. Stone was convicted and sentenced to 40 months prison on felony charges for interfering with a congressional investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election.  He was later pardoned by Trump.
“It’s an interesting strategy,” said Pearson.
Metivier said he was not aware of The League’s ties to the Trump administration, and differentiated an endorsement from being a part of the political organization. 
Endorsed by the District 19 Democratic Committee, as well as the Cumberland and Lincoln Town Democrats, Pearson maintained that his record reflected the priorities of voters in his district. If reelected, he wants to prioritize increasing state Medicaid reimbursement rates for healthcare providers and expanding the purview of the Office of the Health Insurance Commissioner to consider not only insurance premiums, but also provider availability.
The winner of the District 19 Democratic primary is unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election.

title: RFK Jr. announces decertification of KY organ donor group after numerous problems
description: U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy said the decision to decertify the nonprofit was reached after numerous reviews. “Federal reviewers found serious defici[...]
text:
U.S.  Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. came to Lexington on Aug. 5, 2026 to announce the decertification of a Kentucky organ donation group, Network For Hope. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Linda Blackford)U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. traveled to Lexington on Wednesday to announce his office is firing a Kentucky organ donation organization accused of pursuing critically ill patients for their organs.
Kennedy said the decision to decertify the nonprofit was reached after numerous reviews.
“Federal reviewers found serious deficiencies in nearly 30 percent of the cases that they examined,” Kennedy said at a press conference at the University of Kentucky. “We found patients placed on the organ donation pathway who should have never been there. We found cases where the donation process continued despite signs that patients were not appropriate organ donors. We found repeated failures in clinical judgment, oversight, and patient safety, and we found that these problems continued even after the organization promised to correct them.”
Also attending the conference was T.J. Hoover, who was declared brain dead after a drug overdose. His sister, Donna Rhorer, said yesterday that Hoover was being prepped for organ donation when he began to thrash on the operating table. She said the doctors still wanted to move forward.
“My brother almost died that day,” Rhorer said. “That should never happen to anyone. Those responsible must be held accountable.”
Hoover’s case was one of many documented by the New York Times in a series last year about premature attempts to remove organs.
Officials at Network for Hope, which has offices in Louisville and Cincinnati and serves patients throughout the region, did not return calls for comment on Wednesday. 
“Most organ procurement organizations carry out this work with professionalism, compassion, and deep respect for both donors and recipients,” Kennedy said. “A Network For Hope repeatedly failed to meet those standards. It was a bad apple – an organization entrusted with the gift of life repeatedly put patients at risk. The federal government has the duty to act, and that’s why we’re acting today.”
Earlier in the day, Kennedy met with elected officials, including numerous state senators, to talk about nutrition education in medical school curricula.

title: Menhaden management board advances addendum with potential cuts to Chesapeake Bay fishery limits
description: The regional board overseeing menhaden management along the Atlantic coast on Wednesday  advanced a measure to implement new restrictions on Virginia’s only reduction fishery that harvests the oily forage fish within the Chesapeake Bay.  The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission’s draft addendum would reduce the Bay-specific menhaden catch limits for t[...]
text:
Menhaden are small, oily fish that commercial fisheries catch and grind into meal and oil. The tiny fish also support several Chesapeake Bay species including Atlantic striped bass and ospreys. (Photo courtesy of the Chesapeake Bay Program)The regional board overseeing menhaden management along the Atlantic coast on Wednesday  advanced a measure to implement new restrictions on Virginia’s only reduction fishery that harvests the oily forage fish within the Chesapeake Bay. 
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission’s draft addendum would reduce the Bay-specific menhaden catch limits for the fishery, Ocean Harvesters, which contracts with Omega Protein. Other changes include harvest time period quotas to aid in menhaden migration.
Reduction fisheries catch menhaden in purse seine nets to then grind them up into fish meal and oil. Virginia is the only state that allows reduction fishing of menhaden within the Bay.
Currently, the Reedville-based Ocean Harvesters is allowed to catch 51,000 metric tons of menhaden within the Chesapeake Bay annually without any time period quotas. Last October , the menhaden management board voted to reduce the East Coast limit by 20% – bringing the catch limit to 186,840 metric tons for all fisheries, but leaving the Bay cap in place. 
Board members have raised concerns over whether menhaden populations are waning and potential repercussions of a decline. In past meetings, Maryland representatives have warned about impacts to pound net fishermen and small bait fisheries, and said various fish and bird species could go hungry. 
There are several options included in the draft addendum that the public will have a chance to review and respond to. One is to decrease the Bay cap by 10 to 50%.
Another entails quota periods that allow different percentages during certain parts of the harvest season, with special rules regulating the quota process.
The draft also suggests adding language directing the management board to either tie the Bay catch cap to coast-wide cap fluctuations, or to review the Bay cap every three years.
Concerns about catch limits for East Coast fisheries have grown following the decline of striped bass and osprey. Scientists have used those species as proxies for the menhaden population in the Bay, because there hasn’t been a Bay-specific study on the forage fish. 
Osprey flying over the Ware River in Virginia’s Northern Neck. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
Virginia this year allocated funding for in-depth Bay menhaden research, which will support a multi-year study into menhaden within the Chesapeake Bay and how policies could be shaped around the findings.
One of Virginia’s representatives on the board, Del. Adele McClure, D-Arlington, said it would be premature to pass an addendum before the study is completed, since it could have a major impact on the reduction fishery.
“I’ve heard a lot of ‘I think’ and uncertainty versus ‘we know this is happening, and we know this is the cause and the correlation,’ but I need to know that we’re putting out a complete picture to the public,” McClure said.
At the Aug. 5 public hearing, experts on osprey and other wildlife framed the dwindling numbers of these species’ populations as evidence of the need to manage the menhaden, because they are one of the key foods the birds feed on. 
Their observations about ospreys reflect continued debate about how other animals should factor into determining the health of the menhaden population. 
Bryan Watts, who studies ospreys extensively at the Center for Conservation Biology at William & Mary, said in recent years he has seen the number of the birds laying eggs in Virginia decrease by 20 to 30%.
Bryan Watts, a researcher at William & Mary, checks an osprey nest for eggs on the Ware River. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
“They come here, they arrive at the normal time, and they’ll sit there on the nest all season,” Watts said. “But they just won’t lay. And if you go back in time to the 1980s and 1990s, that rate was about 2%. So, it was rare. That’s why it was so surprising to us.”
On a research trip to the Ware River in the Northern Neck, Watts said the nests along the waterfront have lacked eggs and that the osprey are traveling inland to get food. Mehaden haven’t been found in the river for a long time, he said, which is part of the bigger picture of the fish population’s health.
“Menhaden are a public resource, and so it’s up to us, as the public, to decide how we want that resource allocated,” Watts said. “So if we want all of it allocated to industry, that’s a social decision that we can make. But if some of us care about the osprey and what’s happening with them, maybe we would like to allocate some of that public resource to them.”
Ocean Harvesters has vociferously denied the accusations that the fishery could be contributing to the lack of menhaden in the Bay or blocking them from migrating further into the waters towards Maryland. 
Representatives from the company suggested that detractors haven’t fully considered how the environment and other factors contribute to the situation. More data is needed, the company insisted, to make informed decisions on any potential restrictions.
“The addendum says menhaden availability ‘may be affected’ by changes in abundance and distribution and that recent observations ‘suggest that availability of menhaden in Chesapeake Bay may be changing,’” Ocean Harvesters said in an email, highlighting the lack of definite data  “to comprehensively characterize menhaden abundance and distribution in the Bay or the influence of fishing pressure.”
The company urged the board not to adopt the addendum, and flagged the negative economic impact to communities in Virginia that rely on the jobs provided by the fishery if the Bay cap is lowered.
“If Bay harvest were eliminated and vessels could not replace those landings in coastal waters, Northumberland County could lose as many as 176 jobs, including 98 direct jobs,” the company said.
The addendum will be available for the public to view through October and public hearings will be held across all the states represented on the commission before the board will take up the issue for final decision in November.
“You know we’ve worked on this addendum, and I think it’s time for the public to weigh in. The public wants to hear, wants to see this addendum, and they want to help us make a decision,” New Hampshire board member Dennis Abbott said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Feds, DHHS give clear ‘no’ to TANF being used for childcare workforce grants
description: After more than a year of debate, New Hampshire childcare providers received a direct answer this week on childcare workforce grant funding.  In a series of letters exchanged between federal officials, state officials, and an advocacy group, it has been determined that federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF, dollars cannot be used to […]
text:
A childcare provider playing at Rochester Child Care Center. Over the past few days, the federal government and the Department of Health and Human Services gave a clear response on funding for the childcare workforce grant. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)After more than a year of debate, New Hampshire childcare providers received a direct answer this week on childcare workforce grant funding. 
In a series of letters exchanged between federal officials, state officials, and an advocacy group, it has been determined that federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF, dollars cannot be used to fund the childcare workforce grant and that Child Care and Development Fund dollars cannot be used either. 
In the state budget passed in June 2025, the Legislature appropriated $15 million in TANF funds spread over two years to pay for a workforce grant program aimed at improving New Hampshire’s childcare capacity and availability issues. The grant would help childcare programs recruit and retain employees through sign-on bonuses, health savings accounts, childcare tuition discounts, and more. 
However, issues with this funding method arose after the federal government denied the use of TANF funds in October, stating that applying the funds to child care recruitment and retention did not fall under the statutory uses of the TANF program. Some state officials and childcare advocates thought the answer from the Administration of Children and Families, the federal office that oversees childcare funding, was vague, and have been looking for clarity ever since.  



The official exchange
 

Letters exchanged between the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), NH DHHS Commissioner Lori Weaver, Early Learning New Hampshire (ELNH), and Councilor John Stephen regarding workforce grant funding.
June 7: ELNH sends letter to Councilor Stephen asking him to look into workforce grant funding 
July 27: ACF sends letter to Councilor Stephen answering his questions about TANF
July 30: Councilor Stephen sends July 27 ACF letter to DHHS commissioner Weaver, accompanied by a letter from him outlining what he believes can be done for the workforce grant 
August 4: Commissioner Weaver’s response to Councilor Stephen’s letter 
August 4: Commissioner Weaver’s response to ELNH, clearing up “misconceptions” about workforce grant funding 


TANF is a federal program designed to help low-income families achieve economic security and stability. States receive federal TANF grants every year to go toward programming to help achieve TANF’s purposes. The state receives its annual award, and under federal law, 30% of funds can be transferred to a state’s Child Care and Development Fund account, the source of money for state childcare initiatives like the scholarship fund and Granite Steps for Quality. 
Over the past year, various arguments circled the State House on whether and how TANF funds could be used to fund the workforce grant. After the legislative session ended, with no headway on the issue, childcare advocates turned their efforts toward the Executive Council. 
Earlier this summer, Republican Councilor John Stephen of Manchester traveled to Washington, D.C., and spoke about the matter with officials at the Administration for Children and Families. They responded to him in a letter on July 27. 
Wendy Horman, director of the federal Office of Child Care, confirmed that New Hampshire could not transfer extra, or reserve, TANF grant money from previous years into the Child Care and Development Fund, only current-year federal TANF funds, regardless of the amount of TANF money in reserve. This was the primary argument from childcare advocates, who alleged that past TANF funding could be used to fund the workforce grant. 
Horman also said that TANF money transferred into the Child Care and Development Fund, and leftover CCDF funds from previous years, could be used for childcare workforce and retention efforts, since it is an allowable use of the fund’s money. However, TANF funds, as given, cannot be used, as Horman said she still does not see how it meets the federal rules as stated in a letter from the agency in October 2025. 
Stephen sent the letter from the Administration of Children and Families to the state Department of Health and Human Services, along with his interpretation of how the department could move forward with funding the workforce program. Commissioner Lori Weaver responded to Stephen and Early Learning New Hampshire, the advocacy group leading the effort, to clear up “several misconceptions” about the funding matter. 
“While the ACF confirmed two lawful federal pathways — the use of current year TANF transferred to CCDF, and certain CCDF discretionary carryover — the Department is prohibited from utilizing these pathways under New Hampshire’s adopted budget,” Weaver wrote. “The ACF’s additional commentary on federal law does not change the Department’s obligations under state law, the enacted budget, and existing federal program requirements.” 
Weaver said the Administration of Children and Families response did not take into account the state’s Child Care and Development spending plan, approved agency budget, prior transfer decisions, existing federal commitments, remaining available balances, or the fiscal and programmatic tradeoffs associated with redirected limited federal childcare resources. The Legislature and Gov. Kelly Ayotte adopted a budget that maximized the TANF transfer to avoid a waitlist “during a period of significant growth” of the childcare scholarship program. 
“Redirecting those funds to workforce grants would require reducing assistance to eligible families,” Weaver said to Stephen. 
Weaver told Early Learning NH that the department “already committed” available TANF and Child Care and Development Funds to meet state budget and federal requirements, resulting in no leftover funds for the workforce grant. Weaver also said there was no federal waiver to allow extra TANF funds from previous years to fund the program, the initial path the Legislature tried to take in the budget. 
Jackie Cowell, executive director of Early Learning NH, said she was “pleased” with the quick response from the Department and the Administration for Children and Families on the matter. She said her organization still feels “there’s a lot to work out” before she gives up on the workforce grant funding.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: IURC head, governor talk Zay firing and AES hike reconsideration
description: Gov. Mike Braun declined to elaborate on the firing of former Commissioner Andy Zay except to say he disapproved of Zay's approach to affordability.
text:
New Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission leader Anthony Swinger talks to reporters on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana regulators were set to vote Wednesday on whether they should reconsider a contentious $71 million rate increase for AES Indiana customers — but reversed course abruptly Tuesday, the morning after Gov. Mike Braun unceremoniously sacked former regulator Andy Zay.
The governor, meanwhile, declined to elaborate on the firing except to say he disapproved of Zay’s approach to affordability.
New Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission Chair Anthony Swinger said he made the decision to pull the case from the agenda “because there was no consensus among the commissioners.”
Zay fired from utility regulator panel weeks after AES hike demotion

“All I know is that we didn’t have three unanimous voices, and because of that, it’s not ready to move forward,” Swinger told reporters, after the commission’s weekly meeting in downtown Indianapolis.
Swinger has recused himself from the case because he worked on it in his previous role at the Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, which represents ratepayers in IURC matters.
“I have been completely walled off from any internal discussions regarding the AES rate case,” Swinger said. “… I have no participation whatsoever in internal discussions or processes.”
He said it’s “not unusual” to pull an agenda item if commissioners aren’t ready to take action. The IURC has until Sept. 8 to make a decision on the petition.
Firing came after demotion, controversial vote
Zay sparked the governor’s ire in June, when he joined Commissioners David Veleta and David Ziegner in a 3-1 tally to approve the rate increase. Commissioner Bob Deig voted in opposition, with Swinger recused from the vote.
The day after, Braun called on Utility Consumer Counselor Abby Gray to submit a petition for rehearing and reconsideration to the IURC, which she filed last month.
Braun also demoted Zay as chair, six months after appointing him to the commission in that leadership position, and elevated Swinger to the post instead.
Gov. Mike Braun speaks at an event on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
He fired Zay on Monday — the day the IURC’s original meeting agenda featuring the reconsideration vote was released.
Commissioners are appointed to four-year terms and can only be dismissed “for cause” under Indiana law.
The State Personnel Department has alleged Zay “fail(ed) to file a required financial disclosure after his removal as Chair, improperly award(ed) payments and personal gifts to employees, and direct(ed) staff to alter a public meeting agenda without consulting the new Chair.”
Braun, however, focused on the Zay’s vote to raise rates in comments to reporters Wednesday afternoon.
“Next step would be (that) we’ll find a replacement for Andy, and nothing else to announce there other than I was disappointed that he didn’t take on affordability and holding utilities accountable,” Braun said.
Asked what led to the firing, and if he asked Zay to resign beforehand, he replied, “No, it was from the very beginning, when it was clear I was looking for folks (who are) ratepayer-conscious, and the first thing out of the gate was granting a big increase — and that was not part of the interview. … If you don’t have staff, people working with you in the same mindset, it’s better to find somebody that does.”
The governor, who spoke to reporters after an unrelated event, declined to answer questions on the monetary value of the alleged payments and gifts or why the alleged violations were described as “potential.”
IURC remake
Zay’s seat could be filled within the week.
A nominating committee is scheduled to recommend three finalists to Braun on Thursday afternoon, according to a public meeting notice.	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The group of governor-appointed members typically first kicks off an application period, then goes through the submissions before conducting interviews of semi-finalists and then presenting their top three candidates to Braun. But they’ve got a pool of picks left over from last month’s appointment.
Braun in July selected attorney Joby Jerrells to replace Veleta, who announced plans to resign shortly after the AES Indiana vote. Veleta’s last day at the IURC is Aug. 14, with Jerrells starting work Aug. 17.
Zay’s replacement would be this governor’s fifth appointment to the five-member board. Ziegner is the only remaining member appointed before Braun took office in early 2025.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: GOP gubernatorial primary election seems a foregone conclusion
description: Is Donald Trump about to once again hand-select the next leader of Florida? The president has boasted for years that it was his endorsement of Ron DeSantis when he was a longshot in his race against Adam Putnam that boosted his popularity and paved his path to the Governor’s Mansion in 2018. Trump may do […]
text:
Byron Donalds, Jay Collins, James Fishback, Paul Renner. (Photos via U.S. House, Florida House, Office of the Governor, and Fishback campaign)Is Donald Trump about to once again hand-select the next leader of Florida?
The president has boasted for years that it was his endorsement of Ron DeSantis when he was a longshot in his race against Adam Putnam that boosted his popularity and paved his path to the Governor’s Mansion in 2018.
Trump may do that again this year.
There has been no more significant event in Florida politics over the past year-and-a-half than Trump’s endorsement of Byron Donalds in February 2025 for governor, days before the Naples Republican U.S. representative had declared his candidacy to succeed DeSantis. Donalds has been the leading Republican gubernatorial candidate since.
Other Republicans — Paul Renner, Jay Collins, and James Fishback — have been fighting for second place.
That was never more evident than in recent court proceedings in which Collins attempted to get Fishback thrown off the ballot, alleging the 31-year-old investment CEO didn’t meet the state’s seven-year residency requirement. While the story generated headlines, the net result — Fishback remains eligible — won’t likely change the trajectory of the primary race when balloting is finished on Aug. 8.
On the Democratic side, any thoughts of a competitive race dissolved when Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings dropped out two months ago because of poor health, effectively giving the nomination to former Republican U.S. Rep. David Jolly. There remain five other Democrats in the race, however.
They include North Miami Democratic state Rep. Dotie Joseph as well as Dayna Marie Foster, Evelyn Castillo-Bach, Thomas Fernandez, Thomas Fernandez, and Stephann Norman. The Phoenix reported on their candidacies in June.
 Byron Donalds

Donalds maintains a more than 30-point lead, based on an average of the past five polls, according to FiftyPlusOne.
Donalds is at 43%, Fishback at 12.1%, and Collins at 11.5%, according to that compendium of surveys.
An individual poll taken last month by the Tyson Group, considered one of the state’s best polling firms, showed Donalds at 48%, nearly 40 points ahead of Collins (at 9%), Fishback (8%), and former House Speaker Paul Renner (4%). A quarter of the electorate was undecided.
Fishback, Collins, and Renner have attacked Donalds on several fronts during the primary, and yet none of that has appeared to wound the front-runner (or boosted their own campaigns) in any discernible way.
Donalds, the 47-year-old Brooklyn native who moved to Florida three decades ago, has raised more $100 million. That includes a recent $10 million contribution from billionaire hedge fund manager Ken Griffin, who moved from Chicago to Miami several years ago and was a major financial contributor to Ron DeSantis’ bid for president.
Donalds has seen virtually everything go his way since entering the race early last year. DeSantis’ announcement last year that he would not back him appeared to open a pathway for a DeSantis-backed candidate. In fact, First Lady Casey DeSantis polled relatively well compared to Donalds in 2025 surveys. But she never entered the contest, and the governor has declined to endorse any Republican.
Byron Donalds addressing the Republican Party of Florida’s Sunshine State Showdown in Davie on June 27, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
Regarding property tax reductions, Donalds has said that  if voters reject Amendment 3 in November, he intends to revive the issue next year via the Taxation and Budget Reform Commission (a sentiment shared by the Florida Chamber of Commerce and Florida TaxWatch).
On housing policy, Donalds says he intends to reduce permitting times to lower the price of construction to make housing more affordable.
On the contentious issue of data centers, no candidate in Florida running for office this election cycle has received more financial backing from that industry than the GOP gubernatorial front-runner. For months on the campaign trail, Donalds has argued the state needed to lead on the issue.
“Are we going to embrace the next wave of innovation, or are we going to put our heads in the sand?” he said during a campaign appearance in March. But now, with more than 20 local governments in Florida having voted to reject construction of major data centers, Donalds has filed legislation to ensure developers, and not taxpayers, absorb those  costs.
Donalds has also vowed to “enact the Trump agenda,” a line that helps him in the contested GOP primary but could prove a problem in the general election, with the president under water in public approval rankings in the Sunshine State.
 James Fishback

One demographic where Donalds might be shaky is young white men. A certain part of that cohort seems enamored of investment firm CEO James Fishback. 
During a meeting of the Tampa Bay Young Republicans last week at which Donalds spoke, Spectrum News reported that “it wasn’t entirely a friendly crowd.” At the same club in December, several audience members told the Phoenix they supported Fishback and wished Trump hadn’t endorsed Donalds.
James Fishback speaking at Tampa’s Union Station on July 31, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
To say the 31-year-old Fishback’s run for governor has been controversial would be an understatement. Along with some legal problems that have surfaced since he declared his candidacy, he has faced accusations of making racist and antisemitic comments.
Officials with the Republican Party of Florida (RPOF) cited those accusations, along with his alleged “baseless attacks about Florida GOP officials,” as the reason they rescinded their invitation for him to attend their summer convention in South Florida last month. Around the same time, a political committee associated with Texas Republican U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz spent hundreds of thousands of dollars against him in an ad that aired throughout Florida last month. 
“Why would you spend $10 million in the middle of the World Cup running ads against us? Did they run ads against Jay Collins? Did they run ads against Paul Renner? No, they have only run ads against us,” Fishback told the Phoenix last week during a press conference at Tampa’s Union Station. “We are the only campaign who has directly been targeted in attack ads other than Byron Donalds. That should tell you everything that you need to know about the establishment fearing us.”
 Jay Collins

Florida Lt. Gov. and gubernatorial candidate Jay Collins at the Sunshine State Showdown in Davie on June 27, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
When Ron DeSantis chose then-Hillsborough County state Sen. Jay Collins as lieutenant governor a year ago, the conventional wisdom was that with Casey DeSantis no longer considering a run, the retired Special Forces, combat-wounded veteran surely would become the governor’s heir apparent.
That that never happened has hurt his candidacy, as he’s been forced to address the non-endorsement ever since he jumped in the race.
Collins has been aggressive in hammering Donalds on a number of fronts, including holding a press conference in St. Petersburg in April to issue a 13-page document alleging “liabilities,” including references to Donald’s acknowledged arrest record.
Collins supporters produced an AI-created ad depicting a Byron Donalds administration dominated by data centers and marijuana dispensaries.
None of those moves has appeared to move the needle for Collins.
“People are not enamored by Byron. They are not. But those who are voting for him are largely voting for him because of the president’s endorsement, not because of Byron,” Collins lamented during a Tampa press conference last week.
Paul Renner
GOP gubernatorial candidate Paul Renner speaking to reporters in Tallahassee on Feb. 4, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
While all four of the top Republicans insist they admire DeSantis and want to maintain the conservative momentum the governor has imprinted on the state, one could argue no one is more in synch with DeSantis than Renner.
Renner was speaker of the Florida House during the 2023 session when he (and Senate President Kathleen Passidomo) steered major proposals on undocumented immigration, union busting, restrictions on groups registering new voters , and a six-week abortion ban to passage. The session was tailor-made for the governor to launch a presidential bid. 
Renner (and Passidomo) even traveled to freezing Iowa that January to campaign for DeSantis ahead of the caucus. Yet when Renner entered the gubernatorial primary in September, DeSantis’ only comment was, “It was an ill-advised decision.”
On the campaign trail, Renner has laid out policies, including a detailed a plan to reduce homestead property taxes that included details about how to make up the expected loss of funding for local governments — something critics say Ron DeSantis and the GOP-dominated Legislature have failed to do in putting Amendment 3 on the ballot.
There are several other Republicans running in the gubernatorial primary. You can find them on the Florida Division of Elections website.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: The problem with going solar in Indiana
description: Over the past year, I have been noodling over the possibility of installing solar panels on my roof. This simple curiosity eventually turned into action — I got several quotes for what solar installation might cost. It was at that point that I discovered a 2017 Indiana state law that makes installing solar financially difficult […]
text:
Workers install solar power modules for producing electricity on the roof of a house. (Alexandra Beier/Getty Images)Over the past year, I have been noodling over the possibility of installing solar panels on my roof. This simple curiosity eventually turned into action — I got several quotes for what solar installation might cost. It was at that point that I discovered a 2017 Indiana state law that makes installing solar financially difficult for individual homeowners but quite profitable for electric companies.  
I like the idea of being more self-sufficient. I like the fact that, once installed, solar panels provide pretty much free energy for my home that is healthier for our planet. And solar technology has become much better and more affordable over time. As climate author Bill McKibben put it on a podcast: “Sometime earlier this decade, we passed some invisible line where it became cheaper to produce energy from the sun and the wind than from setting stuff on fire.”
While it has become less expensive, installing a solar harvesting system is not cheap in the short term; especially after federal lawmakers abruptly eliminated the 30% residential tax credit at the end of last year. I would have to pay a lot up front for the ability to harvest free photons that would otherwise just warm up the shingles on my roof. Under fair economic conditions, that upfront cost pays for itself over time through drastically lower monthly power bills, eventually earning back every dollar spent and saving money for years to come.
Let’s look at what this should look like for an average Hoosier household.
The average Indiana home uses ~900 kilowatt-hours of energy per month.  At an average cost of $0.15 per kWh, that equates to an average electricity bill of $135 per month (plus a $17 monthly customer fee, totaling $152 monthly) .
Indiana high court sides with utilities on solar power, ending benefits for small owners

To cover 100% of those energy needs, a family would need an 8-kilowatt solar system, which costs around $25,000 to install. 
With fair energy policy, this system would essentially eliminate a family’s electricity charges, leaving them with only the mandatory monthly fee to the electric company required to be connected to the grid. That would drop their $152 monthly energy bill to $17. 
At this savings rate, the payoff horizon is 15.4 years. Assuming a 30-year solar panel lifespan, a solar household would save around $23,650 in energy bills over the last 14.6 years of the system. All while releasing zero carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
While that is how it should happen, a 2017 state law ensures that is not how it works in Indiana. Here’s why.
On a sunny afternoon in July, a home solar array typically makes far more power than the house needs, sending the extra electricity back to the neighborhood power lines. At night, when the sun is shining in Australia instead of Indiana, the family has to pull electricity back off the grid to keep the lights on. 
Think of the power grid like a bank account: with a solar system you make energy “deposits” during the day, and make energy “withdrawals” at night. The system that tracks these deposits and withdrawals is called “net metering”.
In most states, if you deposit 20 kWh of power during the afternoon (as is usual on a typical sunny day), you get a full 1-to-1 credit to withdraw those same 20 kWh later that night. While states like Florida, Ohio, and Iowa protect 1-to-1 net metering as a matter of property rights and energy freedom, Indiana’s Senate Enrolled Act 309 created an artificial government price control that penalizes Hoosier families for investing in their own homes.
Passed in 2017, the law allows electric companies to harvest those same 20 kWh of afternoon power from you and immediately sell them to your neighbors for $3.00 (the full $0.15/kWh retail price), while crediting you just $0.70 (the discounted $0.035/kWh wholesale rate). When you pull that same power back out of the grid that night, they charge you $3.00 once again. That leaves the homeowner getting back less than 25% of the energy value they deposited just hours earlier.
This greatly changes the financial math for solar energy in Indiana. Rather than reducing the previous $152 monthly energy bill for a solar owner to $17, this net metering boondoggle means that the average solar owner in Indiana still pays $85 monthly.  That pushes the payoff horizon to over 31 years, which exceeds the lifespan of the panels entirely. Instead of saving tens of thousands of dollars, Hoosier families actually end up taking a $900 net loss on their investment.
The $23,650 of potential savings that SEA 309 takes from solar households does not disappear into thin air. Those savings become profits for Indiana electric utilities and their (mostly) out-of-state shareholders. Funded out of the pockets of Hoosiers. It’s time for the General Assembly to repeal SEA 309, restore fair 1-to-1 net metering, and give Hoosier families the right to benefit from their own private property investments.
