name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Doctor who worked 18 months for Iowa City VA is denied an Iowa medical license
description: A physician who worked 18 months at Iowa City’s Veterans Administration Medical Center has been denied a license to practice medicine in Iowa. Under federal regulations, doctors who aren’t licensed in a particular state can still work as physicians at federally operated care facilities, such as those run by the VA, within those same states. […]
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Medicine)A physician who worked 18 months at Iowa City’s Veterans Administration Medical Center has been denied a license to practice medicine in Iowa.
Under federal regulations, doctors who aren’t licensed in a particular state can still work as physicians at federally operated care facilities, such as those run by the VA, within those same states.
State and federal records indicate Dr. Odinaka Nwankwo, who worked in women’s health at the VA Medical Center in Iowa City from January 2021 through December 2022, graduated from medical school in the Dominican Republic in August 1999.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the Iowa Board of Medicine, Nwankwo, who is from Nigeria, then took the three-step United States Medical Licensing Examination. The board alleges she took the first-step exam eight times before passing in July 2002, and took the second-step exam four times before passing in October 2004.
The board alleges Nwankwo took the third-step exam seven times between November 2005 and March 2017, but has yet to pass the test.
Board records show that in January 2015, Nwankwo passed the necessary exams for licensure in Puerto Rico, and then, from August 2018 through May 2019, worked in a federal health care facility in Montana.
In May 2021, the same month the Montana Board of Medicine granted her a license to practice in that state, Nwankwo began working at the VA Medical Center in Iowa City. Court records indicate that in December 2022, Nwankwo was fired from the VA Medical Center, which led to her filing a civil rights lawsuit, alleging employment discrimination, against the VA that’s still pending.
In January 2024, Nwankwo began working at a federal facility in Texas, while also providing physicals for military recruits in central Iowa, according to Nwankwo.
In March 2025, she applied for an Iowa medical license, which the board denied, citing her alleged failure to pass the third step of the United States Medical Licensing Examination and her alleged failure to complete two years of acceptable postgraduate residency.
Nwankwo appealed that decision, arguing her work experience in Puerto Rico and in federal health care facilities should serve as the equivalent of postgraduate training. Recently, the board held a hearing on the matter and ruled that Nwankwo does not meet all of the legal requirements to work as a physician in Iowa.
“The board understands Dr. Nwankwo is frustrated with this process and that she will be disappointed with this decision,” the board stated in its ruling. “However, the board has no authority to circumvent the statutory requirements for licensure.”
Nwankwo said Wednesday in an interview she doesn’t understand the board’s reasoning but does not intend to pursue the matter. She said she plans to remain in Iowa while making periodic trips to Puerto Rico, where she can practice medicine and earn a living.
She said she also plans to pursue her civil rights lawsuit against the VA Medical Center in Iowa City. As part of that case, Nwankwo alleges numerous colleagues harassed, belittled and insulted her at work, in part by criticizing her hair, accent and demeanor. The lawsuit, in which Nwankwo represents herself, seeks more than $100 million in damages, which is well above the statutory cap on such claims.
“It is very hard for one person to fight the federal government,” Nwankwo told the Iowa Capital Dispatch on Wednesday, adding that she feels the VA might be behind the licensing board’s recent decision. “Why are they blacklisting me? I cannot get hired anywhere.”
In response to the lawsuit, the Veterans Administration has denied any wrongdoing. The VA alleges a Summary Review Board fired Nwankwo in December 2022 at a time when she was still working as a probationary employee.
In court filings, the VA has objected to Nwankwo’s request for back pay at the level of medical director, a position the VA says she never held, as well as her requests that the VA pay for her future education and provide assistance in obtaining immigration visas for her sister, niece and nephew.
A trial in the matter is scheduled for June 21, 2027.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: What to know about the ban on kratom in North Dakota
description: Kratom and derivative products are now illegal in North Dakota just days after Gov. Kelly Armstrong announced a ban on the substance and related derivatives.  Lawmakers are preparing to draft legislation restricting kratom for a special session. The attorney general has announced how to dispose of kratom products. And police and prosecutors will be dealing [[...]
text:
7-OH products, a concentrated synthetic kratom derivative, are displayed at a retail store in Bismarck on Aug. 5, 2026, hours before a state ban took effect. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Kratom and derivative products are now illegal in North Dakota just days after Gov. Kelly Armstrong announced a ban on the substance and related derivatives. 
Lawmakers are preparing to draft legislation restricting kratom for a special session. The attorney general has announced how to dispose of kratom products. And police and prosecutors will be dealing with enforcement.
Here is what to know about kratom, the ban in North Dakota and what officials are doing.
What is kratom? 
Kratom is a substance derived from leaves of a tropical tree in Southeast Asia. 
People use the substance, such as in capsule form, as an energy booster, for pain management and to cope with withdrawals from drugs such as fentanyl and heroin. Two psychoactive ingredients known as mitragynine and 7-OH are found in kratom leaves.
Gov. Armstrong announces special session, emergency actions to ban kratom in North Dakota

Kratom can act as a stimulant or a depressant, depending on its levels and how it mixes with other drugs.
Why are officials reacting this way? 
The governor linked overdoses and deaths to readily available, unregulated products in gas stations and smoke shops. Officials say those items contain addictive, highly potent, synthetic kratom derivatives, such as 7-OH tablets, often in colorful packaging with candy-like names.
Since 2021, kratom or related substances have been part of the primary cause of 23 deaths in North Dakota, and a contributing cause in one additional death, according to the State Epidemiology Office.
Kratom-related calls to Poison Control leapt from seven in 2024 to 22 in 2025, according to a state epidemiologist report. 
The governor’s actions follow a move by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration last month to temporarily classify 7-OH and three related kratom derivatives – but not certain botanical kratom items – as controlled substances. Ten other states, mostly in the South and parts of the Midwest, have banned kratom products, according to Armstrong’s office. 
In addition to his executive order banning kratom products for 30 days, Armstrong called a special session of the Republican-led Legislature to pass kratom restrictions, beginning Sept. 2.
He also authorized an emergency rule of the state Board of Pharmacy, effective Wednesday, to ban 7-OH as a controlled substance, similar to the DEA. That rule is in effect for about six months as an emergency rulemaking process unfolds, which will include hearings and public comment.
Growing concerns prompt calls to address kratom substances in North Dakota

How to dispose of kratom
Attorney General Drew Wrigley’s office on Wednesday publicized a list of sites where retailers and consumers may dispose of their kratom products. 
The locations include take-back sites at local law enforcement agencies and MedSafe sites at certain pharmacies, comprising about 200 dropoffs statewide.
People also may dispose of kratom products in the trash, per the state Board of Pharmacy.
Wrigley’s office emailed law enforcement agencies Wednesday morning, stating: “During these initial hours and days, we encourage an enforcement approach focused on providing notice and securing voluntary compliance going forward.”
Under Armstrong’s executive order, people may not knowingly or intentionally create, manufacture, deliver, distribute, sell, purchase or possess kratom or related products. Violations are punishable as an infraction up to a $1,000 fine.
Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, who takes natural-leaf kratom capsules for back pain, said he’ll have to dispose of his supply. 
“I’ve always abided by the laws of the land, so I don’t know why I wouldn’t now,” he said.
Under the board’s emergency rule effective Wednesday, 7-OH is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, the same as LSD and heroin, with higher penalties than an infraction, Board Executive Director Mark Hardy said. 
Bismarck police will respond to calls for service related to kratom or kratom products, whether at a smoke shop or on the street, Lt. Luke Gardiner said. 
The Burleigh County Sheriff’s Office plans to “take appropriate action” if officers encounter the substance during traffic stops, Maj. Jim Hulm said.
“Our guys are constantly taking drugs off of traffic stops, so I know they’re already out there looking for anything out of the ordinary,” Hulm said. 
How one seller has responded
Taunya Davenport, co-owner and operator of Smokey’s House of Pipes in Bismarck, said a lot of customers who buy the kratom natural leaf supplement use it for pain management.
The store previously sold 7-OH products, she said, but discontinued those sales after hearing about the addictive and other negative aspects about 7-OH products. Davenport added the store recently brought 7-OH items back due to demand.
Kratom products are displayed at a retail store in Bismarck on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
She was surprised Armstrong banned natural-leaf kratom in addition to 7-OH, especially after he said during a news conference he had learned about kratom three weeks ago.
“How can you make such a quick decision about that, just learning about it?” she said.
Davenport said she hopes lawmakers will take time to learn about natural kratom leaf products before potentially outright banning them.
The store planned to remove and dispose of all of its kratom products and will try to send back its 7-OH items to distributors. The store expected to take a revenue loss on the natural-leaf kratom. Neither substance is a large portion of the store’s revenue, she said.
What are lawmakers doing? 
The Legislature’s Republican majority leaders announced a working group led by Sen. Michelle Axtman and Rep. Pat Heinert, both R-Bismarck, to meet with executive branch agencies to draft legislation for the special session.
The five-member, all-Republican Kratom Working Group is set to meet at 9 a.m. Friday at the state Capitol. The meeting is open to the public and will be livestreamed. The agenda does not include opportunity for public comment.
Armstrong’s executive order calls on the Legislature to consider and pass laws to regulate or ban various activities, such as delivery, distribution, sale, possession and mislabeling, as well as to set criminal penalties. 
Lawmakers are likely to consider something between a complete ban or narrower prohibitions and age restrictions, Axtman said.
Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, who sits on the Senate Judiciary Committee which might hear the legislation, said she leans toward a total kratom ban, but wants to see what the proposed legislation says.
“The drug industry is going to keep coming up with synthetics, and I think synthetics need to be banned outright, period,” Myrdal said.
Legislative Management, a powerful interim committee of lawmakers, meets on Aug. 17 to consider bill drafts for the special session, which might cover other topics.
What about prosecutions?
The kratom ban will be treated no differently than any other law violation, North Dakota Association of Counties Executive Director Aaron Birst said.
“For me, I look at the governor’s action as a temporary ‘take-this-serious, it’s-against-the-law,’ and then the Legislature will deal with it,” said Birst, a former prosecutor.
County state’s attorneys would primarily enforce the governor’s order, Birst said. Given how new the prohibition is, some people might not know of it, but prosecutors have great discretion over what cases they pursue, he said.
Kratom faces increasing scrutiny from states and the feds

What resources do people have? 
State officials have directed people in crisis to call or text 988, which offers support for suicide, mental health, substance use and other crises around the clock, or contact 211, which helps connect callers with local resources.
In anticipation of more awareness of those phone numbers, FirstLink shared information with its helpline specialists, such as educational resources from Parents LEAD and guidance on services, Executive Director Jennifer Illich said. 
“From our perspective at FirstLink, it’s important for people to know that support is available,” she said via email.
The Behavioral Health Division of the state Department of Health and Human Resources offers resources at 701-328-8908 during the week, State Health Officer Sherry Adams said during Monday’s news conference. Adams was not available for an interview Wednesday, a spokesperson said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling contributed to this story.
Reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Epstein commission releases report on investigation so far
description: A New Mexico legislative investigative subcommittee, known as the Truth Commission, on Wednesday issued its interim report on sex offender Jeffrey Epstein's activities in New Mexico.
text:
Members of New Mexico's Truth Commission, a legislative subcommittee investigating Jeffrey Epstein's time in New Mexico, pictured on Aug. 5, 2026. From left to right: state Reps. Marianna Anaya (D-Albuquerque), Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) and Bill Hall (R-Aztec). (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)The chair of a New Mexico House investigatory subcommittee created to probe the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s activities in the state acknowledged Wednesday its first report does not contain major revelations or final findings.
Truth Commission Chair Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) hefts the interim report during the New Mexico House investigatory subcommittee meeting on August 5, 2026. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)
What the interim report does accomplish, state Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) said, is memorializing for the first time what is known about Epstein’s time in New Mexico and his activities at Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County.
The report assembles a timeline for Epstein’s acquisition of the ranch, time spent there, visitors, use of firearms and alleged sexual crimes and human trafficking that took place through a variety of public documents, court records and other materials.
“In the seven years since Jeffrey Epstein died, in the two decades since his crimes first drew attention of law enforcement, no government, federal, state, or local, has ever compiled an account of what he did in New Mexico,” Romero said. “There are some court records that tell pieces of the story in other states’ cases for other states’ victims, but there has never been an official narrative for New Mexico. This report is the first.”
The nearly 120-page interim report prepared by the legal firm contracted by the commission also provides an accounting of the work the commission has done so far to document that narrative.
The New Mexico House of Representatives created the four-person bipartisan investigative subcommittee in its 2026 session. Its final report is due at the end of the year. 
The commission’s work so far has included issuing 20 subpoenas to state agencies and local law enforcement, as well as private institutions such as the Santa Fe Institute, federal agencies and financial institutions J.P. Morgan Chase and Co. and Deutsche Bank.
New Mexico’s Epstein ‘truth commission’ publishes subpoenas, with more on the way

Of those subpoenas, 11 have been met with full compliance, two were met with partial compliance and seven, Romero said, have been ignored, including by the Federal Aviation Administration and by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York. 
The latter agency has been a high-profile foil in New Mexico’s quest to investigate Epstein. 
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas has said he agreed to stop interviewing witnesses in New Mexico’s former investigation of Epstein after coming to an agreement with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York that federal prosecutors would refer state-related matters to the New Mexico attorney general’s office at the end of their case. 
In a July 20 letter to current New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, Balderas said SDNY failed to honor the agreement.
As such, Torrez announced Wednesday his New Mexico Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Justice over what it says has been the federal agency’s withholding of documents.
The Truth Commission also subpoenaed Torrez’s office. In a news conference Wednesday morning regarding the NMDOJ lawsuit and ahead of the commission’s meeting, Torrez said that NMDOJ “complied with that subpoena and provided the information that they’ve asked for, and so I would imagine that we would do so again in the future.”
The commission’s report, however, characterizes NMDOJ’s response as “partial compliance.” Moreover, it says the Truth Commission and NMDOJ are currently involved in negotiations over information-sharing but have thus far “been unable to reach an agreement.”
Torrez noted Wednesday morning that NMDOJ’s criminal investigation into Epstein’s activities, which he announced in February shortly after the Legislature approved the Truth Commission, differs fundamentally from the Truth Commission’s work.
“Our investigation is very much focused on whether or not there is still a viable criminal case to evaluate and prepare,” he said. “Their investigation is much broader into institutional failures, information sharing: who knew what, when, how they acted on it, how they responded to it.”
Thus, he noted, “we have very different objectives, and what that means is we go about our work in…fundamentally different ways, and so part of what that means is that the work that they do is by its nature much more transparent and open to the public.”
All told, Romero said, the commission has thus far received more than 100,000 records in response to the subpoenas issued thus far. The commission voted Wednesday to issue four more: to the state Workforce Solutions, Public Safety and Taxation and Revenue departments, as well as Ten Thousand Waves spa. 
The latter is mentioned in the interim report and has been reported previously as a place from which Epstein recruited massage therapists. The spa in April issued a statement on social media that said it had “never provided therapists for off-premises ‘house calls’, no therapist under the age of 18 has ever worked at the spa, and all therapists work on a contract basis.” It also noted its support for the work of the Truth Commission.
Epstein survivor Rachel Benevidez watches the Truth Commission hearing on Aug. 5, 2026, alongside activist and elementary school teacher Lisa Christopherson, who has organized protests against Zorro Ranch on several occasions. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)
At its meeting on Wednesday, Romero also noted that the Truth Commission is centered on survivors “with a commitment to never asking a survivor to tell their story twice.”
Epstein survivor Rachel Benavidez, who has testified to the commission before, did so on Wednesday as well, in part calling for unreleased evidence to be made available.
“I use this survivor platform to stand on the right side of every survivor’s journey toward truth and justice,” she said. “I am holding onto faith that real accountability will be achieved.”



What’s in the report?

An introduction to Jeffrey Epstein’s biography and his time in New Mexico
Background on the bipartisan New Mexico Truth Commission, approved by the state House of Representatives in the 2026 session as an investigatory subcommittee
Known information about Epstein’s Zorro Ranch
Discussion of the commission’s five investigatory areas: sexual abuse and trafficking; institutional failures; power and motives; medical and scientific improprieties; financial crimes, irregularities and whether victims received damages
Observations and continuing investigation

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Federal judge dismisses part of lawsuit against Arkansas classroom ‘indoctrination’ ban
description: A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed an equal protection claim in a lawsuit challenging Arkansas’ ban on “indoctrination” in public schools and ordered additional briefing on whether the statute is unconstitutionally vague. Filed in March 2024, the lawsuit challenges the constitutionality of Section 16 of an expansive education law called the LEARNS Act th[...]
text:
Little Rock Central High School students pack the school's courtyard during a 20-minute walkout on March 3, 2023. Several student organizations protested Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders' invocation of the school in promoting the LEARNS Act, a new law that changes several aspects of the state's education system.  (Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed an equal protection claim in a lawsuit challenging Arkansas’ ban on “indoctrination” in public schools and ordered additional briefing on whether the statute is unconstitutionally vague.
Filed in March 2024, the lawsuit challenges the constitutionality of Section 16 of an expansive education law called the LEARNS Act that prohibits “indoctrination” in Arkansas schools. 
U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky in May 2024 granted a preliminary injunction against that section of the law. A three-judge panel from the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals tossed out that ruling in July 2025 and sent the case back to the district court for further proceedings.
Arkansas educators examine revised AP African American Studies curriculum

In Wednesday’s 28-page order, Rudofsky disagreed with the Arkansas State Conference NAACP’s argument that the state education department’s removal of an AP African American Studies pilot course from the 2023-2024 approved courses list violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s right to equal protection. 
Rudofsky said the NAACP did not plead facts that make it plausible that Education Secretary Jacob Oliva engaged in intentional or purposeful discrimination when he revoked the course’s approved course status. Rudofsky noted that the NAACP argued the course’s status was revoked because of the governor’s desire to protect Arkansas students from “left-wing political agenda brainwashing.”
“A desire to protect students from ‘left-wing indoctrination’ is not tantamount to a discriminatory intent or purpose to adversely impact African American students. End of story,” he wrote.
Arkansas is among several Republican-led states that have placed limits on how race is taught in public schools, including prohibitions on critical race theory. CRT is an academic framework centering on the idea that racism is systemic in the nation’s institutions, and the theory is not a fixture of K-12 education.
Whatever someone thinks about making credit decisions based on the politics of a class curriculum, such action is not racial discrimination, Rudofsky said. The Equal Protection Clause is about discriminating against people, and discriminating against ideas is not the same as discriminating against people, he said. 
“Because there is no such thing as a ‘black idea’ or a ‘white idea,’ discriminating against ideas cannot in and of itself violate the Equal Protection Clause,” Rudofsky said. “Similarly, because there is no such thing as a ‘black course’ or a ‘white course,’ discriminating against a particular course cannot in and of itself violate the Equal Protection Clause.”


Let us know what you think...


 

Attorneys for the plaintiffs did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday. The attorney general’s office, which is representing the state, praised the judge’s ruling. 
“The court correctly dismissed the plaintiffs’ equal protection claims, and we look forward to continuing to defend the LEARNS Act as the case proceeds,” attorney general spokesperson Jeff LeMaster said. 
Rudofsky ordered parties to file additional briefs on whether that section of the law is so vague it violates the due process rights of teachers challenging the ban.
The ban was challenged by teachers, students and parents at Little Rock Central High School, site of the 1957 desegregation crisis. The teachers have argued they’re self-censoring what and how they teach because they don’t want to suffer the consequences of accidentally running afoul of the law. Rudofsky acknowledged it’s plausible that there was, at some point, a credible threat of disciplinary enforcement. 
However, he said defendants have confirmed the law only prohibits “compel[ling] somebody to adopt, affirm, or profess” a position that otherwise violates Section 16,” and there’s nothing in the operative complaint that suggests the teachers involved in the lawsuit are engaging in or want to engage in that type of compulsion. 
Rudofsky wrote that “it seems fanciful to think that Ms. [Ruthie] Walls or any other teacher would stumble into discipline here.” 
Ruthie Walls, the lead plaintiff in the case, is a teacher at Little Rock Central High School.
There seems to no longer be any real credible threat of enforcement, said Rudofsky, who questioned if that makes the vagueness challenges moot. 
Defendants’ opening brief is due by Aug. 26. Plaintiffs’ response is due 21 days after defendants file their opening brief.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Federal job cuts in Alaska among the deepest in the nation, analysis shows
description: Alaska lost a higher percentage of its federal workforce last year than almost all U.S. states to sweeping Trump administration cuts, according to a newly published analysis by the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development. By the end of 2025, Alaska’s federal workforce was 10.5% smaller than it had been at the end of […]
text:
Fired federal workers formerly with the U.S. Forest Service based at the Mendenhall Glacier in Juneau speak at the Alaska State Capito; on March 21, 2025, about their experiences. The Forest Service was among the federal agencies in Alaska most heavily affected by job cuts. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska lost a higher percentage of its federal workforce last year than almost all U.S. states to sweeping Trump administration cuts, according to a newly published analysis by the Alaska Department of Labor and Workforce Development.
By the end of 2025, Alaska’s federal workforce was 10.5% smaller than it had been at the end of the prior year, according to the analysis, published in Alaska Economic Trends, the monthly magazine of the department’s research section. In the fourth quarter of 2025, after many workers accepted buyouts or early retirement, the state’s federal workforce had dropped by 1,607 from the total in the fourth quarter of 2024, to 13,767 from 15,374 the year prior, according to the analysis.
The job losses came through mass firings and cuts made by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, the government-reducing campaign led by trillionaire Elon Musk that started shortly after Donald Trump took office for his second term. To a large extent, job losses were concentrated at the end of the year.
Calculated by the annual average, Alaska lost about 4.5% of its federal jobs in 2025. Only Maryland, which lost 6.5% of its federal jobs, and New Mexico, which lost 5.8% of its federal jobs, lost more. 
Federal job losses reduced Alaska’s total earnings by $36.5 million on average in 2025, according to the Department of Labor and Workforce Development analysis, and they brought federal employment in Alaska to the lowest level since at least 1990.
Much of the cutting in Alaska came in the U.S. Department of Defense’s civilian workforce. Calculated by annual average, 340 defense related jobs were lost to the DOGE cuts, but the fourth-quarter loss was calculated at 755 jobs.
The large amount of job losses in the Department of Defense category was a bit surprising, said Karinne Wiebold, the state labor economist who wrote the Trends article. “I assumed early on that the DoD might be one of the less affected departments and that our strong military presence might insulate us,” she said by email.
Federal agencies that sustained high numbers of job losses included the U.S. Forest Service, which had 180 fewer employees at the end of 2025 than in late 2024, the Bureau of Land Management, which had lost 133 jobs at the end of the year, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which had lost 101 of its workers by the end of 2025.
Job losses in the Forest Service and NOAA have affected important Alaska industries and services, including fishery science, weather forecasting, scientific research and tourism.
The fallout from the job losses continues, and the public does not yet have a complete picture, Wiebold said. “I do think the public is aware of the federal job losses and that they have been deep and a bit unpredictable,” she said. “I don’t know if the public generally understands what the ramifications of the cuts will be — federal employees perform a wide variety of oftentimes highly specialized work.”
Certain parts of the state were harder hit than others. The Southeast Fairbanks Census Area, which has been reliant on military-related employment, and parts of Southeast Alaska, where employment related to the Tongass National Forest is important, are among those regions with steeper job losses by percentage, according to the analysis.
Alaska’s ranking among states hit by DOGE-related job cuts could change, Wiebold said. Data from this year has yet to be fully analyzed, she said. “Even in the first parts of 2026, there are reports of the rankings shifting somewhat,” she said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida opens civil probe into Anthony Fauci
description: In response to release by Republican U.S. senators of a diary attributed to former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Director Anthony Fauci, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is subpoenaing the former President Joe Biden adviser.  This is “as part of an official investigation into awards, professional opportunities, financia[...]
text:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier wants to know more about Anthony Fauci's personal endeavors. (Photo by Jackie Llanos/Florida Phoenix)In response to release by Republican U.S. senators of a diary attributed to former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Director Anthony Fauci, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is subpoenaing the former President Joe Biden adviser. 
This is “as part of an official investigation into awards, professional opportunities, financial incentives, grants, and COVID-19 guidance that impacted Florida businesses and consumers,” Uthmeier’s office said. 
The office allege Fauci received financial and professional opportunities concurrent with his federal job, which entailed making recommendations that affected Floridians.
“Government officials have a certain level of immunity in their official capacities, but if Fauci personally profited off of the ‘guidance’ he issued, that very well could have broken Florida law,” Uthmeier said in a news release. 
“Fauci’s diary focused more on self-promotion than the legitimate safety concerns from the mRNA vaccines. While Fauci was pushing for book deals, awards, and fortune and fame, Floridians were being deceived and harmed by his misrepresentations.”
Among those awards Uthmeier pointed to was a NIAID research grant to the University of Florida biomedical research program.
Uthmeier alleged on Fox News Wednesday the subpoena could uncover deceptive trade practices, fraud, or public nuisance.
Uthmeier is asking for documents since Jan 3, 2020, that detail which awards Fauci applied for and received related to the COVID-19 pandemic, efforts seeking personal financial benefits, interactions with Florida businesses or news organizations regarding COVID-19 protocols, and communications with vaccine manufacturers. 
Attorneys general from Louisiana and West Virginia contributed statements of support for Uthmeier’s move.
Fauci has not held a government position since Biden was in office. However, last week he was summoned to appear before a U.S. Senate committee. He invoked his Fifth Amendment right during the hearing, refusing to answer questions.
Fauci held his role at NIAID for nearly 40 years. Former President George W. Bush, a Republican, gave Fauci the Presidential Medal of Freedom. 
In an uncommon move, before leaving office Biden granted Fauci a preemptive pardon, in anticipation of political attacks on his former adviser.
Uthmeier will face his first election in November. He’s been attorney general since February 2025, when DeSantis appointed him.
Uthmeier made $100,000 teaching a course per semester this past academic year. During the year, as the News Service of Florida reported, Uthmeier’s office issued an opinion to the university for which he works about how to handle its search for a new president.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: If anything can bring the people of New Hampshire together, it’s the threat of a data center
description: When technical adjustments are made to the website you’re reading right now, they are typically considered to be either back-end changes or front-end changes. When the change is on the back end, that means that while the manner in which a reader’s experience is delivered might be different, the experience itself isn’t.  But a front-end […]
text:
A data center in northeast Oregon on May 18, 2026. (Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle)When technical adjustments are made to the website you’re reading right now, they are typically considered to be either back-end changes or front-end changes. When the change is on the back end, that means that while the manner in which a reader’s experience is delivered might be different, the experience itself isn’t. 
But a front-end change? Regular readers would indeed notice, and they would have feelings. Probably strong ones.
What makes the uproar over data centers unique is that they are, in many ways, the epitome of the back end. The computer networks they house are what make so much of modernity possible, from shopping on Amazon to posting vacation photos on Instagram to the storage of those photos in the cloud. But with the march of artificial intelligence requiring more and more networking capacity, and larger and larger physical structures, data centers have become a very big front-end issue.
The short of it is that AI is likely to dramatically change lives — and lives are already changing because of the data centers they require.
Unlike the debate over how governments should respond to climate change, which very quickly devolved into a partisan issue because of fossil fuel companies’ influence over the Republican Party, a bipartisan public consensus on data centers is emerging. As Jasmine Sun told Ezra Klein of The New York Times this week upon returning from a Midwest reporting trip, she heard one phrase over and over again: “Nobody wants this.”
The Bulletin’s own reporting backs that up. In a May story about the uproar over a proposed data center in Nottingham, partisan divides were absent.
“A lot of times I’ll get emails that are, you know, chain emails that are just being dumped to the Legislature, but these were all local people,” said Rep. Paul Tudor, a Northwood Republican, of the Nottingham proposal. “And there wasn’t one person that was for this.”
Last September, ahead of the most recent legislative session and well before Nottingham, the political debate over data centers in New Hampshire fell upon familiar lines — a left-right divide with a little bit of centrist overlap. 
“I think New Hampshire should court any business into the state,” Londonderry Republican Rep. Doug Thomas, vice chair of the House Science, Technology, and Energy Committee, told the Bulletin at the time. “In order for them to come here, there has to be a market. And so we have to … show them that we’re interested.” 
The main Democratic position was decidedly more cautious, and led to an ill-fated effort to prohibit data centers outright and form a committee to study their environmental impacts. The Republican-majority House ultimately voted that bill “inexpedient to legislate.” A Senate bill with a narrower aim, to allow “municipalities to regulate data centers in commercial and industrial zones,” also failed to advance. It will likely be a different kind of debate in the next session as local opposition grows, and New Hampshire is not alone in its conundrum: The National Conference of State Legislatures reports that 15 states are considering or have considered a ban on the centers, while only New York has enacted a moratorium.
New Hampshire already has 10 data centers, according to the Data Center Map, but the Nottingham proposal arrived in a charged atmosphere in which the general public seems to be well aware that they are witnessing the possible villain origins of Silicon Valley giants like OpenAI and Anthropic. There’s a NIMBY aspect to the local opposition for sure, which New Hampshire saw play out similarly with an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center proposed for Merrimack. Data centers are unattractive, carry environmental and energy concerns, and are noisy — hardly the kind of new neighbor a small town like Nottingham is looking for. 
But as Sun and Klein discussed at length, there’s something deeper at play.
People, regardless of political affiliation or any of the other ways we mentally carve up communities, are wary of AI in general and how aggressively it’s being inserted into their lives.
“I think it feels to a lot of these folks like they are pawns in some tech billionaire’s game, and they do not like to feel that way,” Sun said.
In trying to frame the tech billionaires’ pro-AI rationale, besides the desire to accumulate even more wealth and power, she boils it all down to one big con and one big pro: Yes, AI might kill us all; but then again, it could create utopia.
For the tech bros, the promise of some form of utopia outweighs the risk of annihilation.
But even that ultimate pro feels like a big stretch in a world where wealth inequality is very much trending in the wrong direction. The smart bet is that AI will crown a few winners, and most everybody else will lose. Dreaming of and striving for utopia is one thing, but trying to establish a version of it, especially when the model is designed, implemented, and unleashed by powerful others, is something else entirely.
An artificial paradise is not what we need. We need better and more affordable access to housing and healthcare. We need wages that keep pace with rising consumer prices. We need less profiteering by elected officials, less war, less pollution. We need more time in the sun and the rain, and less time behind screens. We need to be more human, and it’s hard to see how AI can ever deliver that.
Amid all that trepidation, it’s still not difficult to imagine the ways AI could benefit humanity broadly. Medical advancements, scientific discoveries, and, perhaps most importantly, more time for everybody. More time for the people and activities that bring them the most joy, that make life worth living.
And that is largely what’s being sold.
But what the public seems to collectively understand, across every kind of human divide imaginable, is that this limited promise of AI is not what is truly being offered. What is being proposed is a new kind of economy, a new kind of workforce, a new kind of relationship with machines — or nothing short of a remaking of what it means to be human.
If there’s a positive to be found in the fact that we are not so much riding the AI wave as being swept away by it, maybe it’s this: For the first time in a long time people seem to be focused on how we are different from what is artificial and inhuman rather than how we are different from each other.
I don’t expect that new understanding to translate into the easy resolution of our fundamental back-end debates about the direction of this state or this country, nor do I expect our harmful front-end culture wars to abate any time soon. But maybe the narrowest of common paths has opened up, built on some of the things the majority of us cherish regardless of how we vote: the natural beauty of the world we inhabit, the well-being of our loved ones, the strength of community, and the sweet unpredictability of human imperfection. 
The AI genie may be out of the bottle, but so are we.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: More Rhode Island students taking — and earning college credit — on AP exams
description: More of Rhode Island’s high-schoolers are taking Advanced Placement exams in hopes of earning college credits. Rhode Island students earned potentially college-credit-qualifying scores on 10,427 exams during the 2025-26 school year — more than double the number recorded in 2021 — according to preliminary data released by the Rhode Island Department of Educat[...]
text:
More Rhode Island high schoolers are taking AP exams. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)More of Rhode Island’s high-schoolers are taking Advanced Placement exams in hopes of earning college credits.
Rhode Island students earned potentially college-credit-qualifying scores on 10,427 exams during the 2025-26 school year — more than double the number recorded in 2021 — according to preliminary data released by the Rhode Island Department of Education (RIDE) on Monday.
AP exams, which are managed by the College Board, range in score from 1 (no recommendation) to 5 (“extremely well qualified”) and cover collegiate-level math, science, history, English and world languages. The College Board classifies a score of 3 as “qualified,” and it’s roughly equivalent to a B-minus, C-plus or C in a college course. 
The education not-for-profit organization as well as the American Council on Education recommend that college credit be awarded for scores of 3 or higher, although policies vary by institution. A 2023 College Board survey of 1,300 nonprofit four-year campuses noted that about 70% of responding institutions awarded credit for exams scoring at least 3 or higher.
Strong AP scores can substitute for some introductory college courses, allowing students to skip these basic classes, lowering the number of credits they need to complete which could lower the cost of their college degree as well. 
The latest preliminary data from the education department show that over 70% of exams achieved this benchmark score of 3 in the 2025-2026 school year — an 11% increase over the previous year and more than double from five years ago.
RIDE noted that more than 14,500 AP exams were taken in the 2025-2026 school year, which represented an 8% increase over the previous year, although the department did not provide an exact total of exams taken.
“Rhode Island’s latest AP results reflect the tremendous momentum our state is experiencing and are a testament to the hard work of Rhode Island students, educators, school leaders, and families,” Education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green said in a statement.
The commissioner noted the state has worked on “expanding access to rigorous, engaging coursework,” and cited the AP outcomes as evidence “that when students are provided with opportunity, support, and high-quality learning experiences, they rise to the challenge and excel.”
RIDE also highlighted that Providence — whose schools returned to local control on July 1 after nearly seven years under state control — also saw a rise in qualifying scores.
Providence Public Schools students took 2,210 AP exams in the 2025-2026 school year, up from 1,961 the previous year — an increase of 249 exams, or about 12.7%.
The number of Providence exams earning a score of at least 3 also increased from 1,109 to 1,215, a gain of 106 exams, or about 9.6%. But participation grew slightly more quickly than the number of qualifying scores, and the percentage of the district’s qualifying scores fell from 56.6% to 55%. 
The preliminary AP results arrive as Rhode Island also reported its highest graduation rate on record — a statewide figure of 85.5% who graduated on time during the 2025-2026 school year, according to RIDE’s data. 
Gov. Dan McKee said in a statement that the scores “reflect years of intentional work.”
“My administration will continue to support our students and educators as we work to strengthen academic achievement and close the achievement gap with Massachusetts,” he said.
Finalized College Board figures from the 2024-25 school year showed that 70.8% of Rhode Island AP scores were 3 or higher, compared with 76.6% in Massachusetts. Bay State students also took more exams: About 841 AP exams were recorded per 1,000 public high school juniors and seniors, compared with 513 in Rhode Island.
The education department noted that the figures remain preliminary and may change when the College Board releases its validated data this fall.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: First 2026 case of West Nile virus reported in Iowa
description: The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services reported a case of West Nile virus in an eastern Iowa adult Wednesday, marking the state’s first reported case in 2026.  West Nile virus is most commonly transmitted to people via infected mosquitoes and can cause mild symptoms such as a fever or headache, though many infected […]
text:
Iowa HHS reported the first 2026 case of West Nile virus, which is transmitted to humans via mosquito bites. (Photo courtesy of CDC)The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services reported a case of West Nile virus in an eastern Iowa adult Wednesday, marking the state’s first reported case in 2026. 
West Nile virus is most commonly transmitted to people via infected mosquitoes and can cause mild symptoms such as a fever or headache, though many infected people have no symptoms. While not common, the virus can manifest into more serious diseases that impact a person’s nervous system, according to HHS. 
Fifty-seven Iowans were diagnosed with West Nile virus in 2025, according to a news release from HHS. 
The first human case of West Nile virus in Iowa was detected in 2002, when nearly 150 human cases of the virus were reported. 
The virus is carried by birds and has been identified in more than 200 bird species in the U.S. Mosquitoes typically pick up the disease from feeding on infected birds and some varieties of mosquitoes will pass the virus to other hosts they feed on. 
HHS said the best protection against the virus is to avoid mosquito bites. Insect repellents with DEET, picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus, para-menthane-diol, 2-undecanone or IR3535 can lower the risk of a mosquito bite. 
“We want Iowans to enjoy the outdoors and to protect themselves from mosquito bites, which can spread illnesses like West Nile Virus,” Iowa’s State Medical Director Dr. Robert Kruse said in the news release. 
Covering up with long-sleeved shirts, pants, shoes and socks can also lower the risk of mosquito bites. Iowans can also empty standing water from their yards to keep mosquitoes from laying eggs in the water, and use screens on windows and doors to keep mosquitoes out. 
The department said people with mild symptoms of a West Nile virus infection generally recover without medical attention, but immediate medical attention is required for any illness that causes severe headache, disorientation or sudden weakness. 
According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, no vaccines or medicines are available to treat or prevent West Nile virus infections.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Benson snags Whitmer endorsement at post-primary event, positioning herself as a party unifier
description: The day after Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson took home a resounding primary victory in her bid to be Michigan’s next governor, the woman who she hopes to succeed, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, came out to endorse her at a campaign event in Lansing. Whitmer emphasized the victories that her administration, which Benson has been a […]
text:
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer campaigns with Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson the day following the August primary elections. Aug. 5, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. The day after Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson took home a resounding primary victory in her bid to be Michigan’s next governor, the woman who she hopes to succeed, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, came out to endorse her at a campaign event in Lansing.
Whitmer emphasized the victories that her administration, which Benson has been a part of, has won over the last eight years in power, specifically highlighting free breakfast and lunch for all public school students, free pre-K, and free community college, as well as expansions of reproductive rights and protections for the LGBTQ+ community. 
“We solved problems, and we always, always put Michigan first. Michigan’s next governor needs to build on this progress,” Whitmer said. “Can you imagine if we go from one administration to another that continues the work instead of undoes it? Michigan needs a fighter, someone who gets it, someone who will wake up every day and work her tail off to cut costs and put more money in your pocket.”
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer campaigns with Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson the day following the August primary elections. Aug. 5, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Benson thanked Whitmer for her support, recognizing that when they first ran together in 2018, “a lot of people thought it was impossible to see more than one woman leading our state.”
Benson is now the top of the ticket for a Democratic slate that saw deep divisions in the primaries, especially in the contentious U.S. Senate primary between Abdul El-Sayed, who won the nomination, and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who Whitmer had endorsed in the primary. Now, Benson faces the challenge of unifying the party behind the candidates chosen in Tuesday’s election and driving turnout among supporters in November, a key point that she emphasized at the event. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I intend to be a unifier, but I think if you actually listen to what we’re all saying, we’re all talking about the same things,” Benson said to reporters following the event. “That’s what everyone’s talking about in different ways: putting money back in our pocket, getting money out of politics, healthcare for all. That’s stuff we all can agree on. We’re all going to be talking about it because we recognize that’s also what the people of Michigan want us to be doing, want us to be delivering on, and I think you’ll see Democrats proudly champion that message together, unified as one ticket.”
Whitmer and Benson also both criticized U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), the Republican nominee for governor, who will face Benson in the general election. James, in his victory speech and in campaign materials leading up to the primary, has claimed that Democrats, including Benson, are pushing an agenda of “socialism,” which he has said is an evil that he wants to defeat. 
Asked about that framing of her platform, Benson said to reporters, “I think the only thing evil is when leaders claim to work for the people, but then they don’t.”
Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson speaks to supporters at an event the day after the August primary elections. Aug. 5, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Whitmer also hit James on his effectiveness as a lawmaker, saying that he is “like a fancy sports car in a Michigan winter, looks real sharp parked in the driveway, but the second there’s slush on the road, no help at all.”
“He likes to talk tough in 30-second commercials, but when he gets to Washington, he turns out to be just like every other Republican in D.C. with no backbone,” she continued. “The second party bosses or the DeVos donors demand a vote to cut healthcare or to raise prices on working families. He folds like a lawn chair.”
Meanwhile, Benson contrasted herself, especially in her response to President Donald Trump — who endorsed James in the primary election — and his administration’s efforts to force her department to turn over Michigan’s voter rolls. Whitmer received pushback at the start of Trump’s second term after a visit to the Oval Office that some Democrats saw as taking too soft a stance against him.
“Time and time again, we all as leaders have chances to show who we are, and he has shown us who he is and who he prioritizes,” Benson said. “It’s not the people of Michigan. It’s himself, his donors and Donald Trump, sometimes even at the expense of Michigan families. I’ll tell you, that makes me angry because I know when I see in the eyes of Michiganders all across the state, Democrats, independents and Republicans, what they need, they need leaders who are thinking about them, their kids, their future when they come to Lansing.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Hopes grow for higher ethanol blend with inclusion in US Senate farm bill
description: South Dakota’s congressional delegation is hopeful that year-round, nationwide approval of E15 — a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol — will clear Congress this year, bolstered by its inclusion in the latest Senate version of the farm bill. Ethanol is a fuel additive made primarily from corn, and a lower E10 blend is already available […]
text:
A fuel pump includes E15 in August 2025 in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. The state's congressional delegation is optimistic that year-round, nationwide sales of E15 could soon be approved. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s congressional delegation is hopeful that year-round, nationwide approval of E15 — a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol — will clear Congress this year, bolstered by its inclusion in the latest Senate version of the farm bill.
Ethanol is a fuel additive made primarily from corn, and a lower E10 blend is already available year-round. Supporters of year-round E15 availability say it would strengthen the farm economy and make the country more energy independent. Without a law authorizing year-round E15, summertime sales require a federal waiver.
Opponents point to research showing emissions from higher blends could worsen summer smog while encouraging the conversion of grasslands for corn farming. Some lawmakers from oil-producing and refining states also oppose the expansion.
The House pulled year-round E15 from its version of the farm bill earlier this year, instead approving it as separate legislation amending the Clean Air Act. 
The farm bill is multi-year legislation that determines federal agriculture, food and nutrition policies. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, voted in favor of both bills.

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, speaks with a constituent at the Sioux Empire Fair in Sioux Falls on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

The Senate Agriculture Committee included year-round E15 when it released its version of the farm bill last week ahead of the committee’s hearing this Thursday. The House’s standalone E15 bill awaits a hearing in another Senate committee.
The last farm bill was signed into law in 2018 and has been extended after Congress failed to pass a new version. Johnson spoke to South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday at the Sioux Empire Fair in Sioux Falls about the legislation’s progress, including the Senate version. 
“In general, I don’t think the House is going to love this version compared to what we passed, but at some point we’ll figure out a way to get to yes, collectively,” Johnson said. “We need to. This is really important if we care about American energy dominance, and we just can’t get there without E15.”
Year-round E15 sales have been a longstanding goal of the ethanol industry. Ethanol plants process more than half of South Dakota-grown corn.
Rising gas prices this summer and the ongoing war with Iran have drawn attention to the United States’ continued reliance on liquid fuels in cars and airplanes — and its entanglement in Middle East oil markets, Johnson said.  
“I would rather wake up every morning worried about the price of corn in a South Dakota field than worried about the price of oil in an Iranian oil field,” said Johnson, who will leave Congress in January after his failed run for governor.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, said in a statement that year-round E15 is a boost for agriculture and rural communities across South Dakota and the country.
“I remain committed to getting the farm bill and E15 to the president’s desk to secure these critical wins for South Dakota’s farmers and ranchers,” Thune said.
South Dakota Republican Sen. Mike Rounds has also spoken in support of year-round E15.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: As Meta data center expands, advocates push harder for transparency
description: Consumer, science and environmental advocates are pushing harder for transparency from Meta and the utility that will power its expanding Hyperion data center in Northeast Louisiana.
text:
Smoke rises from distant stacks at Entergy's power plant in Reserve, Louisiana, on Wednesday, Nov. 10, 2021. (Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator).Consumer, science and environmental advocates are pushing harder for transparency from Meta and the utility that will power its expanding Hyperion data center in Northeast Louisiana.
The Alliance for Affordable Energy and Union of Concerned Scientists held a joint news conference Monday to address what they consider an ongoing lack of public information available about the sprawling data center campus in Richland Parish and Entergy Louisiana’s plans to meet its massive electricity needs. 
The latest updates to its footprint call for more than 10 million square feet of building space on a site covering 3,650 acres. It will require 7.5 gigawatts of electricity to operate — enough to power up to 7.5 million households. 
The data center is among the largest industrial development deals in Louisiana history, and much of its key aspects have been cloaked through nondisclosure agreements state and local leaders have signed with Meta. NDAs reached in recent months under the Landry administration have severely limited what elected officials will say about major projects around the state, including the Amazon data center campus in Northwest Louisiana and the Hyundai steel mill near Donaldsonville. 
“Louisiana officials and industry have used secrecy and deals made behind closed doors to move projects forward before communities are even aware or have a chance to object,” Logan Burke, executive director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy, said at the news conference.
“The process and the purpose are clear: Hide the ball until it’s already in the goal,” she added. 
Burke’s group and others are asking state regulators to further scrutinize the proposals from Meta and Entergy. 
The Alliance for Affordable Energy and Union of Concern Scientists submitted written testimony and exhibits Friday to the Louisiana Public Service Commission that are critical of the power generation plans for the Hyperion campus. The documents call into question Entergy’s projections and claims for its proposal to build seven additional natural gas-powered turbines — in addition to the three originally planned — to power the Meta data center. 
The plans are on an expedited schedule as part of Gov. Jeff Landry’s Lightning Speed Initiative to fast-track the utility regulatory process in the name of economic development. 
Specifically, the two groups say Entergy’s claims that ratepayers and the public will benefit from the additional power plants are unrealistic. Paul Arbaje, a senior analyst with the Union of Concerned Scientists, said Entergy’s projections are “based on a flimsy analysis that leaves little to no room for deviating from expectations.”
“Entergy has deemed so much of the information in these filings confidential,” Arbaje said, “but also because they indicated … they haven’t even quantified themselves the impact this project will have on an average residential electric bill.”
A spokesperson for Entergy said the company is currently reviewing the groups’ submissions to the Public Service Commission and plans to respond to regulators by an Aug. 14 deadline.  
Meta did not respond to multiple emails requesting comment. 
Entergy and Meta have said in prior filings with the Louisiana Public Service Commission that a fast-track regulatory process for the natural gas plants is justified because the job creation from the projects will benefit the public.
Advocates are also suspicious of this claim. 
“Meta has provided no information regarding the number of permanent jobs and refuses to tell whether these jobs will be in Louisiana or remote or will be part-time or full-time,” said Susan Stevens Miller, a senior attorney at Earthjustice who filed the testimony for the Alliance for Affordable Energy and Union of Concerned Scientists. 
“There’s really no way of knowing how many jobs will be permanently created by these data centers,” she added. 
In last week’s Public Service Commission filings, both advocacy groups cautioned there is no guarantee from Entergy that its other utility customers won’t end up bearing some portion of the cost for the $15 billion being spent to provide power to the Hyperion campus. 
Meta and Entergy have promised to ensure Meta covers all power service costs throughout the end of its contract with Entergy. 
A spokesperson for Entergy reiterated that the company expects Meta’s coming to Louisiana means “customer bills will be lower than they otherwise would have been … generating approximately $2.6 billion in savings for Entergy Louisiana customers over the next two decades.”
The advocacy groups said they have little faith in an executive order the governor issued earlier this year to protect ratepayers from the risk of increased costs from the data center’s increased energy demand. President Donald Trump’s ratepayer protection pledge connected to data centers and their power needs, made soon after Landry’s executive order, carries the same weight for the groups. 
“The problem is this executive order has roughly the same force of law as does the president’s ratepayer protection pledge, which is to say zero,” Burke said. 
The alliance and scientists’ group aren’t alone in their concerns. The Sierra Club also submitted testimony Friday to the Public Service Commission questioning the lack of transparency and the potential costs for other ratepayers. 
“Entergy’s proposal to build even more gas plants and transmission for Meta’s Hyperion project is a huge risk to existing customers,” Tony Mendoza, a senior attorney for the Sierra Club’s Environmental Law Program, said in a news release. 
The Sierra Club is urging the Public Service Commission to significantly change Entergy’s proposal to make Meta more directly responsible for costs associated with the buildout of the new power plants.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey and Minogue agree to fall debates, but not the same ones
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: In a June Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll of 500 Massachusetts registered voters, Minogue and Shortsleeve received 31 percent and 29 percent of support, respectively, to Healey's 56 percent.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY and GOP gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue announced that they’ve agreed to participate in general election debates this fall – just not the same ones.
Healey has committed to participating in two October debates, her campaign announced Monday around 2:50 p.m. WBZ-TV will host one moderated by political analyst Jon Keller. WCVB, WBUR and The Boston Globe, in partnership with The Bay State Banner and El Planeta, will host the other.
Minogue’s campaign just after 4:30 p.m. Monday announced that he had agreed to a general election debate hosted by Boston 25, GBH and New England Public Media in partnership with El Planeta and The Bay State Banner. The campaign said it’s expected to take place after Labor Day, though the date, time and format will be finalized “once confirmed by the candidates and the participating media organizations.”
Asked if GOP gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve has agreed to any general election debates, the Shortsleeve campaign said he has agreed to all of them. 
While Minogue said in a statement that he looks “forward to debating” Healey, Minogue and Shortsleeve will have to first go head-to-head in the September 1 GOP primary election. Minogue clinched the GOP endorsement after the party’s April convention, at which he received 70.38 percent of delegate votes to Shortsleeve’s 15.5 percent. In a June Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll of 500 Massachusetts registered voters, Minogue and Shortsleeve received 31 percent and 29 percent of support, respectively, to Healey’s 56 percent.
The two Republicans are not slated to debate each other before the primary election. Shortsleeve has called on Minogue to participate in primary debates, arguing that the lack of debate hurts the Republican party at large, though Minogue said during a radio appearance in July that there will be “no debate” ahead of September 1 and that he is “very focused on the general election.”
The Minogue campaign did not immediately reply to inquiries about whether Minogue was also invited to the debates Healey agreed to, and if so, why he declined to commit to them. The Healey campaign also did not provide an answer as to whether Healey was invited to the debate Minogue agreed to, and why she declined if so.
Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll has also agreed to face “her eventual Republican opponent” in a debate hosted by GBH and Boston Public Radio’s Jim Braude and Margery Eagan, according to the Healey-Driscoll campaign. The GOP-endorsed candidate for lieutenant governor, Anne Brensley, pivoted her campaign to run for secretary of state as a write-in candidate in the primary. Now-former candidate Anne Manning-Martin was kicked off the ballot after the state’s highest court issued a ruling in a signature fraud case – one of several that has exposed rifts within the party. The remaining Republican LG candidate, New Bedford city councilor and state correction officer Shawn Oliver, has been running a campaign aligned with Shortsleeve.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Judge orders release of Providence man ICE seeks to deport to Cambodia
description: A Rhode Island federal judge on Tuesday ordered federal immigration officials to release a Cambodian refugee who has lived in Providence since arriving in the United States as an infant and whose detention last month prompted appeals from advocates and elected officials. Chansareth Hong’s petition for a writ of habeas corpus was granted by U.S. […]
text:
A protester outside U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's field office in Warwick, Rhode Island, on July 22, 2026. Demonstrators had hoped to keep ICE agents from detaining a Cambodian man who has lived in the state since he was an infant. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) A Rhode Island federal judge on Tuesday ordered federal immigration officials to release a Cambodian refugee who has lived in Providence since arriving in the United States as an infant and whose detention last month prompted appeals from advocates and elected officials.
Chansareth Hong’s petition for a writ of habeas corpus was granted by U.S. District Judge Mary S. McElroy nearly two weeks after Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained him during a scheduled check-in at the agency’s Warwick field office on July 22 and transferred him to the Wyatt Detention Facility in Central Falls. 
Habeas corpus is the legal procedure used by people who believe they are being unlawfully detained to petition for their release in court. In turn, the federal government must justify why that individual is being held. 
Hans J. Bremer, Hong’s attorney, did not immediately respond to an inquiry from Rhode Island Current about whether his client had been released from federal detention. 
Jenni Nguyen, a community organizer from the Providence Youth Student Movement who Hong’s family has authorized to speak on their behalf, declined to confirm whether Hong had been released. She told Rhode Island Current the family would provide an update later in the week.
Demonstrators had tried to prevent Hong from being taken by immigration agents by blocking the entrance to the parking lot of the Warwick field office on the day of his check-in and held a protest outside the field office, but were unsuccessful. Local, state and federal leaders also tried to intervene in ensuring Hong remains in Rhode Island by writing pleas to ICE.
ICE detains Providence man facing deportation to country he has never known

An ICE spokesperson did not immediately respond to request for comment on Hong’s release.
Hong, 50, immigrated to the United States in June 1976 after his family fled the Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia. He is now the primary caregiver for his 9-year-old autistic son and his elderly mother, responsibilities that grew after the deaths of his son’s mother in 2025 and his own father in June.
Hong’s immigration status was complicated by drug convictions he received as a teenager in 1997, which resulted in a deportation order two years later. Court filings from the federal government show that an immigration judge granted deferral of removal under the United Nation’s Convention Against Torture treaty.
Following a ruling by the Department of Justice’s Board of Immigration Appeals in 2002, Hong was released under an order of supervision rather than immediately deported. The federal filing and habeas petition both note the arrangement required him to regularly report to ICE and assist in obtaining any necessary travel documents, among other conditions.
But on July 10, Hong was notified by ICE the federal government was going to revoke his order of supervision during his July 22 check-in at the Warwick field office. A declaration filed by Brian E. Sullivan, acting assistant field office director for ICE in Burlington, Massachusetts, states Hong’s status was changed essentially because Cambodia resumed cooperating with U.S. removals last year.
“ICE expects that the government of Cambodia will likely schedule a nationality interview at which the petitioner must appear to assist in the issuance of a travel document within approximately two to three weeks,” Sullivan wrote.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: USC celebrates record $358M in fundraising, other SC colleges also set records
description: The University of South Carolina is touting a record breaking year of fundraising, with $357.6 million in gifts.
text:
Scenes from The University of South Carolina's Horseshoe in Columbia, S.C. in October of 2024. (Photo by Travis Bell/SIDELINE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The University of South Carolina is touting a record-breaking year of fundraising.
The eight-school system, with a main campus in Columbia and seven other two- and four-year schools scattered around the state, raised $357.6 million in the budget year that ended June 30, according to a statement Wednesday.
That’s nearly $100 million more than the record set by the college system last year.
“This historic year reflects great confidence in the mission of the University of South Carolina,” USC President Michael Amiridis said in a statement. “Our alumni, friends and partners are investing in the people, ideas and discoveries that will shape USC’s future. Their generosity is expanding opportunity, accelerating innovation and strengthening our impact across South Carolina and beyond.”
Most of the money raised will go to athletics: $81 million for scholarships across all sports and $147 million for improvements to Williams-Brice football stadium.
The remaining $129 million is academic-related.
The largest gift of the year — $30 million — went to the medical school, named in honor of the late Kay Floyd, who died in 2023, and the late Dr. Eddie Floyd of Florence, who died in January at age 91.
The Floyd family made the donation in May in the name of Eddie Floyd, a retired heart surgeon, alumnus and the longest-serving member of the college’s governing boare, and his wife, a graduate of both Saint Mary’s College in Raleigh and USC.
Beyond medicine, the Floyds also ran one of the largest farming operations in the state and were major Republican fundraisers.
“My parents loved this university with all of their hearts. They believed deeply in improving lives and expanding opportunity,” said Dr. Coleman Floyd Buckhouse, the Floyd’s daughter who in 2024 succeeded her father on the school’s governing board.
The gift will fund scholarships for medical students and surgery, neurosurgery, neurology, sports medicine and science faculty at the school.
A separate, $22 million, anonymous gift to the medical school this year also will fund scholarships and clinical training for students.
The Robert and Janice McNair Foundation were the college’s second-largest donors of the year, giving $25 million.
The late Bob McNair, a 1958 graduate and founder of the Houston Texans, and his late wife, Janice McNair, who died last month at age 89, were prolific donors to the college, giving $20 million in 1998 to establish a scholarship fund. That was followed by $8 million in 2016 to found the McNair Institute for Entrepreneurism and Free Enterprise and an additional $18 million commitment by the family in 2019, following McNair’s death.
Other landmark gifts this year included:

$5 million to the College of Hospitality, Retail and Sport Management for the new David and Nicole Tepper Department of Sport and Entertainment Management
$5 million to USC Beaufort for the Jonathan Green Maritime Cultural Center
A $7 million unnamed gift to the Molinaroli College of Engineering and Computing.
$1.5 million unnamed gift to the School of Music, one of the largest gifts in the school’s history, for Baroque and early music faculty
A $2.5 million unnamed gift to the College of Pharmacy for pediatric oncology research

Carolina Panthers owner donates $5M to USC for scholarships, professorships

Other colleges
In the Upstate, Clemson University celebrated its sixth consecutive year of raising more than $200 million.
Clemson’s fundraising peaked in 2024 at $259 million. This year, the school raised $202 million.
Major gifts included $16.5 million from Don Quattlebaum, alumnus and owner of White House Farms in Georgetown, to the college’s new veterinary college.
The funding will pay for the Quattlebaum Hub, featuring classroom space, conference rooms, a library and a bookstore, as well as a pavilion for students to relax outdoors and money to hire faculty.
Michelin and the Bezos Earth Foundation Fund also donated $11 million to the school for sustainable cotton research.
In all, the school raised enough for 178 new scholarships and fellowships and nine new endowed professorships.
In addition to the fundraising record set at USC, the College of Charleston raised a record $47 million and Winthrop University raised a record $11.7 million.

title: Price tag for Trump's D.C. deployment of National Guard: $1.4B more through 2029
text: WASHINGTON — The deployment of National Guard troops hailing from all across the country to Washington, D.C. is expected to cost taxpayers more than $1.4 billion in additional funds through 2029. The estimate from Jules Hurst III, President Donald Trump’s nominee to be the Pentagon’s comptroller, came in response to a series of questions from Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., as a part of Hurt’s confirmation process. “While American families are getting flattened by skyrocketing costs, Donald Trump is spending $1.4 billion to keep troops on the streets in Washington for years on end. The National Guard are not pawns and taxpayer dollars are not a piggy bank for Trump’s political stunts,” Warren wrote in a statement.According to the information provided by Hurst, the National Guard deployment is planned to continue until January 2029, the end of Trump’s second term. D.C. missionUnder Trump’s requested budget for the next fiscal year, his Make DC Safe and Beautiful mission — which has led renovation efforts of many of the city’s iconic landmarks and sought to reduce crime —  would receive $605 million in funding. That would include more $375 million for payroll expenses and travel allowances and nearly $230 million for operational expenses, such as housing and meals. Trump first deployed around 800 National Guard troops in Washington in August 2025, an effort to tackle what he called a “crime emergency” in the city. The move came after similar deployments in many Democratic-led cities across the country, including in Los Angeles and Chicago. He also sought to federalize and deploy troops in Portland, Oregon, but was later blocked in the federal courts. He threatened similar actions in locations including New York and Baltimore, often following with political battles with those states' Democratic leaders. National Guard deployments across the country cost nearly $500 million in 2025, according to the Congressional Budget Office.  In general, the office estimated, deploying 1,000 National Guard troops to a U.S. city costs between $18 million and $21 million each month. D.C. deployment grows The initial deployment in Washington has since grown, with thousands of troops from states all across the country now deployed in the nation’s capital.As of Aug. 1, there are more than 4,600 National Guard members deployed in Washington. About 680 of those guardsmen are from the District itself, while most are predominantly from the South. Georgia, South Carolina and Missisppi have sent the most guard members. But that total headcount has risen as many states and territories sent additional troops to help support events as part of the Trump-led Freedom250 celebration of the nation’s semiquincentennial in July. For some states, their National Guard members have been deployed quietly to the nation’s capital, including in Idaho, where the state made no formal announcement of the move. The Department of Defense’s budget estimates for fiscal years 2028 and 2029 assume a total headcount of approximately 2,500 National Guard personnel in Washington through January 2029. Future funding includes a planned $625.8 million for fiscal 2028 and $198.3 million for fiscal 2029.
