name: Maryland Matters
title: Commission to assess tragedy of Black youth at former reform school holds first meeting
description: At their first meeting, members of a panel cresearching "the history, operations, and resident deaths” at the site of a formerly segregated Maryland reform school were thanked for their service and warned to steel themselves to what they might find.
text:
Linda Gorham, right, chats with Deputy Attorney General Zenita Wickham Hurley on Tuesday. Gorham's cousin, Richard Saunders, died in the 1930s at age 15 in the former House of Reformation in Prince George's County. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)After visiting the site of a formerly segregated reform school in Prince George’s County where at least 230 Black youths are buried, Phyllis Hammond wrote a poem.
Hammond, 69, read “If these woods could talk” Tuesday, at the first meeting of the commission that has been charged with researching “the history, operations, and resident deaths” at the former House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children in Cheltenham. Hammond, one of nearly two dozen members of that commission, wrote the poem in honor of her uncle, Amos Hammond, who died at the age of 18 in 1921, and other children who died at the reform school.
“If these woods could talk, would they share how brutal and cruel they were treated by these corrupt authoritarians day in and day out without any justices in place to protect them from harm?” she said at the People’s Resource Center in Crownsville. “If these woods could talk, do you think they could share each of these young boys’ tragic lives and deaths while entrusted in the hands of the juvenile system?”
Phyllis Hammond introduces herself at the first meeting of the Commission on the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The commission’s goal is to “provide a complete and public accounting of the children who died and were buried on the grounds” of the reform school, located on land between the current Cheltenham Youth Detention Center and the manicured Cheltenham Veterans Cemetery along Route 301.
The commission was established through legislation sponsored this year by Sen. William C. Smith (D-Montgomery) and Del. Jeffrie Long Jr. (D-Calvert and Prince George’s). Both lawmakers are members of the commission, but were not able to attend Tuesday organizational meeting because they were in Annapolis for the last day of the special session considering a constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting.
Before members introduced themselves, Attorney General Anthony Brown (D), the commission chair, thanked those who volunteered to serve. Brown said that part of the commission’s work, thanks to more than $1 million approved in this year’s state budget and another $200,000, will be to secure a genealogical research contract.
“That contract is prioritizing one thing: Finding the names of the boys who died here and finding their families. That’s where we’re starting,” he said.
Brown also offered a warning about some of the initial findings by the state Department of Juvenile Services (DJS), that Black boys were used as manual labor, beaten, and worse.
“I want to prepare you. You’ll be outraged. You’ll be saddened. You may be horrified,” Brown said. “But I hope, I believe you’ll also be energized because these children are depending on us to do this work. Their families are watching.”
The Commission on the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children meets Tuesday at the People’s Resource Center in Crownsville. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Crystal Foretia , who worked as a fellow with DJS and led the research into the 230 boys at the school that started in 1873, said Tuesday that available death certificates showed the majority of deaths at the facility were from tuberculosis, pneumonia, typhoid fever and meningitis.
But Foretia, a Montgomery County native and current Yale Law School student, said while during her PowerPoint presentation that researchers must dig deeper on official causes of death, assessing the living conditions of the youth, for example, and comparing the death rate to that at an all-white reform school.
That’s why Linda Gorham wants to know more about the death of her 15-year-old cousin, Richard Saunders, who died at the House of Reformation in 1939. Gorham, who will serve as one of 10 advisory members to the commission, said after the more than two-hour meeting that her cousin’s death certificate said he died of tuberculosis.
“But we heard today, it could be something else,” said Gorham, a licensed psychologist with two sons, ages 40 and 49. “Again and again and again, this trauma that’s happened to Black boys over and over and over again in our society. [Serving as a member] is about giving voice to Richard and the other children harmed.”
A preliminary report from the commission is due by Dec. 31, 2027, documenting the progress of the investigation, with recommendations to the governor and General Assembly.
The commission plans to visit the House of Reformation site sometime next month.
Anyone who may be family member or a descendant of a child who died at the House of Reformation can contact the commission at HORCommission@oag.maryland.gov.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Risch v. Achilles may be Idaho’s most active US Senate race in years. Here’s where they stand.
description: Idaho Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, 83, has been in his position for nearly 20 years. In reliably red Idaho, he has won his previous general election contests by comfortable margins.  His independent challenger, former Boise Democratic state legislator Todd Achilles, 58, has raised nearly $700,000 this year and is arguing that he presents the […]
text:
Independent candidate Todd Achilles, left, and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch. (photos courtesy of the candidates) Idaho Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, 83, has been in his position for nearly 20 years. In reliably red Idaho, he has won his previous general election contests by comfortable margins. 
His independent challenger, former Boise Democratic state legislator Todd Achilles, 58, has raised nearly $700,000 this year and is arguing that he presents the alternative for people who aren’t happy with either party. 
“I’m speaking to roomfuls of Republicans who are just tired of the Idaho GOP, and they’re ready for something new,” Achilles told the Idaho Capital Sun. “And I think they’re really excited about what we’re talking about in this campaign. There’s a lot of angry Republicans in Idaho right now.” 
Idaho Democrat David Roth ends campaign for US Senate seat held by Risch

After the Democrat in the race, David Roth, ended his campaign late last month, Achilles has said his chances are better.
Risch said the race doesn’t feel any different. 
“I know people are getting excited all of a sudden because I was running against two Democrats, and now I’m running against one Democrat,” Risch told the Sun, referencing that Achilles was a Democratic state legislator. “I’ve done that all my life.”
The candidates agree that unaffordable healthcare and the nation’s agricultural migrant worker visa program are problems that need to be addressed, and that Idaho’s public lands need to be protected. They differ greatly about how they want to go about addressing those issues. 
Libertarian candidate Matt Loesby and independent Natalie Fleming are also running for the seat; neither candidate responded to requests for interviews. Roth has not yet filed the paperwork to formally withdraw from the race, the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office confirmed Tuesday. He has until Sept. 4 to do so, otherwise his name will still appear on the ballot. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Achilles wants to reform the Affordable Health Care Act. Risch wants to return it to private sector. 

Risch and Achilles agree that healthcare affordability is a problem, and it’s something they hear about from voters. 
“We talk about it all the time,” Risch said. “I think the problem, to be solved, the healthcare system is going to have to be moved significantly more back into the private sector.” 
Risch said the Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare, is “a mess.” 



Quotation







I am always ranked as one of the most conservative U.S. senators, sometimes the most conservative U.S. senator. And that's because I consistently deliver a conservative vote, and as a result of that, they send me back to office every time because I do what I say I'm going to do. And man, have they got a clear choice to make this time.


– Idaho Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, incumbent candidate running for re-election


“Whether you’re inside the system or whether you’re outside the system, people complain about it,” he said, “and it needs work, but it needs the private sector.” 
Achilles said, “the Affordable Care Act is not working, it needs to be reformed.”  
He criticized Congress for allowing the expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits, which were implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic to make insurance purchased through the statewide healthcare marketplace more affordable. 
People purchasing this insurance with the credits received a boost in 2021, but the larger credit expired at the end of 2025 when Congress did not extend the program. The U.S. House voted on a bill to extend the enhanced credits, but it did not move forward in the Senate. 



Who are the candidates? 
Risch is in his third, six-year term in the U.S. Senate. Prior to that, he served as an Idaho state senator, lieutenant governor and governor. Risch received a bachelor’s degree in forestry and later a law degree from the University of Idaho. 
He was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 2008 and is chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and serves on the Energy and Natural Resources, Small Business and Entrepreneurship, Intelligence, and Ethics committees.
Risch said he’s running again because, “The state’s been incredibly good to me. I’ve offered myself for public service over and over again, and the voters have always accepted me, and primarily because I did what I told them I’d do. And I’m very clear on that. And I enjoy what I’m doing.” 
Achilles, previously served as a Democrat in the Idaho House of Representatives after he was appointed to fill a District 16 vacancy and then won his November 2024 election for the seat. Achilles in July last year announced he left the Democratic Party to become an unaffiliated voter and run as an independent because he said he was unhappy with either party. 
Achilles is a former tank commander and armor officer in the U.S. Army and worked for Hewlett-Packard. He obtained a bachelor’s from Claremont McKenna College in California, master’s in public administration and master of arts in international studies from the University of Washington, and master of public administration from University of California Berkeley. 
“The vast majority of people in Idaho, we’re all profoundly worried about the state of the federal government, Congress,” Achilles said. “What’s happening with the country right now is not what any of us believe we should be doing. And we know it’s not working like it should, and we need to fix it.” 
Loesby moved to Idaho in 2020 and works in video game development, according to his campaign website. Fleming graduated from Moscow High School, worked in the tech industry, raised four children as a single mother, and later received degrees in information technology management and supply chain management from Boise State University, according to her website. 



 Risch is ‘all in’ on SAVE Act. Achilles says it’s ‘federal overreach’ 

The voter identification bill called the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, or SAVE Act, is under consideration in the U.S. Senate. The bill includes specific voter ID requirements to prove citizenship to register to vote. It is currently illegal for people who aren’t citizens to register to vote or to vote in a federal election. 
Risch said that Idaho’s elections are “rock solid safe.” 



Quotation







The vast majority of people in Idaho, we're all profoundly worried about the state of the federal government, Congress. What's happening with the country right now is not what any of us believe we should be doing. And we know it's not working like it should, and we need to fix it.


– Todd Achilles, independent candidate for U.S. Senate


“That is not true all over America, and we as Idahoans have the right to demand that other states do not allow people who are not citizens of this country to vote,” Risch said. “I’m all in on that. I’m all in on the Save Act.” 
He said he wasn’t persuaded by the argument that the bill may limit eligible citizens’ ability to vote, such as married women who have changed their names. Risch said that argument was a “red herring.” 
“That’s a manufactured complaint by people who are opposed to it,” he said. “If you’re going to go get a driver’s license, you’ve got to go get those documents. You can’t just walk in and say, ‘I’m here to get a driver’s license’ and not give them backup to document it. So I don’t buy that argument. … I’m not in favor of anything that keeps a person from voting who is eligible to vote.” 
Achilles said Idaho already had appropriate identification requirements for voting. 
“The SAVE Act is federal overreach,” Achilles said. “And I mean, everyone in the state rejects a federal gun registry. The SAVE Act is the equivalent of a federal voter registry. Same principle.” 
The Boise National Forest covers more than 2.5 million acres and includes more than 500 trails. More than 60% of Idaho is federal public land. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)
 Public lands protection is a top issue for both candidates 

Risch and Achilles both named protection of Idaho’s vast public lands as a top priority. 
Achilles said the federal agencies that manage those lands, such as the Bureau of Land Management and U.S. Forest Service, need to be properly staffed. 
“The first responsibility is: make sure we don’t sell any lands,” Achilles said. “The second responsibility is to make sure the agencies are resourced to actually take care of lands.” 
He criticized massive staffing cuts at the Forest Service that took place to those agencies last year, led by the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, which was spearheaded by billionaire Elon Musk. He also criticized reductions in staffing at the Bureau of Land Management. He said poor staffing is contributing to challenges during an active fire season this year. 
Achilles said he supports raising the federal payments local governments received to offset lost revenue from the lack of property taxes collected on federal lands within their borders, called Payment in Lieu of Taxes, or PILT.  
Risch also opposes the sale of public lands.
Independent challenger calls on Risch to do three public debates ahead of Idaho’s general election 

 “It’ll be over my dead body that we sell off public lands,” Risch said. 
He underscored his efforts to fight off a proposal year to sell off large swaths of public lands. He and two other members of Idaho’s four-member congressional delegation all opposed the sale, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Risch also underscored his work while he served as Idaho governor to craft Idaho’s own Roadless Rule — which was finalized in 2008 and outlines conservation and management of around 9 million acres of roadless federal lands in Idaho. 
Idaho was the first state to adopt its own Roadless Rule. The Trump administration has taken steps to consider rescinding the federal Roadless Rule, but has exempted Idaho and Colorado — the two states with their own guidelines. 
Risch acknowledged that management, especially in regard to wildfire prevention, could be better. 
“We can do it better than what we have been, and we’re going to continue to work at it,” he said. “There’s no magic silver bullet for this.” 


Let us know what you think...


 

 Candidates support immigration reforms for ag workers, disagree on other related policies

Risch said that work has been done for years to try and make changes to the nation’s immigration system. He said he supports legal immigration, and wants to improve the H-2A visa program for migrant agricultural workers. He said he supports the longtime effort of leaders in the Idaho dairy industry to change the program to allow the visa to be used for year-round work, instead of only temporary, seasonal work as it is now. 
“We’re not getting enough in, but we pressure the administration to get the workforce here necessary,” Risch said, “because there are certain sectors in the agricultural economy that you can’t get Americans to do the work, and you’ve got to have an immigrant force to do it.” 
He said his issue with proposals in the past is they would create a path to citizenship for those who entered the U.S. illegally.

“That is a non-starter for us,” he said of himself and many other Republicans. 
Achilles highlighted the 2013 bipartisan immigration reform bill, H.R. 744, which would’ve made a number of changes to boost support for border patrol and immigration enforcement as well as made significant changes to the legal immigration process. Risch and his Senate counterpart Idaho Republican Sen. Mike Crapo voted against the 2013 legislation. 
“That got politicized,” Achilles said of the bill. “The same principles apply now. We still don’t have a working immigration system. We still don’t have a working visa system, and it’s been that way for you know the entire time he’s been in the Senate. So somebody needs to get this addressed.”
Achilles said he also supports making changes to the H-2A program to allow for year-round labor. 
“Any policy we do has got to be centered on livable livable-wage jobs for Idahoans first,” he said. “And if then they can’t get filled, then you can make them available to a visa system, and the producer could be accountable for any guest workers that come out of the country.” 
 Is this race more competitive than past Idaho U.S. Senate elections?  

Between Risch’s first general election contest for U.S. Senate in 2008 and his last one in 2020, he has won with at least 58% of the vote each time. In 2020, he defeated Democrat Paulette Jordan, the independent Fleming, and Constitution Party candidate Ray Writz with 62.6% of the vote, according to records from the Idaho Secretary of State. 
Achilles argues that his campaign presents a more serious challenger in deep red Idaho than Risch has had before. 
He said negative messaging he’s seen about his campaign that didn’t mention other candidates is “a good sign that they’re taking it seriously.” 
“But even if they’re not, that’s their mistake,” he said. 
The Achilles campaign has raised $692,245.06 in contributions and spent just over $500,000 of that, according to Federal Election Commission data as of Aug. 4. Achilles has contributed $10,500 from himself toward the campaign. 
Risch’s campaign has garnered more than $4.4 million, FEC data as of Aug 4 showed. Risch said this race “doesn’t feel any different at all” from his past races. 
Achilles said he believes he’s the more conservative candidate, pointing to the increasing national debt over the years. He criticized Risch’s vote to confirm Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, a former Fox News host and Army National Guard veteran with limited military leadership experience compared to his predecessors, and initial vote to not release files related to the investigation of Jeffrey Epstein. 
“Why is he doing absolutely nothing about this ridiculous corruption that’s happening within this administration?” Achilles said. “There’s nothing conservative about looking the other way when you know people are stealing taxpayer dollars. So, the reality is I’m the better conservative candidate in this race.” 
Risch said Achilles’ votes on a number of issues during his time in the state Legislature were “exactly the opposite,” of how the senator would’ve voted. He included votes such as Achilles voting against: House Bill 93, which allowed for the first time in Idaho state funding to go to private K-12  education; HB 32 to prohibit any government entity from creating a mask mandate; and HB 83, which created new state-level immigration crimes and penalties. 
“I represent the most conservative state in America,” Risch said. “I am always ranked as one of the most conservative U.S. senators, sometimes the most conservative U.S. senator. And that’s because I consistently deliver a conservative vote, and as a result of that, they send me back to office every time because I do what I say I’m going to do. And man, have they got a clear choice to make this time.” 
A billboard purchased by the Todd Achilles campaign for Sen. Jim Risch’s 83rd birthday, calling the senator the state’s “oldest and richest.” (Photo courtesy of the Achilles campaign)
 The race has been marked by a billboard dispute, age-related questions, and dueling polls 

Amid the race, there’s been contradictory polls, a campaign billboard taken down, and a major emphasis by Achilles about Risch’s age. 
On May 4, the Achilles campaign sent a press release about a billboard it had paid for that said “Happy 83rd Birthday” to Risch had been removed. The billboard company leased a parcel of land in Boise owned by an investment company run by Risch and his wife Vicki.  
“It looks like Senator Risch proudly stands for free speech — as long as it’s speech he agrees with,” Achilles said in the press release.
Risch told the Sun he “didn’t really care” about the billboard and that he wasn’t the one to request its removal. 
“The company that did it, the property’s rented to a billboard agency, and they put the thing up,” he said. “When they found out about it, they went out and took it down. I didn’t ask them to take it down.” 
Achilles, told the Sun in an interview that he’s concerned about Risch’s age. One of his priorities is to set an age limit of 72 for members of Congress. 
“Sen. Risch is the oldest, wealthiest senator in Idaho history,” Achilles said. “He’s had a good run, but it’s time for somebody new.” 
Risch said, “there’s nothing I can do about it,” regarding his age. 
“It is a high-energy job,” he said. “There’s no question about it. I’m incredibly active. Have been all my life. … I’m not going to apologize for the people of Idaho sending me back there over and over again.” 
The Achilles campaign on June 4 released results from a poll of 774 registered voters in Idaho. The survey first asked respondents to pick among Risch, Achilles, and the Democrat David Roth. Roth has since dropped out of the race.  
It did not include the other independent candidate Fleming or the Libertarian Loesby. The first results showed Risch winning with 41% of those polled choosing him. 
The survey questions later highlight Risch’s connection to the confirmation of Bureau of Land Management Director Steve Pearce, “who has a record of supporting the sale of public lands,” Risch’s age, and that “technology and artificial intelligence are rapidly changing the Idaho economy and American workforce.” 
The survey then provides a paragraph of information about Achilles’ background and his priorities. Survey respondents later chose Achilles with 39% of the vote in a three-way race. In a head-to-head contest between Risch and Achilles, 51% of  survey respondents selected Achilles. 
On June 11, the Risch campaign released its own survey results from 500 “likely general election voters” in Idaho. The poll asked voters to choose among all of the candidates with no additional information about them. Poll respondents selected Risch as their top choice with 55% of the vote, Roth receiving 15%, and Achilles getting 7%.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Report: Tennessee’s lottery-funded scholarship program faces revenue shortfalls
description: Tennessee Lottery proceeds that fund many of the state’s college and technical education scholarships are projected to fall short of covering those programs’ costs each year through 2030, according to a report released Tuesday. Net lottery proceeds — the money left over after prizes and operating costs are covered — have fallen 21.9% since fiscal […]
text:
The Tennessee Education Lottery has funded college scholarships since its launch in 2003. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout) 
Tennessee Lottery proceeds that fund many of the state’s college and technical education scholarships are projected to fall short of covering those programs’ costs each year through 2030, according to a report released Tuesday.
Net lottery proceeds — the money left over after prizes and operating costs are covered — have fallen 21.9% since fiscal year 2022, while scholarship enrollment and spending have continued to grow, according to the report produced by nonpartisan think tank ThinkTennessee and the Tennessee Skills Coalition. The report projects a funding shortfall of up to $344 million by fiscal year 2030.
The advent of sports wagering in Tennessee is at least partially responsible for the drop in lottery ticket revenue, a University of Tennessee professor told lawmakers in March. And the sports gambling proceeds that backstopped the lottery’s scholarship programs are now also steered toward construction and maintenance for K-12 schools after Tennessee lawmakers struck a deal to secure the votes needed to pass a statewide private school voucher program in 2025.
The Tennessee Education Lottery Scholarship system offers 12 programs funded directly through lottery revenue to students pursuing two- and four-year degrees, workforce certificates and credentials. Another program, Tennessee Promise, is funded by a $1.3 billion endowment, but also historically received surplus funds from the lottery.
In 2025, the 13 programs together spent $505 million supporting 169,412 students. This also marked the first time that lottery proceeds fell short of scholarship spending, creating a multi-million-dollar funding gap.
Tennessee lottery proceeds fell short of scholarship costs for the first time in 2025. (Courtesy of ThinkTennessee)
These programs fund merit-based HOPE scholarships for students, help high school students earn college credits before they graduate, allow adult and independent learners to return to Tennessee’s community colleges and technical schools for education, and fund scholarships benefitting students with intellectual disabilities and veterans.
The Tennessee Education Lottery recently announced fiscal year-end results that show an increase of $15.2 million toward education funding over the previous year.
But even if lottery proceeds grow faster than Tennessee’s scholarship spending over the next four years, proceeds will likely fall short of costs, the report states.
In previous years, any lottery proceeds left over after scholarships were paid for went toward the Tennessee Promise program, a “last dollar” program which gives high school graduates an opportunity to attend any community college, Tennessee College of Applied Technology or other eligible institution offering associate degrees for free by covering any remaining costs not paid for by other scholarship programs. Between 2022 and 2025, transfers to the Tennessee Promise program ranged between $124 million and $151 million. Now, such annual transfers are capped at $10 million.
Scholarship spending in Tennessee is projected to outpace lottery proceeds every year through 2030, according to a report by ThinkTennessee. (Courtesy of ThinkTennessee)
If the lottery account no longer generates a surplus, this program too will receive less funding. And if funding for Tennessee’s other scholarship programs does fall, it could put more pressure on the Tennessee Promise program to fill in those gaps, according to the report.
Tennessee launched online-only sports betting in 2020, and the state designated those proceeds to the lottery’s college scholarship program as backup funds. With that money now going toward K-12 school construction, if lottery proceeds fall short of scholarship spending in the future — as they are projected to do — money would be pulled “dollar-for-dollar” from the construction and maintenance fund to cover the gap, the report states.
A new federal Workforce Pell grant, a needs-based program, may help offset costs of some short-term TCAT programs, the report notes. Other states facing shortfalls in lottery funding for scholarships have allowed retailers to accept debit cards instead of cash, or launched digital instant games in an attempt to improve lottery revenue. Some states supplemented lottery-funded scholarships with general fund allocations, and some switched to fixed, formula-based scholarship awards to keep costs from rising with tuition, the report states. But the report also says none of these approaches alone is enough to close Tennessee’s funding gap.
“Tennessee has built one of the nation’s strongest postsecondary scholarship systems, and that success has helped more students pursue education and training after high school,” Erin Hafkenschiel, president of ThinkTennessee, said in a news release. “By understanding the structural pressures on the system today, Tennessee can thoughtfully address these emerging funding challenges now in order to preserve access to postsecondary education for future generations.”

description: EUFALA — Five of the six Republican candidates in a special primary in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District made their pitch to voters in Barbour County Tuesday night, one week before the election.  The district, which covers the Wiregrass, the eastern portion of the Black Belt and the capital city, was redrawn by a May U.S. […]
text:
Republican voters in the Wiregrass on Tuesday will choose between (clockwise) Hampton Harris, Christian Horn, Rhett Marques, James Richardson, Joshua McKee or David Matthews in a special primary election. Five of the candidates pitched their platforms to voters in Eufala on Tuesday evening, one week before the election. (photos by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector and courtesy of Christian Horn; graphic by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)EUFALA — Five of the six Republican candidates in a special primary in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District made their pitch to voters in Barbour County Tuesday night, one week before the election. 
The district, which covers the Wiregrass, the eastern portion of the Black Belt and the capital city, was redrawn by a May U.S. Supreme Court order. The order allowed the state to use a Legislature-passed congressional map, which had previously been ruled racially discriminatory, instead of a court-ordered one. 
Following a special session of the Legislature, Gov. Kay Ivey in May called a special primary election for the district, along with Alabama’s 1st, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The candidate with the most votes will be the party’s nominee; the legislation setting the election did not provide for a runoff. The winner will face U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, in November.
The candidates
Candidates randomly selected speaking order at the event Tuesday evening, hosted by the Barbour County Republican Party. Joshua McKee, a U.S. Army veteran and business owner, said voters should choose a candidate that will go to D.C. for them, not themselves.
“I’ve sat on the sidelines, and I’ve been just as angry by electing someone that self-serves. How about having a servant that serves you, transparent, available and serving you?” McKee said. 
He said he would make his campaign finances into a non-profit organization so that voters would be able to see where his money came from and where it is being spent. 
In an impromptu question-and-answer segment, McKee promised to “stop investing in corporations and start investing in the communities.”
“The money needs to go to you,” he said. “It needs to go to the mom and pop shops, the brick and mortar that sustain the communities.”
Hampton Harris, a small business owner and part-time lawyer, promised that if elected, he would not raise taxes for Alabamians and would support abortion restrictions.
“I will stand to fight for the life of the unborn and for our children to make sure that we protect every life, that we protect our children, that we keep the government from telling parents how they should raise their children and how they should educate their children,” Harris said. “I will fight to make sure we take care of our military.”
Harris qualified for the race before the Legislature redrew the district in May. Like McKee, he urged voters to choose a candidate who is running “for the right reasons.” 
“I jumped in this race because it was the right thing to do. It was going to be an uphill battle, but I wanted to do it to fight, and I will continue that fight. If you send me to D.C., we will win,” he said. “We’ll carry on the tradition and the legacy of Charlie Kirk and get young people involved, and we will take this district back.”
David Matthews, a former Trump appointee in the U.S. Department of Agriculture, said he understands the inner workings of D.C. policy. 
“We haven’t had a farm bill since 2018, and our farmers need help. I have experience that can help get the farm bill passed,” Matthews said.
The bill would provide support for farmers, including improved access to credit, expanded investments in specialty crops, increased transparency in fertilizer markets and enhanced research and conservation programs.
Matthews said that with a low turnout expected in the primary, it is important to choose a candidate with comparable experience to go against Figures.
“Thirty thousand people or less are going to decide who runs up against a Shomari Figures, and this guy has very similar experience to what I have, just not as useful,” he said.
A message seeking comment with Figures was left Tuesday evening. 
James Richardson, a Marine Corps veteran, said he took an oath when he joined the military and he promised to keep that oath in Congress.
“Freedom is not free, but I felt the call to service again because I felt Washington doesn’t hear us anymore. I feel like we’re treated as numbers on a spreadsheet,” Richardson said. 
Richardson’s top priority is to address veterans’ healthcare. He said he lost his father, a veteran, to suicide because he could not get the mental healthcare he needed at the VA hospital.
“He gave his life to this country, just like I am every single day, willing to give my life for each and every one of you. So I ask on August 11th, send a vet to fight for you who knows the cost of freedom,” he said. “Send a Marine to beat Shomari, because a Marine will hold the line and I’ll never back down.”
Rep. Rhett Marques of Enterprise touted his endorsement from President Donald Trump six times during his short speech. He said his experience as a legislator also makes him the best candidate to beat Figures. 
“I am very proud to have President Trump’s endorsement in this race, and I am. This is not only going to be an important race for the state of Alabama, but it is for this country,” he said. “We have a chance to flip a [Democratic] seat back to the Republicans.”
During the question-and-answer session, each candidate asked about deploying troops to Iran said they did not support that. However, Marques said the priority is to eliminate Iran and groups like Hamas and Hezbollah.
“They are the head of the snake, and we’ve got to cut off the head of the snake,” Marques said. “Obviously, we do not want to send people in there to get that and change the regime, but I’m going to support our troops wherever they go, if that’s what it takes. We cannot continue letting this fester.”
A sixth candidate, Christian Horn, was not present at the forum. 
Jerry McGilvray, chair of the Barbour County Commission, urged attendees to tell everybody they know to go vote. He said that Tabitha Isner, vice chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, is “doing God’s work” by encouraging Democratic voters to cast ballots in the GOP primaries.
“You can take that for what it’s worth, but I think that we need to be very cognizant of the fact that Democrats vote in Republican primaries. I don’t know of any Republicans that dare vote for a Democrat in their primary, because I don’t think it’s anything they believe that we could support,” he said.
The Alabama Republican State Executive Committee on Saturday approved a resolution to add party registration, or closed primaries, to its official party platform.
“The state legislature dropped the ball,” McGilvray said. “If that comes up again in the Legislature, we would need some help to help get that done.”
Campaign finances
According to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission, Marques raised $1.3 million and spent $1.1 million as of July 22. He has $187,000 on hand. 
McKee has raised about $521,000 and spent almost $525,000 through July 22.
Harris has raised $245,500 and spent about $82,000. He has about $163,000 on hand. 
Matthews has raised more than $47,000 and spent about $36,000. He has about $12,000 on hand. 
Richardson has raised about $7,600 and spent about $7,400. He has $26 on hand.
Horn has not reported any fundraising. 
Figures has raised $1.3 million and spent about $700,000 through July 22. He has about $662,000 on hand.
How to vote
Republican voters in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District can choose between Harris, Horn, Marques, Matthews, McKee and Richardson for the Republican nomination on Tuesday. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Polling locations can be found here. The winner will face the Figures in the general election.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: From Idaho pockets to progress: Introducing Gem State’s Housing Network Call
description: Ask anyone in Idaho about the housing shortage and you’ll hear the same thing: We know the problem. We’re stuck on what to do about it.  Idaho’s housing shortage isn’t new anymore. Nonprofits, quasi-governmental groups, city partners, and grassroots coalitions are already working on the issue from their respective corner of the state. Boise has […]
text:
A house for sale in the North End of Boise on March 21, 2021. (Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun)Ask anyone in Idaho about the housing shortage and you’ll hear the same thing: We know the problem. We’re stuck on what to do about it. 
Idaho’s housing shortage isn’t new anymore. Nonprofits, quasi-governmental groups, city partners, and grassroots coalitions are already working on the issue from their respective corner of the state. Boise has its organizers. Coeur d’Alene has its advocates. Twin Falls, Driggs, Pocatello … the work is happening everywhere, often led by people who’ve been at it for years.
Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough.

As the advocacy director for Gem State Housing Alliance, Idaho’s first statewide pro-housing coalition, I hear about Idaho’s housing shortage from just about every person I talk to. 
The population boom has increased competition for Idaho’s available homes, and that competition — coupled with rising costs — has made Idaho the second least affordable housing market in the country, according to the National Association of REALTORS. 
It reminds me of a lesson from my high school math teacher: When there isn’t enough on the market, prices rise. I now see this playing all across the state out in real time in the competition for a starter home and the waitlists for rentals.
Here’s what’s easy to miss in that math: pro-housing solutions already exist in Idaho. What’s missing is a way to connect them so they add up to something bigger than one city’s win. 
Prior to my work with Gem State, I spent years working to preserve Idaho’s agricultural land; sprawl is part of why we’re losing it. Across the state, farmland is being eaten up by subdivisions and apartment buildings, largely because zoning codes limit builders to predominately large-lot detached homes (the most land-intensive, expensive option). Homes like duplexes, townhomes, and starter homes on smaller lots use less land per household, meaning more homes for Idahoans without paving over the farmland we’re trying to protect. 
That’s just one example, and it points to a pattern we see again and again: We’re organized in pockets, but not together. A win in one city rarely reaches a pro-housing group tackling the same issue two counties over. Lessons learned the hard way in one community must be relearned the hard way in another.
 That’s the gap Gem State’s Housing Network Call was built to fill. If you’re already one of the people doing the work, or ready to start, this is where you can join in. 
Pro-housing organizing calls are already happening statewide, but many admire the problem without moving into action. So Gem State asked these community leaders directly: What would actually help you make progress?
Their answer wasn’t more meetings. It wasn’t another organization to report to. It was one thing: a way to connect the conversations already happening, so the people doing this work don’t have to keep discovering the same solutions independently, city by city.
That’s why we’re launching the “Housing Network Call,” a 50-minute, action-driven call bringing pro-housing Idahoans from every corner of the state together. These calls will keep groups working on housing solutions aligned, address policy gaps, and most importantly, get everyone in the boat rowing in the same direction. It’s the first effort of its kind in Idaho, designed by the people already on the ground.
Idahoans take care of each other,  in our neighborhoods, in our small towns, in the way we show up when someone needs a hand. It’s time that instinct showed up in how we organize for housing too. 
You can be part of our first call oat noon Mountain time or 11 a.m. Pacific on Aug. 20. Learn more and register to join us by visiting Gem State’s website gemstatehousing.org/events/.

description: Memphis advocates on Tuesday called on a privately-run aviation company to stop servicing flights that transport detained immigrants out of the state. Volunteers with Vecindarios 901, a Memphis mutual aid organization that coordinates a “rapid response” network to help immigrants impacted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said they have tracked 51 flig[...]
text:
Memphis immigrant advocates are calling on the privately run Wilson Air Center to stop serving plans carrying immigrant detainees out of Memphis. (Photo: Dan DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Memphis advocates on Tuesday called on a privately-run aviation company to stop servicing flights that transport detained immigrants out of the state.
Volunteers with Vecindarios 901, a Memphis mutual aid organization that coordinates a “rapid response” network to help immigrants impacted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said they have tracked 51 flights since March transporting detainees from Wilson Air Center. Using publicly available flight tracking data, the group has traced most of these flight destinations to Alexandria, Louisiana, where ICE has established a large detention facility. 
Maria Oceja, Vecindarios 901 co-founder, urged owners of the Wilson Air Center, located on the site of the Memphis International Airport, to “reconsider your role” in the Trump administration’s mass immigrant detention and deportation operations.
“The Trump administration has separated parents from their children, wives from their husbands and families from their communities,” said Oceja, citing increased detentions as a result of ICE’s participation in the Memphis Safe Task Force and an uptick in detentions statewide that have brought hundreds of immigrants to a detention center in the city of Mason, located about 40 miles from the airport.
“Before they can even contact an attorney to fight their case in court they’re immediately flown out of this airport to a detention center in Louisiana, Alabama or another detention center in another part of the United States.” she said.
“By flying them out they are losing the opportunity to fight  their case in Tennessee so they can stay with their families.”
Neither Wilson Air Center nor ICE responded Tuesday to a request for comment. 
ICE Air Operations, a division of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, coordinates the majority of flights via contracts with airline companies to transport detained immigrants to detention centers within the U.S. and on deportation flights outside the country. 
In June, there were a total of 1,889 immigration enforcement flights — a 59% increase from June 2025, according to ICE Flight Monitor, which tracks flights using publicly available data.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabamians to vote on four statewide constitutional amendments in November
description: The Alabama Fair Ballot Commission on Tuesday approved language to describe four statewide constitutional amendments that will be on the statewide ballot in November.  The amendments, all approved by the Legislature this spring, range from methods to filling a vacancy in the lieutenant governor’s office to requiring schools to regularly play the National Ant[...]
text:
A sign saying "Vote Here" is seen at the Dean Road Recreation Center in Auburn, Alabama, on May 19, 2026. Voters in November will decide on four constitutional amendments, each were approved by the Legislature this spring. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Fair Ballot Commission on Tuesday approved language to describe four statewide constitutional amendments that will be on the statewide ballot in November. 
The amendments, all approved by the Legislature this spring, range from methods to filling a vacancy in the lieutenant governor’s office to requiring schools to regularly play the National Anthem. 
The language that appears on Alabamians’ ballots, chair of the commission Patrick Moody said in an interview after the meeting, will remain identical to the language in the bill passed by the Legislature.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The goal of the commission was to try to write those on about an eighth-grade reading level, because that was the average reading level for the voters in the state,” Moody said during the meeting. “It sounds easy sometimes, but it is hard to put something that’s nonpartisan and concise.”
The explanations of the amendments will be available on the Alabama Secretary of State’s website by the end of the week and at polling locations on Election Day.
Statewide Amendment 1 provides for a method of filling a vacancy in the lieutenant governor’s office, if the vacancy occurs more than 60 days before the next general election, which is usually every two years. 
The amendment, sponsored by Sen. Sam Givhan, R-Huntsville, passed unanimously in both chambers. 
It also allows the Legislature to set the pay of the lieutenant governor and legislative officers by joint resolution. 
Givhan said in a phone interview Tuesday that he proposed the amendment when questions of Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s residency arose. He said that should there be a vacancy – by death, resignation or otherwise – in the beginning of a four-year term, there was no way for the lieutenant governor’s office to be filled until the next midterm election.
“The president pro tem of the Senate does not automatically become lieutenant governor. No one automatically becomes lieutenant governor,” he said. “As far as the president of the Senate, under our rules and statutes, yes, the pro tem would serve lieutenant governor, but the pro tem’s got a lot of other things to do.”
After Gov. Robert Bentley resigned in 2017, then-Lt. Gov. Kay Ivey became the state’s chief executive. The lieutenant governor’s chair remained empty until 2019; then-Senate President Pro Tem Del Marsh presided over the Alabama Senate in the interim. 
The amendment would allow the lieutenant governor’s office to be filled without spending any additional taxpayer money, Givhan said.
“This was kind of a Band-Aid approach, but I’ll probably be coming back with another solution when there’s more time to think about it,” he said. “It’s just an opportunity for the people to elect a lieutenant governor if there’s a vacancy during the last two years of the quadrennium.”
The commission unanimously adopted the language after some minor changes.
Statewide Amendment 2 creates a process for county school boards of education to merge, and requires the State Board of Education to conduct an impact study before a merger. It also ensures a process for protest and requires a referendum election.
“We want people to know that there is a way for people to protest this action or at least have a voice in trying to stop the action, so it’s not an automatic merger,” Moody said.
According to the explainer, if at least 25% of registered voters in an affected county school system submit a written protest, a majority of voters would need to approve the merge at the next general election. 
The amendment, sponsored by Rep. Terri Collins, R-Decatur, passed 96-2 in the House and unanimously in the Senate. 
A message seeking comment from Collins was left Tuesday afternoon.
The commission unanimously adopted the language after some minor changes.
Statewide Amendment 3 would require Alabama school boards of education to adopt a policy requiring public K-12 schools to say the Pledge of Allegiance daily, and allow school boards to adopt policies allowing student-initiated and student-led prayer. 
Students who do not want to participate would be allowed to leave the classroom during the prayer and the pledge. According to the U.S. Department of Education, students may pray in school as long as it does not disrupt school activities.
The amendment, sponsored by Rep. Reed Ingram, passed the House 94-4 and unanimously in the Senate. 
A message seeking comment from Ingram was left Tuesday afternoon.
The commission unanimously adopted the language after no discussion or changes.
Statewide Constitutional Amendment 4 requires local school boards of education to adopt policies requiring public K-12 schools to broadcast the first stanza of The Star-Spangled Banner once per week. 
Under the amendment, the national anthem can be performed by a school-approved band, choir, vocal group or vocalist, as long as they use the version archived by the Library of Congress. 
The amendment, sponsored by Sen. Gerald Allen, R-Cottondale, passed the Senate 22-5 and the House 75-27.
A message seeking comment from Allen was left Tuesday afternoon.
The commission unanimously adopted the language after no discussion or changes.
Moody said that the commission’s work is challenging because they have to explain the amendments clearly, in a nonpartisan manner and at an eighth-grade reading level. 
“Trying to just make it simple, everyday language, sometimes that’s hard if you’re talking about things like bond issues or sometimes even constitutional amendments,” Moody said. “That’s a complicated term, but we just try to take it and work with our different commission members and everybody’s different backgrounds, and try to think about our friends and family and what they’d want to know if they’re voting yes or no on something.”
Voters will see all four amendments on the Nov. 3 ballot. Each requires a simple majority of votes to pass.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado Democrats begin general election with big cash advantages over GOP rivals
description: Republican candidates are entering the 2026 general election at a major fundraising disadvantage as they hope to defy the odds and put an end to nearly a decade of Democratic dominance in Colorado politics. After spending more than $6 million to secure the Democratic nomination for governor, Attorney General Phil Weiser collected another $486,005 in […]
text:
Victor Marx, left, Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, right. (Photo by Chase Woodruff, left, Lindsey Toomer, right)Republican candidates are entering the 2026 general election at a major fundraising disadvantage as they hope to defy the odds and put an end to nearly a decade of Democratic dominance in Colorado politics.
After spending more than $6 million to secure the Democratic nomination for governor, Attorney General Phil Weiser collected another $486,005 in contributions last month, according to his campaign’s latest financial disclosure, and had $369,303 in the bank as of July 27.
His Republican opponent in the governor’s race, first-time candidate Victor Marx, raised less ($185,694) than his campaign spent ($221,627) during the same period, and reported $136,989 in cash on hand.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
It’s the first time in his short political career that Marx, a ministry leader from Colorado Springs, has found himself with less financial firepower than an opponent. He significantly outraised state Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer and state Rep. Scott Bottoms in the GOP’s June primary, collecting nearly $3 million in donations and eking out a victory over Kirkmeyer by fewer than 2,500 votes.
Weiser raised a record $6.7 million en route to his primary win over U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet in June, overcoming a major deficit as he faced over $17 million in combined spending by Bennet’s campaign and a billionaire-funded super PAC supporting Bennet’s candidacy. Weiser collected nearly $1 million in donations in June and July combined, his best two-month fundraising period since the first two months of his campaign in January and February 2025.
The winner of the governor’s race in November will succeed Gov. Jared Polis, who is term-limited.
Greg Lopez, an unaffiliated candidate for governor who briefly served as a Republican member of Congress from Colorado’s 4th District in 2024, trails far behind the two major-party candidates in fundraising. His latest disclosure reports a total of $89,556 in donations received, a personal loan of $65,160 and a cash-on-hand total of $10,390. Lopez, who unsuccessfully sought the GOP nomination for governor in 2018 and 2022, qualified for the ballot through petition signatures last month.
Marx faces a raft of campaign finance complaints filed with the secretary of state’s office in connection with donations in excess of the legal $1,450 contribution limit, and with his claim last week that there is “no limit” to the donations he can receive through his campaign’s online merchandise store.
Fighting for Colorado, a pro-Weiser super PAC, reported $258,790 in receipts for the period ending July 27, while the Freedom Independent Expenditure Committee, which has spent on Marx’s behalf, collected just $31,600.
Other statewide races
Alongside the race for governor, Coloradans in November will elect a new attorney general, secretary of state and treasurer. All four statewide offices have been in Democratic hands since 2019.
Secretary of State Jena Griswold, seeking a promotion to the attorney general’s post, eased to victory in a four-way Democratic primary in June and begins the general election with $158,920 in cash on hand. Her opponent, El Paso County District Attorney Michael Allen, reported $5,732 in the bank.
Democratic candidates also enjoy major financial advantages in the races for secretary of state, where Democrat Amanda Gonzalez has outraised the GOP’s James Wiley by more than a 5-to-1 margin, and treasurer, where Democratic state Sen. Jeff Bridges has amassed more than $237,000 in cash on hand, compared to the $53,247 in the bank for GOP Fremont County Commissioner Kevin Grantham.
The midterm election will be held on Nov. 3, 2026.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Political notes: A special session long on emotion, short on balloons, spot-on in witnesses
authors: William J. Ford, Will Hammann, Danielle J. Brown
description: The special session was focused on one subject, but lawmakers still found time to give fond sendoffs to Sen. Nancy King and Del. Frank Conaway, and to do an abridged balloon drop to wrap it all up, in political notes.
text:
Delegates throw what balloons they could muster without the help of pages after the special session is adjourned Tuesday. (Photo by Will Hammann/Maryland Matters)While the Senate waited Tuesday for a congressional redistricting bill to come across the hall from the House of Delegates, several senators stood up to pay homage to Senate Majority Leader Nancy J. King (D-Montgomery), a longtime lawmaker who will not be returning in January, after losing her primary to Amar Mukunda, a first-time candidate.
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) read a short biography about King, who was elected to the House in 2002 and has served in the Senate since 2007.
After King gave a few remarks that she labeled her “swan song,” the tributes flowed from colleagues for at least 40 minutes.
Senate Majority Leader Nancy King (D-Montgomery) speaks at the rostrum Tuesday next to Senate President Bill Ferugson (D-Baltimore City). (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Sen. Mary Washington (D-Baltimore City and Baltimore County) called King “a history maker” as one of three women to serve as Senate majority leader. Washington also recalled when she served as the floor leader to defend the Freedom to Read Act that was sponsored by King and signed into law in 2024.
“I was so excited and also honored that I could get to do that,” Washington said.
Several Republicans also stood up to praise King. Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore) talked about his Friday morning conversations with King.
“We got to talk about things outside of just the policy and the things that really bring us together,” Hershey said.
Sen. William G. Folden (R-Frederick) said he has attended only two Democratic fundraisers: One for Folden’s good friend, Del. C.T. Wilson (D-Charles), who won the nomination in June to replace outgoing Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) and once for King.
“I always appreciated the value of your word and really just the sincerity in your voice and your touch because some things I wasn’t going to process in a manner that was going to be consistent with your beliefs,” Folden said. “We could always walk away and agree to disagree. I’m very grateful for you. I think we can all learn a lot about dignity and grace in watching Nancy J. and how she handled her time here in the Senate and her relationship with someone that could be potentially polarizing as me.”
Honoring a friendship
It wasn’t just the Senate where the heartfelt speeches were being shared. As the House kicked off the special session Monday morning, Del. Aaron Kaufman (D-Montgomery) offered an ode to an outgoing colleague.
“I want to acknowledge my dear friend Del. Frank Conaway Jr.,” Kaufman said. “Many of you probably don’t know this, but he has been so good to me,” he said of the Baltimore City Democrat, who lost his seat of two decades in the June primary.
“What he would do because he was such a good man … is make sure I got home OK, and he always, also on those late nights, made sure I had something to eat,” Kaufman said.
Del. Aaron Kaufman (D-Montgomery), right, in his seat as the House begins the special session Monday. (Photo by Will Hammann/Maryland Matters)
Kaufman, who doesn’t drive, said Conaway often walked him to his hotel after they left committee late at night when the shuttle was closed.
“He just seemed like he needed my help, so I was there so help him out … but I wouldn’t do it for everybody.” Conaway told Maryland Matters Tuesday. “I have a lot of respect for him.”
Conaway and Kaufman both have spent their entire tenures as delegates on the House Judiciary Committee. But by the time Kaufman joined in 2023, Conaway had more than a decade and a half under his belt.
“You need a lot of mentors when you’re a freshman, and I have many, including the speaker, but also Delegate Conaway,” Kaufman said Tuesday. “I appreciated his veteran insight.”
Conaway recalled times Kaufman left him laughing on the House floor. “I thought he was a funny guy and all that … That’s how we became friends,” he said.
Kaufman shared the same story.
“We just enjoyed busting each others’ chops and developed a fast friendship. He was one of the first friends that I made and he’s really been a pioneer [as a delegate],” he said.
“I’ll miss him very much and I just want to thank him for his 20 years of service to the body and always looking out for me,” Kaufman said, closing his remarks Monday. “Thank you, delegate.”
Maybe they can choose our lottery numbers
There was plenty of hand-wringing from Republicans after Democratic leaders announced last week that testimony in the one committee on a proposed redistricting constitutional amendment would be limited to 50 people, who had a 10-hour window Friday to sign up to speak at Monday’s hearing. Once the limit of 50 was reached, it would be up to committee chairs to pick the speakers.
Critics saw the opportunity for chicanery. But legislative leaders never had the chance.
Exactly 50 people signed up online during the 10-hour window for registration, committee staff members said, and no one was turned away.
Technically, 51 people were registered to speak, but one of those was the bill’s sponsor, House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Anne Arundel and Prince George’s), said Rory Nolan, committee manager for the House Government, Labor and Elections Committee.
1/45th the number of days, 1/45th the amount of balloons and confetti
The Maryland General Assembly typically marks the end of a regular 90-day legislative session by having pages toss balloons and piles of confetti from the galleries of the House and Senate, covering the floors of each chamber.
The special session came to a close with delegates tossing a couple balloons across the floor, a smaller version of celebrations held at the end of the regularly scheduled 90-day session. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
That tradition continued — sort of — in the House Tuesday when delegates adjourned sine die. While the Senate simply gaveled out to end the special session, Del. Joe Vogel (D-Montgomery) brought in a handful of balloons and tossed them out over the desks as delegates hit them across the floor.
The confetti tradition was not missed either — Chief of Staff Michelle Firmin threw a handful of paper scraps over the head of House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel).
The mini celebration for the short special session brought the session to a close on a high note after long hours of tense debate to pass legislation ushering in a constitutional amendment on redistricting.
“If I may have a minute,” Peña-Melnyk said as laughter and applause continued in the chamber. “I just want to thank you sincerely to be here. You took time out of your life, your family. I know it was tough, but I do thank you for doing it in an honorable way.
“I hope you are blessed, that you have an amazing, amazing rest of the summer and fall,” she said.
— Maryland Matters reporter Christine Condon contributed to this report.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado’s new battery recycling bill is a start, but communities still need more protection
description: Colorado’s recently passed battery recycling law defines producer responsibility for end-of-life electric vehicle batteries. And California’s SB 615 may soon follow in a state committed to addressing the problem of large-format battery waste. These laws are an important step toward collecting waste and aiming to recover valuable minerals. But without stronge[...]
text:
An electric car battery is installed with a robotic arm. (Getty Images)Colorado’s recently passed battery recycling law defines producer responsibility for end-of-life electric vehicle batteries. And California’s SB 615 may soon follow in a state committed to addressing the problem of large-format battery waste.
These laws are an important step toward collecting waste and aiming to recover valuable minerals. But without stronger environmental transparency, disclosure and accountability requirements for battery recycling facilities, they fall short of protecting the workers and communities that will bear the industry’s impacts.
Because neither Colorado nor California currently has lithium-ion battery recycling facilities, much of the waste collected under these programs will likely be shipped and processed in Nevada, where Redwood Materials claims about 90% of all lithium-ion batteries in North America are processed.
A recent report from the nonprofit GAIA on battery recycling facilities in Nevada found that community right-to-know laws are outdated to monitor these new technologies, that publicly accessible environmental data is limited or otherwise deemed confidential, and that recent federal deregulation is leaving communities exposed to hazards and risks these facilities may pose.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That information gap matters now because Nevada’s “lithium loop” is the nation’s epicenter for the full electric vehicle battery supply chain. We’ve seen the harm a lead-acid battery recycling industry can cause at the former Exide facility in Vernon, California, which spewed lead over a 1.7-mile radius for over 20 years before it was shut down in 2015. It is considered one of the largest environmental cleanups of residential properties in California’s history, and to date, hasn’t gone so smoothly.
Whether lead-acid or lithium-ion, all batteries are chemically intensive products that use acids, solvents, and high heat in their recycling processes, which generate waste and pollution.
GAIA’s report examines modern lithium-ion battery recycling processes and found that existing federal transparency tools, including the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act and the Toxic Release Inventory, do not actually tell the public what it needs to know. These federal laws are outdated and have weak enforcement. While Colorado’s new law requires some recovery rate reporting, those provisions are limited. Overall, key information about PFAS emissions, hazardous waste generation, water use, energy consumption, and recycling recovery rates remains difficult to access. Recent federal deregulation has further weakened public access to information at the very moment this industry is scaling up.
Recycling companies are not required to publicly report PFAS releases or resource use, such as water consumption and energy consumption, that affect the region. This information is either opaque and voluntary or withheld by companies as proprietary. The GAIA report shows that hazardous waste generation is uneven, while materials-recovery rates are neither transparent nor reliable.
Batteries are essential to the shift away from fossil fuels, and they are an integral part of modern electricity grids, which are central to climate action strategies. But without clear, publicly available standards for reporting environmental impacts, responsible companies cannot be distinguished from risky ones and policymakers and investors lack the information they need to make sound decisions.
Colorado’s new battery recycling law is a welcome start, and California should follow suit to hold producers responsible for collecting spent large-format batteries and sending them for their next best use according to the waste management hierarchy.
But collection and recycling requirements alone will not guarantee a safe and responsible battery industry. As this sector scales up, states must ensure battery recycling facilities are subject to the highest environmental standards and review. Producer responsibility must be paired with stronger transparency, disclosure, and environmental health protections. Otherwise, an industry intended to solve one environmental challenge risks creating new ones.
A truly sustainable battery economy requires not only keeping materials in circulation but also ensuring that workers, communities, and regulators have the information and protections they need.
