title: US Senate stopgap fails to renew more than $38B a year in state transportation funding
text: WASHINGTON — The stopgap spending bill supported by an overwhelming majority of U.S. senators does not address tens of billions in expiring transportation funding, leaving states facing a massive effective budget cut starting Oct. 1.The 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law, which authorized highway and transit programs for five years, expires Sept. 30. Roughly $38.6 billion per year in extra federal transportation funding is set to expire with it, even if the continuing resolution the Senate advanced 89-4 Monday becomes law.The stopgap measure, a version of which has also passed the House, would keep the government funded mostly at current levels, and reauthorize highway and transit programs through Dec. 11. But it would not renew the advance appropriations that provided $184 billion over five years for a host of transportation programs under the infrastructure law President Joe Biden signed in his first year in office.Ben Gilsdorf, an associate legislative director for transportation at the National Association of Counties, said in a Tuesday interview that the advance appropriations funded many of the group’s top transportation priorities.“It's not all of the programs under (the infrastructure law) that would stop without an extension,” he said. “But for us, it's several of the most impactful ones.”The National Association of Counties was part of a broad range of advocacy groups representing business, labor, cities, state departments of transportation and every mode of transportation that signed a letter last month asking Congress to extend the supplemental funding.Funding for Transportation Department programs makes up a bit more than half of the total advance appropriations in the infrastructure law, which also includes major funding for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, Energy Department and telecommunications program. The total advance appropriations for fiscal 2026 were about $66.2 billion, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office.Bridges, airports, transit and moreThe DOT funding largely flows to state departments of transportation. Returning to pre-2021 baseline infrastructure spending would leave every state with less federal funding to cover varied transportation needs.About 30%, $10.8 billion per year, of the extra transportation funding is determined by formula, meaning the amounts sent to each state vary based on population, highway miles and other factors.California is the only state that would lose 10 figures worth of funding, at nearly $1.1 billion. But even Vermont, the state with the lowest total funding lost, would see $55.6 million less in formula funds if the funding is not extended, according to data Senate Appropriations Committee Vice Chair Patty Murray of Washington sent to her fellow Democratic senators last month.A total of 10 formula programs representing different modes of transportation would be affected, according to the fact sheet from Murray’s office.More than half of the formula funding, $5.5 billion, is slated for the Federal Highway Administration’s bridge repair program. Airport construction funds represent the next-greatest funding at $3 billion per year. The Federal Transit Administration’s grant program to maintain transit system infrastructure would lose $950 million and state transportation departments would lose another $900 million in federal funding for electric vehicle charging stations.Other affected programs are for highways in Appalachian states, truck safety inspections, ferry boats and terminals, FTA grants for senior passengers and those with disabilities and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration programs.In addition to formula funds, the remaining 70% of advance appropriations is distributed via 25 competitive grant programs, according to the Murray document.Grant programs to fund ports, large highway and rail projects, transit station upgrades, roadway safety and other projects would be among those losing funding.Complicating spending negotiations While the law that initiated the additional funding was bipartisan, there are indications an extension could be a more partisan issue.Murray said ahead of the Senate floor vote Monday that Republicans did not “agree to our efforts to extend critical advance appropriations for infrastructure” and vowed to continue pursuing the additional funds.Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, a Maine Republican, did not reference advance appropriations in a press release announcing a deal on the stopgap bill. Republicans, who hold majorities in both chambers of Congress, may prefer to settle the future of the funding through a long-term surface transportation bill or full-year appropriations measure, Gilsdorf said.Even if the Senate bill is enacted, there will be an opportunity when it expires to revisit the issue, he said.“There'd be another bite at the apple,” he said.A person familiar with negotiations who was not authorized to speak on the record said Tuesday that the advance appropriations in the 2021 law were meant to be one-time funding, and that extending them in a stopgap measure meant to preserve the status quo would be inappropriate.The funding is part of a larger policy debate than is usually considered in a continuing resolution, the person said.The issue could hang over negotiations for full-year spending bills, likely to begin in earnest after November’s elections. Senate appropriators have not reached a deal for top-line spending levels for fiscal 2027. Republicans, at President Donald Trump’s urging, are seeking a massive boost to defense programs. Democrats historically seek parity between non-defense and defense spending, but have relaxed that stance while the extra infrastructure funds have been flowing. Without that additional funding, Democrats might be less amenable to compromise.

name: Delaware
title: Wilmington shootings raise questions about public safety, enforcement and accountability
description: A series of violent incidents across the city is affecting residents and businesses while renewing debate over declining arrests, detention policies and whether current crime-prevention strategies are producing measurable results. By George D. Rotsch,  Editor, Delaware LIVE WILMINGTON — A series of shootings across Wilmington in recent weeks has renewed conc[...]
text:
A series of violent incidents across the city is affecting residents and businesses while renewing debate over declining arrests, detention policies and whether current crime-prevention strategies are producing measurable results.
By George D. Rotsch,  Editor, Delaware LIVE

WILMINGTON — A series of shootings across Wilmington in recent weeks has renewed concerns about public safety, the effect of violence on neighborhoods and businesses, and whether the criminal justice system is doing enough to identify, detain and prosecute dangerous offenders.
The incidents have not been limited to one neighborhood. Shootings have been reported in West Center City, Price Run, Southbridge, Baynard Village, near Fourth and DuPont streets, and in other parts of the city.
Most of the victims survived, but several suffered serious or critical injuries. A concerning number of the victims were teenagers or young adults.
Shootings reported across the city
On Aug. 1, a 32-year-old woman was shot on West Seventh Street and a 28-year-old man was shot on Vandever Avenue. On Aug. 2, a 52-year-old man was shot near Linden and South Van Buren streets.
All three victims were reported in stable condition.
Those incidents followed the July 31 shooting of a 16-year-old, the July 14 shooting of a 31-year-old man in Price Run and the July 12 shooting of a 17-year-old near Fourth and DuPont streets. The 17-year-old was reported in critical condition.
Other recent victims included a 17-year-old boy shot in Southbridge, an 18-year-old woman seriously injured in Baynard Village, a 29-year-old critically injured in West Center City and a 20-year-old man shot on North DuPont Street.
Police have not publicly indicated that the shootings are connected. However, the incidents show a recurring pattern of gun violence affecting several Wilmington neighborhoods, with multiple victims between the ages of 16 and 19.
Hospital shooting left one employee dead
The most serious recent incident was the June shooting inside Wilmington Hospital.
Two 19-year-old employees were shot. One died and the other was critically injured.
Police arrested 23-year-old John Wallace-Bey in Philadelphia and charged him with first-degree murder and related offenses.
Police described the hospital shooting as an isolated workplace incident rather than part of the city’s street violence. That distinction is important, but it does not lessen the broader effect repeated shootings can have on public confidence.
Residents bear the daily cost
Crime reports often reduce shootings to dates, locations and victim conditions. Residents experience them as part of daily life.
Families living in affected neighborhoods may change their routines after repeated violence. Parents may keep children indoors. Senior citizens may become reluctant to walk to stores, churches or bus stops. Residents may avoid certain streets or stop going outside after dark.
Repeated gunfire can also produce anxiety, sleep disruption and constant concern for children and other family members.
Even when victims survive, the psychological effect can accumulate. Residents may begin to treat fear and disruption as normal conditions of city life.
The burden often falls hardest on people who cannot afford to move. Higher-income families may have the ability to relocate, install additional security, or avoid troubled areas. Lower- and middle-income residents are more likely to remain exposed while continuing to pay taxes and expect basic public services.
Public Safety Committee Chair Yolanda McCoy warned that Wilmington can not allow violence to become normalized.
The first responsibility of government is to protect life, property and the ability of law-abiding citizens to live safely in their communities.
Youth programs, social services and violence-intervention initiatives may play an important role, but they cannot replace consistent law enforcement.
Businesses lose customers and employees
Gun violence also affects Wilmington’s economy.
Small businesses depend on customers who feel safe entering a neighborhood, workers who are willing to accept early or late shifts and property owners who are confident enough to invest.
When residents believe an area is unsafe, they may leave earlier, shop elsewhere or avoid the neighborhood entirely.
Restaurants, convenience stores, service businesses and neighborhood retailers are especially vulnerable. Many operate on narrow profit margins and may struggle to absorb declining foot traffic, higher insurance costs or additional spending on cameras, lighting and private security.
Employers may also have difficulty recruiting and retaining workers who are concerned about traveling to or from work.
Property owners may postpone improvements, and potential tenants may choose other locations. Businesses considering Wilmington may question whether the city can provide a predictable and secure environment for employees and customers.
Public safety is not separate from economic development. It is one of the basic conditions needed for economic growth.
Police have not identified a single cause
Wilmington police have not identified one cause for the recent violence or attributed the shootings to a single citywide trend.
Police and city officials have instead pointed to several overlapping factors, including crime concentrated in particular hotspots, group-related conflicts and opportunistic offenses.
The department’s public strategies have emphasized intelligence-led policing, Group Violence Intervention, GunStat, partnerships with federal agencies and community outreach.
Police should not assign a cause without evidence. Still, residents deserve more than descriptions of strategies. They should receive regular information about arrests, firearms recovered, cases cleared, repeat offenders identified and prosecutions completed.
Officials may accurately describe individual shootings as isolated or unrelated, but residents often experience the incidents as part of a continuing pattern of danger.
The victims may be unrelated. The effect on the public is not.
Declining arrests raise public questions
The brief also describes a longer-term decline in arrests, criminal filings, case dispositions and convictions.
Statewide Court of Common Pleas criminal filings declined from 110,071 in 2014 to 90,410 in 2023, an 18% decrease.
Criminal dispositions fell from 88,507 to 62,211 during the same period, a decline of approximately 30%.
The brief also states that Wilmington arrests declined across violent, property, drug and juvenile offense categories, although it does not include a complete year-by-year city data table.
Those figures require context.
Fewer arrests can reflect lower crime, changes in enforcement priorities, diversion programs, juvenile justice reforms or fewer cases supported by sufficient evidence. A decline in arrests does not, by itself, prove police are refusing to enforce the law.
Lower conviction totals may also result from fewer crimes, fewer arrests or fewer cases entering the courts.
However, the trend raises a legitimate public-policy question.
When residents see repeated shootings while arrests, filings and completed cases decline, they may reasonably ask whether the system is creating enough certainty that dangerous offenders will be arrested, detained when legally justified and prosecuted.
Detention policies deserve scrutiny
The issue is not whether everyone accused of a crime should be jailed. Defendants are entitled to constitutional protections, due process and individual bail decisions.
The issue is whether the system has moved too far toward diversion, reduced detention and noncustodial resolutions, allowing repeat or high-risk offenders to return to the community before cases are resolved.
The source brief does not establish that Wilmington police have adopted a formal policy of refusing to arrest offenders. It also does not prove that prosecutors or judges are routinely releasing dangerous defendants.
Still, city and state officials should provide more detailed information about how the system is functioning.
That should include the number of shooting cases resulting in arrests, the prior records of suspects, the number of defendants released before trial and the outcomes of cases involving serious gun charges.
Without that information, the public is left to choose between official assurances and what residents see happening in their neighborhoods.
Prevention cannot replace enforcement
A balanced public-safety strategy should avoid two extremes.
The first is the assumption that law enforcement alone can solve every underlying social problem. Addiction, unstable families, school failure, untreated mental illness and a lack of opportunity can contribute to crime and should be addressed.
The second is the idea that arrest, detention and prosecution are inherently harmful or ineffective.
When used lawfully and supported by evidence, enforcement protects victims, deters repeat conduct and reinforces basic standards of behavior.
Violence-prevention programs should support enforcement, not replace it.
Wilmington also needs stronger witness protection, closer coordination among police and prosecutors, and better relationships with residents who may have information but fear retaliation.
Results should matter more than programs
Wilmington officials should be judged not only by the offices, partnerships and programs they announce, but by whether residents feel safer and businesses regain confidence.
That means concentrating police resources in repeat hotspots, improving shooting clearance rates, recovering illegal firearms and coordinating with state and federal prosecutors.
It also means imposing meaningful consequences on people convicted of gun crimes.
Officials should not minimize public concern because most recent victims survived or because police have not connected the shootings.
A nonfatal shooting is still a serious violent crime. A teenager in critical condition is not evidence that the public-safety system is succeeding.
The central question is not whether Wilmington has strategies and programs.
It is whether those efforts are preventing the next shooting.
Residents and business owners have a right to expect rehabilitation opportunities for offenders who can change. They also have a right to protection from people who repeatedly threaten the community.
A responsible public-safety policy must recognize both obligations. Wilmington’s recent violence gives residents legitimate reason to question whether the current balance is working.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Rep. Zach Nunn, U.S. labor secretary say 2025 tax cuts help Iowa businesses expand
description: Acting U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said Tuesday that U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn played a key role in passing the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act — a law that he said has helped support and expand Iowa manufacturing sector. Sonderling and Nunn visited Auto-jet, a Clive manufacturing business specializing in exhaust system parts for […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, left, and Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling look at parts manufactured as they tour Auto-Jet, a manufacturer in Clive Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Acting U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said Tuesday that U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn played a key role in passing the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act — a law that he said has helped support and expand Iowa manufacturing sector.
Sonderling and Nunn visited Auto-jet, a Clive manufacturing business specializing in exhaust system parts for school buses, trucks and other vehicles. After Auto-Jet General Manager Kelle Vos gave the two politicians a tour of the facility, Sonderling told reporters the Trump administration is supporting businesses like Auto-jet through components of the 2025 tax and spending law, pointing to the “100% deduction on new business payments” included in the law.
The law included a new 100% bonus depreciation for the entire cost of “qualified production property” — equipment used for manufacturing, production and refining — for the year that the property is placed into service. Sonderling said employees at Auto-jet, as well as other businesses he has visited, say this change allows for the purchase of new machines — and builds off other portions of the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act related to removing taxes on tips and overtime.
“That’s what we were able to see today — this super high-tech equipment, you know, they almost look like a spaceship how to operate this, being able to do some of the advanced welding and CNC,” Sonderling said, referring to computer numerical control. “A company like this can take 100% tax deduction in their first year. What does that mean? More money back into the business that they can reinvest into building more business lines, but more importantly, hiring more workers and giving more workers more hours and more overtime and more money.”
Sonderling pointed to Nunn’s vote in support of the 2025 law as one of the people in Washington, D.C., “actually bringing jobs and more money back to Iowa.”
Nunn, a Republican who represents Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, faces a competitive reelection campaign as he runs against state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott in the 2026 election. He has held the seat since the 2022 election, but some political forecasters predict Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District may be among the most competitive races in the nation in the upcoming midterms.
As he campaigns for a third term, Nunn has spoken about his position as a moderate candidate while also highlighting ways Iowa has benefitted from measures led by the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress. Sonderling is not the only member of President Donald Trump’s administration to visit Iowa to support Nunn — in May, Vice President J.D. Vance also came in Iowa to encourage voters to reelect Nunn to the U.S. House.
While Republicans have highlighted how policies under the Trump administration and the Republican-controlled Congress have supported American businesses and workers, Democrats have argued GOP policies have made life more expensive for Iowans. Trone Garriott and others have criticized the cuts to Medicaid funding made through the 2025 tax and spending law as a policy that is bringing up the costs of healthcare for Iowans, and Democratic leaders have argued the measure does more to help the wealthy than help working class Americans.
General Manager Kelle Vos, center gave U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, right and Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, left, a tour of the facilities at Auto-Jet, a manufacturer in Clive Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Nunn said as he and Sonderling toured Auto-jet, they saw evidence that GOP policies are helping rebuild America’s manufacturing base.
“Like so many companies across the Midwest right now, we’re building again, and we’re building in America,” Nunn said. “It’s a direct reflection of the work that we’ve done, both in Congress, but also most importantly right here on the homefront. The fact that Auto-jet has had one of their best years ever and is on track to have their best record year yet, suggests that, you know, we’re really open for business here.”
Nunn said there’s more work to be done, saying he supports further investments in labor and workforce education, saying he and the labor secretary planned to meet with labor unions and community colleges to speak about workforce development.
Sonderling said workforce development — especially programs like registered apprenticeships — has been a major priority for the current administration as Trump and others aim to “reindustrialize” the U.S. economy.
“You know, in prior administrations, we saw jobs like this being shipped overseas,” Sonderling said. “And because of the president’s policy — because he’s working every single day to bring investments back, –we’re seeing trillions of dollars of investments from foreign companies, foreign countries, and domestic companies saying, ‘you know what, we want products made in America.’ And people want to buy products made in America, just like here, because they’re the best. And more importantly, they want them made by American workers.”
Sonderling was also holding events with Gov. Kim Reynolds and U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon in Iowa Tuesday related to other workforce development initiatives.
Though the leaders pointed to investments made to support the manufacturing industry in recent years, Iowa has also seen a decrease in manufacturing jobs in the past year, alongside other workforce losses as reported by Iowa Workforce Development. Nunn said Republicans’ tax policy is allowing employers and workers to reinvest more money in local businesses.
“The types of tax cuts that we’re doing here with the Department of Labor, with Congress, are putting money directly back in employers’ pockets. Most importantly, they’re putting money back in Americans’ pockets,” Nunn said. “That gives them the ability to invest in their family, invest in their business, invest in the country. Already, we have seen a huge return. Most families are getting $3,500 back in their pocket — that’s something that they can take back home. That has a very positive impact here.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s healthcare crisis needs more than bake sales
description:
As Brattleboro rallies to save its birthing center, the real question is why we keep patching a broken system instead of fixing it.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s healthcare crisis needs more than bake sales.
text:
This commentary is by Manny Mansbach, a member of the Vermont Workers Center, which has been working for economic justice and human dignity, including healthcare as a human right.    
Since Brattleboro Memorial Hospital (BMH) announced they plan to close southeastern Vermont’s only birthing center in the next six to nine months, Windham County residents and officials have begun mobilizing to find a way to keep safe birth alive in our community. It is imperative that these efforts gain steam and this harmful decision is reversed. It is also crucial that we look clearly at how we got into this mess, and how we get out.
The story of the BMH birthing center must be set in the context of an active war on healthcare by the Republican Party, along with a colossal bipartisan failure to act to protect and expand healthcare access for Vermonters over many years. Yes, part of the problem at BMH was undoubtedly mismanagement, but you don’t need to be an expert to see that the healthcare system is badly broken. Birthing centers closed in Springfield in 2019 and at Copley Hospital in Morrisville last November. Springfield Hospital recently announced plans to close adult day services this fall. Without a serious reordering of our priorities, this crisis will almost certainly be followed by more tragic closures all across the state.
Gov. Phil Scott has been in office for about a decade, and in that time our healthcare system has steadily gone downhill. Today, despite the pressure from BMH and community activists, he is sending strong signals that no help will be forthcoming from the state. Democrats, on the other hand, have also not offered any meaningful healthcare policy initiatives in the legislature. Even modest proposals to increase access to healthcare have been watered down, changed to studies, and then shelved without any action. 
Legislators have repeatedly made it clear that leadership has had no appetite for working on anything significant around healthcare. What there has been appetite for is to continue rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic, with payment reform schemes, failed Accountable Care Organizations like OneCareVT and the recently abandoned AHEAD model, and misguided reports from pricey consultants, amounting together to many tens of millions of wasted dollars that in a rational system could have been used to provide actual healthcare. 
Instead of moving towards community-based care, we are left with just a few dominant large hospital systems. Now that some hospitals are stressed and failing, local communities are left underserved and are instructed to tighten their belts and make do with less.
The solution is not imposing austerity and managing the carcass of a healthcare system, but recognizing the band-aids are not enough and insisting on a much better way. Rather than trying to overwork and underpay our healthcare workers, and attempting to cut our way to a less costly system, we need to protect our healthcare dollars from insurance companies, enormous non-profit hospitals and private equity firms that skim millions from the system and rob people and communities of the funds that could otherwise be going toward real care.
While there may be generous donors willing to contribute to save the Brattleboro birthing center, we can’t just fundraise our way out of systemic crises. We should not have to hold bake sales to have dignified healthcare in the richest country in the history of this planet. Delivering healthcare should be the responsibility of our government, funded by our tax dollars.
It’s time to stop viewing healthcare as a product to be sold, to recognize healthcare as a common good and demand it as a human right. We need to insist on a system that is designed to include, rather than exclude, people who need care. The powers that be keep telling us that we can’t do any better than this, when the truth is we can’t do much worse. We can and must aim higher. Let’s come together to demand an equitable, transparent, accountable and accessible system.

READ MORE

As we enter election season in Vermont, it is clear that we need healthcare champions who are willing to do more than offer vague, empty platitudes about favoring healthcare for all. We need leaders who are committed to working toward what we deserve and need: a publicly funded universal healthcare system. 
The inspiring upwelling of energy that is arising to save the BMH birthing center must now also be directed toward demanding a system that puts people first. Instead of accepting a few crumbs from the healthcare table and hoping to call that a victory, we need to rise collectively to insist on the full meal. Only then will we get the kind of healthcare that each one of us absolutely deserves and needs.

title: Democratic Socialists of America wants to abolish the U.S. Senate. Bernie Sanders says ‘No.’
description:
Democrats across the caucus dismissed the idea of restructuring Congress. Even U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who’s long called himself a democratic socialist, isn’t on board with the proposal.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Democratic Socialists of America wants to abolish the U.S. Senate. Bernie Sanders says ‘No.’.
text:
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., leaves a meeting for Senate Democrats at the Capitol in Washington, in Nov. 2025. Photo by J. Scott Applewhite/AP

This story by Igor Bobic was first published in NOTUS on Aug. 2, 2026.
Democratic Socialists of America, a group that’s gaining momentum across the country, is pushing to scrap the U.S. Senate and replace it with a unicameral legislature. Senate Democrats aren’t on board.
“It’s in the Constitution, and it is a critical component of the United States government to pass legislation with the House,” U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Arizona, told NOTUS. “In my view, that is not a serious recommendation.”
“I don’t even know what they mean by that. I don’t have any idea,” added a befuddled Massachusetts Democratic U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren.
Even Vermont’s U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who’s long called himself a democratic socialist, isn’t on board with the proposal.
“No,” Sanders told NOTUS. He declined to elaborate, saying he had a flight to catch.
The DSA’s new platform, unveiled earlier this month, calls for expanding the social safety net and making sweeping changes to the federal government. Those include abolishing the Senate, the presidency and the Supreme Court. Those institutions would be replaced with an “executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress,” as well as an expanded House of Representatives with multiple political parties instead of the current two-party system. Those ideas would require approving an amendment to the U.S. Constitution, a major hurdle in a polarized political environment.
“The Senate is a very undemocratic institution,” Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, said in an interview on C-SPAN. “I talked a bit about democracy, a small ‘d’ democracy, and that’s really important to us. We want democratic representation of all people who live in this country.”
The DSA platform, titled “Workers Deserve More,” has drawn attacks and ridicule from top Republicans who are seeking to tie some of its controversial ideas, such as abolishing the police, to the Democratic Party and its candidates ahead of November’s midterm elections. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist and front-runner in the Wisconsin governor’s Democratic primary race, for example, is facing questions about the platform and her past comments calling to abolish the police.
“I do not support the full platform of the national DSA, and I am not endorsed by DSA national. What democratic socialism is, is a form of government that puts working-class people first,” Hong said in a debate last week, backing away from a 2020 social media post in which she called to abolish the police.
Some Democrats believe their party isn’t doing enough to marginalize the democratic socialist movement, which recently claimed victories in local and congressional races in New York, Pennsylvania, Colorado and Washington, D.C. According to a recent CNN poll, about a third of Democrats now identify as democratic socialists.
“These people sat in a room and said, ‘How much crazy shit can we cram into a platform?’ Like, ‘Yeah, abolish the Senate? Sure, why not. Hey, abolish the presidency? Yeah, sure, why not?’ That’s crazy shit,” Pennsylvania U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, who has broken with fellow Democrats on several key issues, told NOTUS. “I’m unique, I’m the only Democrat that will call it out.”
But other Democrats downplayed the rise of DSA, arguing that most people who consider themselves to be far-left progressives ascribe to more popular ideas like taxing the rich and providing universal healthcare.
“I know people in Richmond who align with DSA who don’t want to abolish the Senate,” said Virginia U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine. “They don’t want to abolish the presidency. If you ask them, ‘Why are you DSA?’ they will say, ‘I’m a Democrat, but I like DSA because I don’t like the concentration of wealth.’”
New Jersey U.S. Sen. Cory Booker, a Democrat, said his constituents are more concerned about their economic situation and having healthcare rather than “proposing things that would require a constitutional amendment,” which he called “farcical at this point.”
Still, Booker, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, said he did support other structural reforms such as granting statehood to Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, as well as changing equal state apportionment, which gives every state two senators, no matter its population.
“The Senate does have things that our founders never imagined, like the fact that North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming, Idaho and Montana have 10 senators and they have less population than Los Angeles County, and that’s really problematic,” Booker said. “But there are things that really focus on the real issues of people that we can get done here, that I think we should be organizing around.”
Georgia Democratic U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, meanwhile, argued that voter frustration with how the Senate operates could be addressed if its members stood up for the system of checks and balances as laid out in the U.S. Constitution.
“I think that we need to do something about a supine Senate. There’s a lot of madness happening right now in the White House that this body could do something to address if there was any courage,” Warnock said, before adding, “If my Republican colleagues had any moral courage.”

title: NC Governor Stein voices reservations about hemp bill
description: Governor Josh Stein said Tuesday it is “premature” to say if he will sign House Bill 328, legislation that would ban intoxicating hemp products in the state. Stein, a Democrat, has long called on state lawmakers to ban the sale of intoxicating hemp products to anyone under 21. H328 would go a step beyond that, […]
text:
Governor Josh Stein explains his reservations about House Bill 328 following an August 4, 2026 N.C. Council of State meeting. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) Governor Josh Stein said Tuesday it is “premature” to say if he will sign House Bill 328, legislation that would ban intoxicating hemp products in the state.
Stein, a Democrat, has long called on state lawmakers to ban the sale of intoxicating hemp products to anyone under 21. H328 would go a step beyond that, banning their sale to anyone.
Hemp business owners who gathered at the General Assembly Tuesday to voice their opposition to H328 say the bill would amount to a near ban on all hemp products, harming what advocates say has grown into a $4 billion industry.
As law enforcement backs a hemp ban, protestors push NC lawmakers to vote no

Stein told reporters after the North Carolina Council of State meeting that while he is supportive of the hemp industry, he must also weigh if the bill appropriately addresses public health and public safety.
Stein agrees the current marketplace offers no consumer protection for kids or adults (21 and over) who choose to use these products. He said he supports a well-regulated THC market for adults, so they know exactly what they are buying and know what the ingredients are.
Stein said while the majority of the bill is intended to promote public safety, he has reservations about allowing the sale of kratom to people 21 and over.
“If you take a lot of it, it will act as an opioid. It is commonly called on the street ‘gas station heroin.’ This bill legalizes that in North Carolina,” said Stein.
The bill makes a distinction between natural kratom and synthetic kratom. Natural kratom would be legal to sell to adults, but  synthetic kratom would be classified as a controlled substance and not legal for sale to anyone.
Chuck Spahos, general counsel to the North Carolina Conference of District Attorneys, said the bill does define kratom for the first time in state statute.
“It does not legalize kratom, but it does define it, so that it also can define synthetic kratom products,” said Spahos. “It does not legalize a substance that you can’t go buy right now.”
Stein views the language of the bill differently. He also says it doesn’t include a strict requirement for sellers of kratom or hemp products to check every purchaser’s ID before sale, as is required for the sale of alcohol or cigarettes. 
“We need to completely protect kids. That is not happening with the law today. Unfortunately, that bill that the legislature is thinking about doesn’t get us there,” Stein said.

title: State-employed physician associate accused of having sex with prison-inmate patient
description: Iowa regulators have issued an emergency order suspending the license of a physician associate who was accused of having sex with a prison-inmate patient while working for the Iowa Department of Corrections. The Iowa Board of Physician Associates has charged Kyle L. Parks with unethical conduct, an offense the board describes as including verbally or […]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing is responsible for overseeing Iowa's licensing boards. (Photo illustration via Getty Images; logo courtesy of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing) Iowa regulators have issued an emergency order suspending the license of a physician associate who was accused of having sex with a prison-inmate patient while working for the Iowa Department of Corrections.
The Iowa Board of Physician Associates has charged Kyle L. Parks with unethical conduct, an offense the board describes as including verbally or physically abusing a patient and improper sexual contact with a patient.
The board alleges it has investigated complaints related to Parks’ conduct in his practice as a physician associate and concluded that Parks had an improper sexual relationship with a patient who was an inmate at the Iowa Medical and Classification Center where Parks worked at the time.
The board has opted not to publicly disclose when the alleged conduct took place.
In choosing to impose an emergency suspension of Parks’ license while the disciplinary charge is pending, the board stated “there is credible information to demonstrate that (Parks) had an inappropriate sexual relationship with a patient” and that “the matter has been sufficiently investigated to ensure the board is proceeding on the basis of reliable information.”
The board also said it had concluded that “the circumstances which pose immediate danger to the public are continuing,” and that the immediate suspension of Parks’ license is “necessary to protect the public health, safety, or welfare until this case is resolved.”
A board hearing on the matter is scheduled for Sept. 9, 2026.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Parks for comment.
State employment records show Parks worked for the Iowa Department of Corrections from 2008 until sometime in 2025 when he was separated from employment. His annual salary in 2025 was reported to be $134,256.

text:
The Itasca County Courthouse and offices in Grand Rapids. (Photo courtesy of KAXE)Reprinted with permission from KAXE.
GRAND RAPIDS — An Itasca County judge heeded the requests of both the prosecution and defense by granting a lighter sentence Monday, Aug. 3, for a rural Grand Rapids woman who pleaded guilty to felony criminal vehicular homicide.


Cynthia “Cyndy” Martin, a well known northern Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor activist, was sentenced to 364 days in the Itasca County Jail for leaving the scene the night of July 3, 2024, after she struck a 19-year-old pedestrian on Highway 169 near Nashwauk.
Martin must also spend each Fourth of July holiday in jail during her five-year probation period, complete 100 hours of community service, pay a $1,085 fine and comply with several other conditions of probation upon release.
Judge Heidi Chandler explained to about 45 people in attendance how she reached her decision to grant a downward dispositional departure, or less than the recommended sentence. She said Martin has shown remorse and accepted responsibility for her actions that led to Carter Haithcock’s death, is particularly amenable to complying with probation and has broad support of friends and family.
Ahead of Monday’s hearing, Martin’s defense team submitted 38 letters of support that attested to her selfless and kind character, her volunteerism and strong work ethic, and her commitment to the community.
Chandler acknowledged Martin has struggled immensely because of her actions in this case, but not before addressing the extreme hardships faced by the victim’s family.
“Nothing that can happen out of this courtroom will ever bring Carter back,” Chandler said. “I don’t know what the right word is for Carter’s family. … I truly feel for you. I have lost family members, but not in the way you have. … He was a young man with a lot of life ahead of him.”
Chandler made the ruling at the end of an emotional hearing in a courtroom filled with the families and supporters of both Martin and Haithcock. Many cried throughout the proceedings.
John Haithcock Jr. spoke of his family’s loss while making a victim impact statement about his son, a 2023 Nashwauk High School graduate and young father who worked at Yanmar.
“There are three other parents whose lives are destroyed. He had 14 nieces and nephews who don’t understand,” Haithcock Jr. said. “ … He has a son growing up without a father, whose life is also destroyed.”
Haithcock Jr. expressed frustration with Martin’s plea deal, noting Minnesota Sentencing Guidelines call for a four-year prison sentence for someone like Martin, with no criminal history. He suggested she was getting a “slap on the wrist” because of her political affiliation.
“That’s what the guidelines are for,” Haithcock Jr. said. “ … Try her like you try everybody.”
Assistant County Attorney Courtney Beck described the unusual circumstances of the case, which was heavily scrutinized because of Martin’s volunteer roles in local political party leadership. Martin was the chair of the 8th Congressional District DFL Party and vice-chair of the Itasca County DFL Party. Martin resigned from those positions in December 2025, shortly after reporting from the Reformer highlighted a split in party support.
Beck said Martin was put to trial through social media, and both prosecutors and law enforcement received an extreme number of tips and letters calling her a murderer, accusing her of being intoxicated and demanding her imprisonment. She said none of these claims reflect the evidence the state actually possesses.
“She did not intend to hit Mr. Haithcock,” Beck said. “Ms. Martin did stop for 25 seconds, but she failed to investigate. If she had done so, we wouldn’t be sitting here today. A tragic accident became a criminal matter.”
Beck outlined each of the reasons the state agreed to Martin’s deal to plead guilty and why it also agreed Martin should receive a lighter sentence than usual. Defense Attorney Derek Hansen thanked Beck for explaining the sentencing guidelines and the reasons judges may depart from them.
“Nobody is going to walk out of his courtroom feeling like they won,” Hansen said.
He said Martin had unequivocally accepted responsibility at the time of her plea hearing and described a woman whose life was turned upside down by the collision. He said Martin had attempted to take her own life on one or two occasions since.
Martin choked back tears as she read a prepared statement expressing her sincere condolences and apologizing to Haithcock’s family.
“I think of Carter all the time,” Martin said. “Not only was a life lost, but a family was forever changed.”
Martin described her grief and shame, saying she’s been forced to confront the consequences of her actions.
“I should have stopped. I should have done more. I deeply regret that decision,” she said. “ … I understand my suffering does not compare to the suffering of Carter’s family. I am so, truly sorry. If I could change what happened, I would do it immediately.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC utility regulators set January deadline for decision on Dominion, NextEra merger
description: South Carolina regulators are expected to make a decision inside of the next six months on whether to approve a utility mega merger.
text:
Dominion Energy is headquartered in Richmond, Virginia. (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce for The Virginia Mercury)COLUMBIA — South Carolina regulators are expected to make a decision within six months on whether to approve a utility mega merger valued at $67 billion.
The state Public Service Commission voted unanimously Tuesday to adopt a regulatory schedule proposed by Florida-based NextEra Energy and Virginia-headquartered Dominion Energy, setting a Jan. 29, 2027, deadline for a final determination on the merits of a merger and potential impacts on the 820,000 customers it serves across the Lowcountry and Midlands.
If approved, the newly combined company would serve a total of 10 million customers across four of the nation’s fastest-growing states — Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina and Virginia. The companies hope to close the deal sometime in the second half of 2027.
Dominion Energy, NextEra seek to merge, creating world’s largest electric utility

Commissioners in South Carolina’s capital approved the timeline without comment Tuesday after delaying its decision by a week to give members more time to think it over.
The timeline can still change. Participants can ask the commission to alter the schedule as needed.
“This schedule provides all parties with adequate opportunity to meaningfully participate in this proceeding,” Commissioner Delton Powers said in his motion, noting South Carolina’s utility watchdog had agreed to the timeline.
So did House Speaker Murrell Smith and Senate President Thomas Alexander, who filed petitions two weeks ago asking to be part of the proceedings.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In letters to the commission, whose members are elected by the General Assembly, the Sumter and Walhalla Republicans cited the large number of South Carolinians potentially impacted. Both said in the July 21 filings they don’t have a position for or against the merger but don’t oppose the utilities’ proposed timeline.
Alexander declined to comment further Tuesday, citing the ongoing regulatory procedures.
Smith was traveling overseas and not immediately available to respond to questions submitted by the SC Daily Gazette.
Consumer and environmental groups criticized the involvement of the Legislature’s top GOP leaders, saying the politicians were putting their fingers on the scale in favor of utilities.
It’s not the first time a state House speaker has gotten involved in Public Service Commission proceedings.
In 2017 and 2018, when Dominion was in the process of buying out bankrupt SCANA Corp. following the state’s failed nuclear expansion at VC Summer nuclear site, then-Speaker Jay Lucas filed a similar petition.
Here’s how much SC power customers are still paying for a failed nuclear project

That was also a much different situation. The state still had direct skin in the game, as the partially built reactors were jointly owned by SCANA and state-owned utility Santee Cooper.
While the potential deal between Dominion and NextEra is massive, it is unclear what makes this merger rise to the same level as the fallout from the failed nuclear project so as to warrant legislative involvement.
On the same day utility regulators met, state business, utility and government leaders gathered in Columbia to talk about South Carolina’s energy needs during a summit hosted by the state’s joint manufacturing and chamber of commerce organization.
Sen. Tom Davis told the SC Daily Gazette he did not know the exact reason behind leaderships’ decision to participate.
“If it’s so the Legislature is better informed about what occurs, I think that’s a helpful thing,” the Beaufort Republican said. “And I think that probably is the intent.”
But Davis, who has led legislative efforts related to energy in the state, also said he would not want to see any interference or influence on the commission’s process, “because they’re the ones that have been delegated this power to make these decisions.”
This is not NextEra’s first foray into South Carolina. The company also tried and failed to buy Santee Cooper in the wake of the failed V.C. Summer nuclear expansion.
The Dominion deal, as proposed, would take place through a stock swap — eight-tenths of a share of NextEra’s stock for each outstanding share of Dominion — so NextEra shareholders would own about 75% of the combined company.
“This is a combination centered on customers, communities and employees. It preserves the Dominion Energy utilities our customers know — the same local leaders, employees, regulatory oversight and commitment to an all-of-the-above energy mix — while adding capabilities that can help us build needed infrastructure more efficiently and keep bills affordable,” Dominion CEO Robert Blue said in a statement following the filing with the Public Service Commission last month.
Dominion will maintain its Virginia headquarters, as well as its South Carolina offices, and customers across Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina would see a total $2.25 billion in discounts on their monthly bills over two years, according to a joint statement by the companies.
South Carolina’s Public Service Commission is far from the only agency that must sign off on the proposed merger of $67 billion in stocks.
The two utilities also need approvals from the Virginia State Corporation Commission, the North Carolina Utilities Commission, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The deal also is subject to antitrust oversight by the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice.
But South Carolina could end up the first to weigh in from a utility regulations standpoint.
Virginia law requires its state utility regulators to make a decision within six months of a company filing. (Dominion and NextEra filed on July 15.) But some Virginia lawmakers have sought to extend that.
The Virginia House tried to add a clause to the state budget giving themselves the ability to weigh in. And last month, two Republican legislators wrote the governor asking her to call a special legislative session to extend the time limit.
Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi last month also urged the commissioners to more closely scrutinize the planned merger.
If the commonwealth’s leaders don’t act, Virginia’s decision could still come down two weeks ahead of the Palmetto State’s.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida’s no-children-at-drag shows law upheld by federal appeals court
description: A federal appeals court has upheld a Florida law banning children from attending drag shows, a measure put in place with the support of Gov. Ron DeSantis. In an 8-5 opinion handed down Tuesday, the majority ruled the law was constitutional, while those on the dissenting side criticized the measure as overreach. “The act is […]
text:
Rose Duvall performing at Drag Brunch of Bay County Florida on Sunday April 26th 2026 (Photo credit:  Kassy Byrd)A federal appeals court has upheld a Florida law banning children from attending drag shows, a measure put in place with the support of Gov. Ron DeSantis.
In an 8-5 opinion handed down Tuesday, the majority ruled the law was constitutional, while those on the dissenting side criticized the measure as overreach.
“The act is a straight forward regulation of obscenity,” wrote Judge Andrew Brasher, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, on behalf of the majority. “Preventing children from attending adult live performances obscene for them is rationally related to Florida’s interest in safeguarding the well-being of minors.”
DeSantis posted on X that “this shouldn’t even be controversial, yet our law protecting kids required to fend off lawsuits and win a case before a divided appellate court.”
The Legislature in 2023 passed SB 1438, the “Protection of Children Act.” 
The law threatens fines, loss of operating licenses, and criminal penalties against any venues that expose any “child” to “lewd” performances, even if the child has parental consent.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Dissenting opinions
Hamburger Mary’s is a chain restaurant with locations across the nation including in Florida. The restaurant’s Orlando location (which closed in 2024) hosted drag shows including “family friendly” performances to which children were invited. Its parent company filed the underlying lawsuit seeking to bar DeSantis from enforcing the law.
Judge Robin Rosenbaum issued a scathing 27-page page dissenting opinion criticizing the majority for upholding the statute, which she described as wielding a “Titanic-sized iceberg of chilling power” against freedom of speech.
“Today our Court embraces mess-around-and-find-out (“MAFO”) First Amendment jurisprudence. Under this form of jurisprudence, a citizen can learn whether a law prohibits their speech only by taking a wild guess, presenting their speech, and then seeing if they get arrested and face imprisonment, thousands of dollars in fines, and loss of their business license,” she wrote.
“And it doesn’t tolerate statutes that create prosecutorial skeleton keys allowing “policemen, judges, and juries” to unlock penalties and punish speech on “an ad hoc and subjective basis. Yet today we endorse [the law] even though it’s a MAFO statute that does all these unconstitutional things.”
Rosenbaum, appointed by former President Barack Obama, also took aim at the majority for weighing in on the availability of universal injunctions in overbreadth cases. In her opinion, Rosenberg said it “should go without saying, of course,” that the court shouldn’t consider the scope of an injunction it isn’t upholding.”
Rosenberg wasn’t the only judge to dissent with an opinion.
Judge Nancy Abudu concurred with Rosenberg’s lengthy dissenting opinion but drafted her own focusing on what she said was the growing tendency of judges “as demonstrated in the majority’s opinion” to ignore legislative history in their analyses of state laws.
Rep. Randy Fine introduces HB 1423 while several drag queens sit behind him. Credit: Screenshot/Florida Channel
“Legislative history is not a competing authority to statutory text, but a source of context that can illuminate statutory purpose, help reveal and resolve interpretive ambiguities, and guard against selective or contextual readings that distort legislative design,” he wrote in her nine-page dissent.
Abudu noted that a review of the legislative history shows that both DeSantis and bill sponsor then Rep. Randy Fine had espoused “anti-drag motivations that precipitated the Act’s introduction, debate and passage.”
A review of the legislative history also, she said, showed the state understood the law was vague and “would lead to uncertainty for Hamburger Mary’s and similar establishments, thereby chilling protected as well as unprotected expression.”
An analysis for the bill prepared by the legislative staff cautions the bill’s “indeterminate scope could lead venues to cancel performances based on a justified fear of prosecution simply for engaging in otherwise lawful behavior. That concern goes to the heart of Hamburger Mary’s challenge: the Act’s ambiguity does not merely create difficult line-drawing questions; it encourages speakers to selfcensor,” Agudu wrote.
A three-year legal journey
Following passage of the law in 2023, Hamburger Mary’s sued the state alleging the law violated its free speech and was vague, and sought an injunction, which  U.S. District Judge Gregory Presnell granted.
The state appealed to a three-judge U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit panel, which affirmed the lower court decision in a 2-1 opinion.  
The DeSantis administration appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking it to reinstate the law pending the legal challenges, but the justices declined to do so in a 6-3 ruling, with justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch dissenting
The case wound up back before the 11th Circuit, which agreed to hear it en banc, with all circuit judges participating.
“After additional briefing and with the benefit of oral argument, we are convinced the district court erred in preliminarily enjoining the enforcement of the Act,” a majority of the court opined.

title: Report: State probing overdoses at Morgan County prison
description: The Tennessee Department of Correction is believed to be investigating a series of overdoses at the Morgan County prison, based on reports from other media outlets. A spokesperson for the state declined to confirm the overdoses, saying only that the department doesn’t allow drugs in prisons and uses several methods to prevent illicit substances from […]
text:
According to reports from media outlets, the Tennesee Department of Correction is investigating a series of overdoses at the state's prison in Morgan County. (Photo: Tennessee Department of Correction) The Tennessee Department of Correction is believed to be investigating a series of overdoses at the Morgan County prison, based on reports from other media outlets.
A spokesperson for the state declined to confirm the overdoses, saying only that the department doesn’t allow drugs in prisons and uses several methods to prevent illicit substances from being smuggled into prisons. But WBIR reported obtaining an employee’s 911 call from the correctional complex last week in which two to three ambulances were requested for “multiple overdoses” at the prison. The employee told dispatchers he thought the overdoses involved a synthetic form of marijuana called K2 and that and said staff administered Narcan to several inmates, according to the report.
Asked about the reported overdoses, a Department of Correction spokesperson issued a statement saying the state is investigating an incident that occurred at the Morgan County prison last week.
“TDOC maintains a zero-tolerance policy for contraband and remains committed to aggressively preventing its entry into our facilities. Through routine searches, intelligence-led operations, and collaboration with our law enforcement partners, we continually work to identify, intercept, and remove contraband while protecting the safety of our staff and those in our custody.”
Correction officials also told WBIR that no staff members were hurt in the incident.
The investigation comes about six months after an inmate allegedly killed officer Dustin Pedigo. Reginald Steed is under indictment on a first-degree murder charge and moved to Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Faulty locks on prison cell doors were blamed.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT groups will receive $3.1M to help prevent gun violence
description: The goal is to identify root causes of gun violence, build trust with the community and intervene before violence occurs.
text:
The Connecticut Department of Public Health is funding 33 organizations statewide to prevent gun violence.
Groups operating in and around Bridgeport, Hartford, New London, New Haven, Stamford and Waterbury are set to receive $3.1 million to pay for mentoring and afterschool programs, hospital-based violence intervention programs and street outreach. The goal is to identify root causes of gun violence, build trust with the community and intervene before violence occurs.
The state will distribute the money through agreements with five of the cities, and with the Ledge Light Health District, which will focus on the New London area.
“Gun violence is a public health crisis, and addressing it requires the same coordinated, community-driven approach we use for any public health threat,” DPH Commissioner Dr. Manisha Juthani said in a statement. “These agreements put resources directly into the hands of the communities and organizations that know their neighborhoods best.”
Connecticut had the sixth lowest gun death rate in the country in 2023 according to data from Johns Hopkins University. But firearms were the third leading cause of death in the 1-17 age group from 2019 to 2023. Overall, the gun death rate increased by 24% from 2014 to 2023.
[RELATED: CT sues Trump administration, again, over withheld school mental health grants]
Recipients of the DPH grants are engaged in an array of violence-prevention initiatives.
The local Police Athletic League in Waterbury will use the grant money to provide recreational and educational activities to youth, as well as emergency services for victims of violence.
In the Stamford area, Hoops4All will provide life skills, conflict resolution and leadership development sessions.
In the Hartford region, the Justice Education Center will host weekly midnight basketball games. An organization called the AASAASKA Foundation will provide apprenticeships in urban farming and beekeeping.
COMPASS Youth Collaborative will offer case management, mental health services and career preparation to gunshot victims.
Another organization, 4-CT, will offer direct cash assistance to victims of violence.
“Recipients have used these funds to secure housing, cover lost wages, reconnect with family, and build the stability and peace of mind needed to move forward,” said Sarah Blanton, CEO of 4-CT. “Research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also shows that reducing financial stress can lower the risk of violence and suicide.”
Blanton said that 4-CT recently signed a $104,000 contract with the city of Waterbury and a $40,000 contract with the city of New Haven for DPH grant funding, and is awaiting a contract with the city of Hartford.
The organization currently works in Hartford through the Connecticut Children’s Violence Intervention Program. Its direct cash payments have been used as a tool to support families impacted by violence in Hartford for years now, Blanton said.
This story was first published Aug. 4, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

title: US House Ethics starts probe of abuse allegations against Ohio Rep. Max Miller at his request
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. House Ethics Committee announced Tuesday that it will review allegations that Republican Rep. Max Miller of Ohio may have “engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use.” The announcement came shortly after Miller said on X earlier Tuesday he was planning on filing paperwork requesting that the committee investigate him, as he has “nothing to hide” and wants to “clear (his) name from these horrific attacks” on him and his family.  “We will be providing the committee all necessary documents needed for a detail(ed) examination,” he wrote. “The accusations continue to change, but my facts stay the same. I am looking forward to my colleagues reading everything for themselves.”The second-term lawmaker is facing intense public scrutiny over allegations that he abused his ex-wife, who is the daughter of fellow Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, and the couple’s 2-year-old daughter. Miller strongly denies the allegations. In a statement Sunday, his former father-in-law said Miller “needs serious psychological help” and should not serve in Congress.After filing for divorce from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, in 2024, Miller has been embroiled in divorce proceedings and a custody battle over their child. The allegations have been public for several months. But in July, the magazine Mother Jones reported on court documents in which Moreno told police detectives investigating their daughter’s broken collarbone that he was abusive and may have been responsible for the injury. According to the report, Moreno said that Miller had thrown scalding water from a pan at her, pushed her and pointed a gun at her head during an argument. ‘Total and complete depravity’Speaking to reporters in Washington Tuesday, Bernie Moreno said his daughter Emily “lives in constant fear” of Miller, CBS News reported. “Deeply in her heart, she fears what this guy is capable of,” he said. Moreno said that he picked up his granddaughter from Miller this week at a police station so Emily Moreno didn’t have to interact with him. He said Miller wouldn’t hand over their toddler’s favorite stuffed animal, and she spent the next couple days unable to sleep. “This is the level of total and complete depravity,” he said. The remarks came after Moreno spoke publicly about his former son-in-law for the first time on Sunday, issuing a scathing indictment of Miller, who he described as a danger to his daughter who should not be serving in Congress. Miller is currently running for reelection in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District. Moreno has received criticism of his own — including from Miller — for not publicly addressing the allegations sooner. Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Moreno said his daughter had explicitly asked him to turn down the temperature and avoid drawing attention. But since rising again in mid-July, the attention on Miller has reached a fever pitch as the allegations mounted.Miller has been vocal about it on his social media pages. He hosted a 20-minute livestream on X in which he defended himself from the allegations and announced he had no intention of dropping his reelection bid. He also released a DropBox page containing scores of documents he said were proof against the allegations. But some of those documents contained deeply personal information, including sensitive photos of the child, Politico reported Tuesday. A lawyer for Miller has taken responsibility for the inadvertent inclusion of the photos in the documents, Politico reported, and has apologized to Emily Moreno. In his remarks to reporters, Bernie Moreno said he believes the publication of the photo is a felony, and anyone that touched it or transmitted it electronically should be jailed. “Now you have hundreds of thousands of psychotic human beings that have that,” he said. “To say, ‘Oops’ is grotesque.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico state veterinarian says more screwworm cases ‘headed this way’
description: While no new cases of New World screwworm have been detected in New Mexico for more than a month, the parasitic fly “definitely is headed this way,” and a widespread infection would quickly exhaust the state’s resources, the state’s top veterinarian told state lawmakers Tuesday.
text:
New Mexico’s state veterinarian outlined her office’s plans to address a potential outbreak of New World screwworm, pictured above, in a presentation to state legislators on Aug. 4, 2026. (Courtesy USDA)While no new cases of New World screwworm have been detected in New Mexico for more than a month, the parasitic fly “definitely is headed this way,” and a widespread infection would quickly exhaust the state’s resources, the state’s top veterinarian told state lawmakers Tuesday.
Samantha Holeck, state veterinarian with the New Mexico Livestock Board, told legislators that the state is urgently finalizing a program that would increase the number of certified livestock inspectors to help private veterinarians, along with state and federal officials, contain a screwworm outbreak.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The pest, which has advanced rapidly through Mexico after being mainly contained in Central America for several decades, is named for the maggot’s behavior of feeding on live tissue. The fly made its first new incursion to the United States in early June, when it was detected in a south Texas calf, and then officials identified a separate infection in a Lea County dog in New Mexico a few days later. 
Since then, the number of cases has increased in Texas and in Mexican states along the U.S.-Mexico border. As of Monday, Texas tallied 43 total infections, including eight new cases. Chihuahua, which borders New Mexico, has 57 cases, a case count Holeck said has “risen rather quickly.” 
As a result of those spikes in cases, Hoseck said more infections in New Mexico are inevitable. 
“We’ll have much more than just a single isolated case,” she said. 
The infestation of maggots causes severe wounds that can result in injury and deaths of pets, wildlife, livestock and — in rare cases — people. The risks to livestock, especially in the eastern part of the state where cattle operations are most concentrated, have state officials most worried, Holeck told lawmakers on the interim Federal Funding Stabilization and Affordability Subcommittee.
The lack of federal support adds to her concern, she said. The United States Agriculture Department currently employs three federal field veterinarians for the whole state, she said, following widespread cuts to the department last year. 
While the USDA is rapidly trying to hire new staff in New Mexico and along the U.S.-Mexico border, Hoseck said that process could take up to four more months. The state, which also has only three field veterinarians, will likely have to recruit private veterinarians if the screwworm outbreak worsens. 
New Mexico reports first New World screwworm case in Lea County dog

“If it becomes much more prevalent here, similar to what’s going on in Texas, even our accredited veterinarians will be tapped out fairly quickly,” she said. “Imagine if this gets into the east side of the state, into our very concentrated dairy population. It’s going to be a challenge, significantly.”
The state is finalizing curriculum to certify additional inspectors, she said, through a one-day course in which students will conduct “nose-to-tail” inspections of cattle and also learn about the biology of the fly. Texas launched a similar program in early June. The free, online course grants recipients the authority to certify that animals are safe to be transported, among other duties. 
Hesock said launching a similar program in New Mexico is “critical.”
“If the outbreak expands here, then we can activate additional individuals to help maintain the continuity of business for the livestock industry in New Mexico,” she said.

name: National
title: AG nominee tells faith leaders he will take action to restrict abortion drug access
description: Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche is one step closer to confirmation after the Republican Judiciary Committee voted to advance his appointment on a party-line vote on Tuesday, and based on promises he made to faith leaders around the country last week, that means national anti-abortion actions may be one step closer as well. In […]
text:
Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, whose nomination advanced in the Senate on Tuesday, told faith leaders in a call on July 30 that he would take action to restrict mail-order access to abortion medication. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche is one step closer to confirmation after the Republican Judiciary Committee voted to advance his appointment on a party-line vote on Tuesday, and based on promises he made to faith leaders around the country last week, that means national anti-abortion actions may be one step closer as well.
In a conference call hosted by the White House Faith Office on July 30 with thousands of religious leaders around the country, Blanche said he was committed to achieving policy solutions so that the U.S. Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision “becomes permanent in every single state.”
A recording of the call was publicly available on YouTube as of Tuesday, posted by Intercessors of America, a religious group in Virginia.
US Supreme Court rules telehealth abortion can resume while lawsuit continues

Blanche told the participants he is working “hand in hand” with U.S. Health and Human Services, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and President Donald Trump’s White House team to fulfill those goals.
His comments come amid ongoing attempts to restrict access to mifepristone, one of two drugs approved by the FDA to terminate early pregnancies and to treat miscarriages. The state of Louisiana sued the FDA in October seeking to rescind a 2023 rule that allowed mifepristone to be dispensed without a visit to a provider in person. That rule has allowed people in states with abortion bans to order the pills by mail through telehealth visits with providers in states that don’t have bans.
The FDA has said it is conducting a safety review of mifepristone that won’t be ready until at least December.
“If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that and they can’t do things like they’re doing with mail-order drugs,” Blanche said on the faith call.
Health care providers who support abortion care have said they intend to keep prescribing misoprostol, the other drug used to end a pregnancy or treat miscarriages, even if mifepristone is restricted.
But anti-abortion activists and others have also called on the Trump administration to enforce the Comstock Act, a long-dormant law passed in 1873 that restricted the mailing of “obscene” materials. The law includes language prohibiting mailing anything “designed, adapted, or intended for preventing conception or producing abortion.” If that law were to be enforced, it could bar access to the mailing of both medications.
Blanche did not mention the Comstock Act in the call, but the administration has been pressured by anti-abortion groups to do more.
Blanche said the process of achieving his goals takes a lot of time, but he assured the faith leaders it will happen.
“We don’t have complete victory yet, but we will have victory, and victory will be soon and it will be permanent,” he said.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.
