name: WyoFile
title: Ann and Al Simpson were each other’s ‘greatest champions’
description:
Their 70 years of marriage were defined by appreciating what each brought to the table, writes columnist Kerry Drake.
The post Ann and Al Simpson were each other’s ‘greatest champions’ appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Several photographs accompanied articles about the death of Ann Simpson last week that aptly illustrated the love between her and her husband of 70 years, the late U.S. Sen. Al Simpson. 

Opinion

That includes one of them smooching in their later years, with the senator looking like he still couldn’t believe how lucky he was.
I realize that’s probably the sentimental favorite of everyone who knew the couple. But there’s an image of Ann highlighted by WyoFile that’s even more emblematic of her courage and the devotion and love she had for him. Ann was at the senator’s funeral last year, looking elegant as always and beaming with pride that so many people in their lives honored him as he was laid to rest.
I hope Ann realized that she was being honored too, because having each other gave them their best chance at happiness in all their endeavors, including her love of the arts and advocacy for mental health. They were a team that rooted for each other, even in politically taxing times.
I didn’t know Ann well, even after covering Al’s political career for many years. But I do know how much he loved her, because it was evident every time he spoke her name or talked about what she was doing.
In 2011, Al’s press secretary and then chief of staff, Donald Hardy, wrote the appropriately titled “Shooting From the Lip” about his former boss, who could be cranky about the political scene in Washington as being too polarizing and at odds with his life in Wyoming.
Hardy’s book is a great read about a politician who frequently got into trouble for expressing views that were often unflinchingly honest but unpopular. To me, it’s a much better look at the man than the book Simpson wrote about his often combative relationship with the media, “Right in the Old Gazoo.”
But I hadn’t re-read Hardy’s book, even after Al died at age 93 last year. When I wrote a column about my relationship with the politician I admired but also shared some combative times with, I relied on the recollections and articles I’d written. My conclusion was Simpson is a “prime example of precisely what American politics are missing today.”
When I read about Ann’s death at age 94, though, I knew I had to look at Hardy’s book in a new light, because I had forgotten some great anecdotes the author recounted about her influence on Al. I offer a sample with the hope that anyone curious about the life and times of the Simpsons will check it out.
Ann Schroll entered the picture when she and Al were in high school; he in Cody and his future wife in Greybull. She was a tall cheerleader who, like her twin sister Nan, was on the lookout for tall boys.
“Back in high school, we had been on the lookout for the Simpson boys [Al and his brother Pete] at the next basketball tournament,” she told Hardy. “We spotted them, and they spotted us. Unfortunately, they didn’t know how to dance. 
“Right away we ruled them completely off our list,” Ann added.
Al copped to his failure, and listed a few more of them. “We were the ‘zit kings’ of the world,” he recalled. “I was knock-kneed and heavy. I had good hair, though — like Tony Curtis! Ann didn’t mind that, but was unimpressed once she found out I couldn’t dance.”
So Ann knew exactly what she wanted, but she didn’t realize until they started dating at the University of Wyoming that Al would endear himself in ways that earned him a second chance. 
I forgot about this entry, but once I saw “port-a-potty incident” in the index, I had to check it out. It involved the 1986 wedding of their eldest son Bill, in the far reaches of the Cody countryside, hence the need for rented portable toilets.
In the book, Al notes with laughter that Ann discovered the toilets lacked chemical deodorants, prompting behavior that didn’t match her refined image. 
“Ann, in a magnificent pink silk dress, was galloping around the outdoor toilets in her slippers, with this rich, blue deodorant elixir, which, if you spilled it, would probably eat through your epidermis,” Al said. “Quite a sight it was.”
One of the things that endeared me most to what Ann represented in Al’s life was the heavy criticism he received in 1991 for badgering law professor Anita Hill when she told a Senate panel and national TV audience that Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas had allegedly sexually harassed her.
Al was unrelenting in his hostile questioning of Hill. During the hearings, Al referred to Ann as “the most important person and the brightest guiding light” of his life.
But while it might have been easier to “stand by her man,” Ann couldn’t sit back and watch the damage without telling him what she thought.
“He was so defensive during the hearings that I finally said to him, ‘You’ve had such a great reputation here, and now you are destroying it by the way you are behaving. Why don’t you just shut up?’”
Al, Hardy wrote, was stunned: “That’s the first time you’ve ever told me to shut up.”
Ann responded, “Well, you need it.”
Al came to the same realization, but probably only because of Ann’s stinging rebuke. “I have been riding high, a bit too cocky, arrogant, yeah, too smart by half sometimes,” he later admitted at a GOP fundraiser in Cheyenne.
Except for that incident, though, I couldn’t find a single reference where Ann did not stick up for her husband, no matter how much he was getting beaten up by the press. But she knew where to draw the line.
In Ann’s obituary, she was deservedly praised for her work to promote the arts in Wyoming. She founded the Artmobile more than 30 years ago, bringing some of the art objects in the University of Wyoming’s collections to people statewide. It was named in her honor, and the Ann Simpson Artmobile was an enormous gift to Wyomingites; it won’t stop traveling with her passing.
A mental health advocate, Ann was said to be passionately involved in the Congressional Wives Mental Health Group. She was co-chair of the group and focused on legislative support for mental health issues.
The Simpsons were both highly quotable, and each one said poignant things about the longevity of their marriage and gave advice to couples, especially when they were playing matchmakers. But their daughter, Sue Simpson Gallagher, has a special insight into her parents that she expressed on June 21, 2024, on their 70th wedding anniversary.
“My parents recognize each other’s gifts,” she said. “They are appreciative of what they each bring to the table. They don’t try and be everything to each other either. They know how important it is to have friends but to have each other as their greatest champions.”

text:
Voters cast their ballots for the May 19, 2026, primary election at Fox Hollow Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner said they each will run active, statewide campaigns in their efforts to unseat incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little, who is seeking a third term. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Little, Pickens, Stegner, a Constitution Party candidate who legally changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life and Libertarian Paul Sand are all running for governor in Idaho’s Nov. 3 general election. 
“I got into this race because I think Idaho is worth fighting for, and I didn’t see anybody else willing to take up the mantle in the way that I thought it needed to be taken up,” Stegner said in a July 10 interview. 
Pickens, an attorney who owns her own business, is also optimistic about winning. Pickens described Little as an unpopular incumbent governor who has tied himself fully to President Donald Trump just as what Pickens described as a “Trump slump” is playing out across the country.
“We have built momentum, both face-to-face and also with our social media,” Pickens said July 15. “I can’t go anywhere in the state of Idaho without people recognizing me, and that is really huge for a candidate going in. We also have a wildly unpopular governor (in Little).”
Efforts to reach Little and Sand were unsuccessful. 
“It’s a hard job. It’s a thankless job in many respects,” Stegner said, of running for governor. “But I’ve also had any number of people come up to me and tell me that I’ve given them hope. And if that’s all I get to do, I would consider this candidacy a success. But I aspire to more. I aspire to be governor, and I think there’s a path to victory in the way that the team that we’ve built and the campaign that we’ve constructed is working.”
Former Idaho Supreme Court Justice John Stegner is running for governor as an independent candidate. (Photo courtesy of John Stegner)
While Stegner served as a judge for 25 years in Idaho, including as a member of the Idaho Supreme Court, this would be the first statewide elected political office. 
“Running for governor as the first political office out of the blocks is a little aspirational,” Stegener said. “I shouldn’t say a little; it’s quite aspirational to start at the top. But I think having been on the Supreme Court and having seen how government works, I have a solid understanding of how things work. And I think being governor at this juncture is an important office and an important place for somebody with my background because I sincerely believe that neither the Democrats nor the Republicans have a lock on good ideas. And as a governor, I would aspire to implement good ideas irrespective of their source.”
To do that, Stegner said he will launch a series of campaign events this summer and fall. 
“Our goal is to reach every one of the 44 counties,” Stegner said.
 Pickens says contested primary election and her unsuccessful 2022 campaign made her a stronger candidate

Pickens knows that any Democrat running for statewide office faces an uphill challenge. No Democrat has been elected governor in Idaho since 1990, when the late former Gov. Cecil Andrus won his fourth and final term. 
In 2022, Pickens ran unsuccessfully for lieutenant governor – losing to incumbent Republican Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke. 
Pickens said her experience as a candidate has helped her grow. She said her unsuccessful 2022 campaign for lieutenant governor helped her gain name recognition. And she said this spring’s contested Democratic primary for governor, which Pickens won, helped her improve as a candidate. 
Pickens said she has already campaigned across Idaho three times, held events in 30 counties and has plans to have visited all 44 counties before Election Day. 
Terri Pickens is a Democrat running for Idaho governor. (Photo courtesy of Terri Pickens)
“I will tell you that having to have an active, healthy primary was not just good for the party, but it was good for me,” Pickens said in a July 15 interview. “It taught me to be a better candidate. I got the opportunity to have three forum town hall debates with the candidates, and it allowed me to kind of fine-tune my message and get ready for what I perceive is going to be an uphill battle in the general election.”
Pickens said she doesn’t think Stegner’s independent campaign hurts her chances as the Democrat.
“I’m actually looking at this as a good thing for my campaign,” Pickens said in a July 15 interview.
Pickens said she thinks Stegner will pull Republican voters away from Little, drawing down Little’s support and making it easier for Pickens to win as a Democrat in the minority party. 
“We are jumping after different demographics,” Pickens said. “I’m going for the 18- to 30-year olds. I’m going for all of the women who are going to show up to vote for their bodily autonomy, and I’m going for every Democrat in the room.”
“I think (Stegner) is really going to pull those Republicans who would never vote for a Democrat anyway,” Pickens said. “But they’re so disappointed in Brad Little that they want 2018 Brad Little, and I think that’s what John Stegner offers them.”
 At least one Idaho candidate for governor does not plan an active political campaign

In contrast to Stegner and Pickens, the Constitution Party candidate who changed his name to Pro-Life does not plan to run an active campaign and does not think anyone will beat Little. 
“We already know who’s going to win,” Pro-Life said July 16. “We know that Brad Little’s going to be our governor and everybody else is maybe dreaming or faking that they might be able to somehow pull off a win, but it’s not going to happen.”
Pro-Life said he would agree to a debate or a town hall event with gubernatorial candidates, but he does not anticipate mounting an active campaign of his own. 
“Probably not,” said Pro-Life, who has not reported raising any campaign money this year. “I’m old and I have to work on my farm and I can’t hire labor, so I don’t think I am going to do anything.”
Instead Pro-Life said he is running to bring public accountability to political candidates and to encourage Christian morality.

Independent John Stegner: $410,332

title: Idaho AG releases list with 39 hazardous items facing federal recall, including 10 products for kids
description: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador has released a list of 39 hazardous products subject to a federal recall from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission for the month of July. text:
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 National Police Week roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C., alongside Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and other officials. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General's Office)Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador has released a list of 39 hazardous products subject to a federal recall from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission for the month of July.
The recalled products include household appliances, electronics, and furniture, and 10 items specifically designed for infants and toddlers.
“Idahoans need to know when everyday products put their families at risk,” Labrador said in a July 30 press release. “This month’s 39 recalls include ten products made for infants and toddlers, from baby loungers to dressers to pool drain covers. Check this list, check your home, and take action.”
The Consumer Product Safety Commission reports the following products were recalled in July:

Heated Sherpa Throws and Blankets Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards: The electrical cord on the recalled throws and blankets can detach and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire, burn and shock hazards.
Galanz Americas Recalls Retro Refrigerators Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards; One Death Reported: The recalled refrigerators’ internal electrical components can short circuit and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
Jake’s Fireworks Recalls World Class Fireworks “Skull Strobe” Rockets Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Explosion and Burn Hazards: The recalled fireworks rockets can explode prematurely before reaching their intended height, posing explosion and burn hazards.
Trsmima Zipline Kits and Zipline Spring Brakes Recalled Due to Fall and Collision Hazards: The zipline kit’s steel cable, turnbuckle and seat can detach or break during use, posing a fall hazard. The zipline spring brakes are not stiff enough to safely slow a rider down and the kit design does not include an emergency brake, posing collision and fall hazards.
HARPPA Recalls Nordi Toddler Tower Stools Due to Risk of Serious Injury and Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled tower stools can collapse or tip over while in use, and a child’s torso can fit through the openings on the front and back sides, posing a risk of serious injury and death due to tip over, fall and entrapment hazards.
Mangohood Direct Kids Kitchen Standing Towers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury and Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled tower stools can collapse or tip over while in use, and a child’s torso can fit through the openings on the front and back sides, posing a risk of serious injury and death due to tip over, fall and entrapment hazards.
Recall of Cpzzkq Baby Loungers Expanded Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Suffocation Hazard: The recalled baby loungers violate the mandatory safety standard for infant support cushions because the padding can obstruct an infant’s breathing, posing a serious risk of injury or deadly suffocation hazard.
Golden Link Recalls Fantastic Four Cups and Captain America Popcorn Helmet Containers with LED Lights Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Battery Ingestion Hazard: The cups and containers violate the mandatory standard for consumer products with button cell and coin batteries because they contain button cell batteries that can be accessed easily by children.
BenQ America Recalls GV31 Portable Projectors Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards: The recalled projectors’ lithium-ion battery can overheat, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
15-Drawer Dressers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Tip-Over and Entrapment Hazards: The recalled dressers are unstable if they are not anchored to the wall, posing tip-over and entrapment hazards that can result in risks of serious injuries or death to children. The dressers violate the mandatory safety standards as required by the STURDY Act.
OCOOPA Direct Recalls 1.5 Million Rechargeable Hand Warmers Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards; One Death Reported: The lithium-ion battery in the recalled hand warmers can overheat and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
Woodure Toddler Kitchen Step Stools Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury and Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled tower stools can collapse or tip over while in use, and a child’s torso can fit through the openings on the front and back sides, posing a risk of serious injury and death due to tip over, fall and entrapment hazards.
Mommy’s Baby Lovely Deluxe Baby Doll Playsets Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Choking Hazard; Violate Small Parts Ban: The recalled doll playsets violate the small parts ban because the toys are for children under three years old and some of the accessories are small parts, posing a deadly choking hazard.
5-Drawer Dressers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Tip-Over and Entrapment Hazards: The recalled dressers are unstable if they are not anchored to the wall, posing tip-over and entrapment hazards that can result in risks of serious injuries or death to children. The dressers violate the mandatory safety standards as required by the STURDY Act.
Peony Design Recalls Personalized Baby Bibs and Stroller Bags Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Choking Hazard: The snap can detach from the recalled bibs and stroller bags, posing a risk of serious injury or death from a choking hazard to young children.
12-Drawer Fabric Dressers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Tip-Over and Entrapment Hazards: The recalled dressers are unstable if they are not anchored to the wall, posing tip-over and entrapment hazards that can result in risks of serious injuries or death to children. The dressers violate the mandatory safety standards as required by the STURDY Act.
CuddleCubs Creations Teething Toy Sets Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Choking: The recalled teething toy sets contain a pull string teething toy that violates the mandatory standard for toys because the silicone strings are smaller and longer than permitted. The strings can reach the back of a child’s throat and become lodged, posing a risk of respiratory distress and a deadly choking hazard.
Sviyatp Pool Drain Covers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Drowning Hazards: The recalled drain covers violate the entrapment protection standards of the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGBA), posing deadly entrapment and drowning hazards to consumers.
OeyUoc Pool Drain Covers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Drowning Hazards: The recalled drain covers violate the entrapment protection standards of the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGBA), posing deadly entrapment and drowning hazards to consumers.
Noerishia Adult Portable Bed Rails Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Asphyxiation: The recalled bed rails violate the mandatory standard for adult portable bed rails because users can become entrapped within the bed rail or between the bed rail and the side of the mattress, posing a serious entrapment hazard and risk of death by asphyxiation. In addition, the bed rails do not bear the required hazard warning labels.
Conair Recalls Cuisinart Propel+ Four Burner 3-In-1 Gas Grills Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Laceration Hazard: The tempered glass window in the pizza oven can shatter during use, posing a risk of serious injury from laceration hazard.
Greenworks Tools Recalls 24V and 48V Kobalt Yard Power Tools with USB-C Batteries Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Fire Hazard: Charging the lithium-ion batteries through the USB-C port while the batteries are inserted in the yard power tools can cause the batteries to short-circuit, posing a risk of serious injury from fire hazard.
WonderStone Infant Walkers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fall Hazard; Violate Mandatory Standard for Infant Walkers: The recalled infant walkers violate the mandatory standard for infant walkers because they can fit through a standard doorway and fail to stop at the edge of a step, posing a risk of serious injury or death due to a fall hazard.
Best Buy Recalls Insignia® Gas Ranges Due to Risk of Serious Injury from a Fire Hazard: The recalled ranges’ front-mounted knobs can be activated accidentally by humans or pets, posing a risk of serious injury from a fire hazard.
Moodooy Bed Rails Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Asphyxiation: The recalled bed rails violate the mandatory standard for adult portable bed rails because users can become entrapped within the bed rail or between the bed rail and the side of the mattress, posing a serious entrapment hazard and risk of death by asphyxiation. In addition, the bed rails do not bear the required hazard warning labels.
Flaunt Recalls Magsafe Battery Chargers Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire and Burn Hazards: The lithium-ion battery in the recalled power banks (chargers) can overheat and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury or death from fire and burn hazards.
Biometric Gun Safes Recalled Due to Serious Injury Hazard and Risk of Death: The biometric lock on the gun safes can be opened by unauthorized users, posing a serious injury hazard and risk of death.
Rowenta Recalls Cordless Vacuum Cleaners Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Fire and Burn Hazards: The recalled lithium-ion battery in the vacuum cleaner can overheat and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury from fire and burn hazards.
Vevor Recalls Baby Loungers Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Fall Hazards: The recalled baby loungers violate the mandatory safety standard for infant sleep products. The sides are too low to contain an infant and the enclosed openings at the foot of the loungers are wider than allowed, posing serious risks of fall and entrapment hazards to infants. In addition, the baby loungers do not have a stand, posing a fall hazard if used on elevated surfaces. These violations create an unsafe sleeping environment and can cause death or serious injury.
Conair Recalls Over One Million Cuisinart Grill Brushes Due to Ingestion Hazard: Small metal wire bristles can detach from the brushes and stick to the grill or food, posing an ingestion hazard and risk of serious internal injuries that could require surgery.
Winco Fireworks International Recalls Unity 7 Shot 200 Gram Aerial Cake Fireworks Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Explosion and Burn Hazards: The recalled fireworks can tip over, posing a risk of serious injury from explosion and burn hazards.
Junpower CR2032 Lithium Coin Batteries Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Battery Ingestion Hazard: The lithium coin batteries are not sold in child-resistant packaging and do not bear the warning labels as required under Reese’s Law. When button cell or coin batteries are swallowed, the ingested batteries can cause serious injuries, including internal chemical burns and death.
AMASKY Nursing Pillows Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Suffocation: The recalled nursing pillows advertised for infant feeding and tummy time violate the mandatory safety standards for nursing pillows and infant support cushions because they can obstruct an infant’s breathing, posing a serious risk of injury or death from suffocation.
Winco Fireworks International Recalls Roman Candles 8 Shot Fireworks Due to Risk of Serious Injury from Explosion and Burn Hazards: The recalled fireworks can malfunction, and shots can blow out the side of the tube, posing a risk of serious injury from explosion and burn hazards.
Projecting LED Finger Light Toys Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Battery Ingestion: The recalled LED finger lights violate the mandatory safety standard for toys because they contain button cell batteries that can be easily accessed by children. If button cell or coin batteries are swallowed, the ingested batteries can cause serious injuries, including internal chemical burns, and death.
Cooper Lighting Recalls Metalux Optimized High Bay LED Light Fixtures Due to Fire Hazard: The LED’s board can overheat or come into contact with the lens or nearby combustible materials, posing a fire hazard.
Topyond Pool Drain Ports with Covers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Entrapment and Drowning Hazards: The recalled drain ports with covers violate the entrapment protection standards of the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act (VGBA), posing deadly entrapment and drowning hazards to consumers.
Target Recalls Gigglescape Under the Sea Popping Toy Due to Choking Hazard: The clear plastic dome can detach from the blue plastic base, making the small plastic balls inside the toy accessible to children, posing a choking hazard.
Diamond Wipes International Recalls CVS Health Medicated Hemorrhoidal Wipes Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Child Poisoning: The recalled medicated wipes contain lidocaine, which must be in child-resistant packaging, as required by the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. The packaging of the wipes is not child-resistant, posing a risk of serious injury or death from poisoning if the contents of the wipes are ingested by young children.

“If you believe you recently purchased a recalled product, stop using it, and check its recall notice,” the AG’s press release said. “Follow the notice’s instructions, including where to return the product, how to get the product fixed, how to dispose of the product, how to receive a refund for the product, or what steps must be taken to receive a replacement product.”
To file a complaint about a defective product, go to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission website.

text:
The Aug. 6, 2026 Republican primary for Tennessee governor includes U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, left; U.S. Rep. John Rose, top right; and state Rep. Monty Fritts, bottom right. (Photos: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Cookeville U.S. Rep. John Rose loaned his gubernatorial campaign an additional $4 million in the final days of the Republican primary, bringing his total in self-funding to $13 million. 
For U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn the Tennessee Freedom Fund and Team Tennessee political action committees, PACs, backing her bid have consolidated under one entity after raising a total of $12 million this cycle so far. This includes a recent donation of $250,000 from San Francisco-based artificial intelligence company Anthropic.
Anthropic’s primary product is the AI agent Claude, and with its contribution, it’s one of the top spenders backing Blackburn. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Candidates filed their final campaign finance reports to the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance on Friday, detailing their contributions and spending one week before the August 6 primary. 
Blackburn, Rose and Kingston state Rep. Monty Fritts are running for the Republican nomination to replace term-limited Gov. Bill Lee. The winner of the Republican primary is widely considered to be the favorite to become the state’s next governor, as Tennessee voters haven’t elected a Democratic candidate to a statewide office since 2006 and has never elected an independent one.
For much of the last year, Blackburn held a significant polling advantage over Rose. But in the last few weeks, Rose’s campaign released polling showing the race tightening, which Blackburn disputed. There has only been one non-campaign-funded independent poll conducted, which shows a close race. 
Blackburn has raised $10.8 million for the election, and Rose has raised $15 million, including his self-funding. Fritts has raised close to $300,000.
Blackburn has raised money from more individuals, and Tennesseans specifically. But the largest checks supporting her have gone to the independent expenditure PACs backing her. 
The top donor to the two PACs is the pro-private school voucher group affiliated with Club For Growth called the School Freedom Fund. The group donated $4.81 million to a PAC backing Blackburn a month after her federal Senate campaign donated a nearly identical amount to the organization’s primary PAC.
Blackburn moves $4.8M from US Senate campaign account in apparent legal ‘workaround’

Other top donors to Blackburn’s PACs are Club for Growth funder Jeff Yass ($1 million), payday lender Advance Financial ($800,000), Tamara Stephens ($279,000) and logistics entrepreneur Spencer Patton ($250,000)
Rose doesn’t have a PAC, and has used his used his personal wealth, estimated at $55 million, to counter the disadvantage.
But a dark-money group called the American Exceptionalism Institute has been running advertisements attacking Blackburn. The group has not registered with the state under its legal requirement to disclose its spending, leaving its donors unknown. A Blackburn campaign surrogate filed a complaint with the state agency in charge of overseeing campaign finance.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina continues to be ruled and held back by the party of fear
description: It would be silly to claim that there aren’t a lot of things in the modern world about which to be deeply concerned or even, at times, fearful. There’s the ongoing global environmental emergency, the resurgence of war and authoritarianism, the many uncertainties surrounding the rapid development of artificial intelligence, the plague of poverty and […]
text:
The North Carolina Legislative Building - Photo: Clayton Henkel. It would be silly to claim that there aren’t a lot of things in the modern world about which to be deeply concerned or even, at times, fearful.
There’s the ongoing global environmental emergency, the resurgence of war and authoritarianism, the many uncertainties surrounding the rapid development of artificial intelligence, the plague of poverty and homelessness and, as even a few moments of three-o’clock-in-the morning reflection will confirm for most of us, dozens of other legitimate worries.
If ever we try to put these things out of our minds, the little devices in our pockets and purses will prevent any sustained success.
All that said, it’s also true that, as one of the greatest American presidents so eloquently reminded the nation in the depths of the Great Depression 93 years ago, allowing ourselves to be overwhelmed and ruled by fear is a recipe for disaster. For a nation, a state, a people to move forward when times are tough, it’s essential that fear be managed and kept in check.
And it’s in light of this simple truth that North Carolinians find themselves sorely burdened these days by the policies and politics of what can be best described as the party of fear.
Think about it for a moment. If there’s a single unifying theme at the core of the policies and politics of the Republican leaders who’ve dominated state lawmaking for the past 16 years, it’s fear. Fear of different people. Fear of science. Fear of corporate bosses. Fear of Donald Trump. Fear of new ideas. Fear of voters. And most of all, fear of change.
The examples go on and on, even in just the past few days.
Take Wake County State Rep. Erin Paré’s new half-baked plan for legislation that would micromanage the clothing worn by transgender teachers.
Rep. Erin Paré, R-Wake County (Photo: NC Newsline)
It’s hard to know whether to laugh or cry at such a preposterous idea. Setting aside the absurd notion that in 2026, clothing must or even can match one’s gender — what, no pants for you and your fellow female legislators, Rep. Paré? – the proposal highlights just how fear and utter cluelessness can feed off each other.
Earth to Rep. Paré: there are hundreds – probably thousands – of trans people right there in your comfy Wake County district who have lived as their true selves for decades and who neither you nor anyone else in the broader public would ever know started life labeled with a different gender. Is it really your plan to revive the old HB2 craziness of the last decade by somehow requiring them to masquerade in an identity they abandoned long ago? Why? How?
Of course, the good news here is that, even under the current GOP leadership in the legislature, Paré’s silly idea seems unlikely to proceed very far anytime soon. Would that this were the case for another fear-based GOP policy of even greater long-term consequence that’s been advancing in Raleigh in recent days.
As NC Newsline has reported, Republican lawmakers are, for what seems like the umpteenth time in recent years, advancing yet more legislation that would erect roadblocks to voting. And as always, the stated excuse – somehow boosting “election integrity” – has absolutely nothing to do with the what’s really going on. Rather, as nakedly transparent ideas like reducing the window for early voting confirm, the new proposals are about one thing and one thing only: doing anything possible to blunt the voter backlash the GOP fears is coming this fall in response to the chaotic Trump presidency.
As with the embarrassingly partisan moves of state Auditor Dave Boliek and his minions, these proposals are all premised on one thing: the Republican fear that certain voters – young people, people of color, and people of low income – will reject them.
It’s the same fear of voters that one sees in the repeated efforts to seize powers from Democratic officials elected by large majorities in statewide elections, as is being pursued yet again in pending “technical corrections” legislation.
And, in a sobering way, it’s the same kind of fear that one sees in policies like those that deny the reality of climate change, that seek to deport millions of immigrants, and that cozy up to corporate plutocrats with ceaseless tax cuts and other giveaways.
Rather than acknowledging, accepting and confronting head-on the formidable challenges we face as a state, nation and species, and promoting participatory, collective action, it’s the policy of the party of fear – indeed, the guiding premise of the whole “MAGA” movement – that Americans can avoid the change that makes many fearful and uncomfortable by somehow keeping it at bay or denying its existence.
And ultimately, it’s not going to work.
As with so many reactionary movements and regimes throughout history, the policies of the party of fear will cause delays, some of them hugely destructive, in addressing the most important issues of our time. But in the long run, change is coming regardless and the sooner we come to recognize the truth in FDR’s warning that “the only thing we have to fear its fear itself,” the much better off we will be.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: University of Alabama schools remove LGBTQ+ language from non-discrimination policies
description: Schools  in the University of Alabama System have removed LGBTQ+ inclusive language in their non-discrimination policies. The University of Alabama, the University of Alabama Birmingham and the University of Alabama Huntsville’s revisions to the policy include removing language including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression.  According t[...]
text:
An aerial view of the University of Alabama campus in Tuscaloosa, Alabama. The University of Alabama System schools have updated their non-discrimination policy to remove language that was LGBTQ+ inclusive.(Jacob Boomsma/Getty Images)Schools  in the University of Alabama System have removed LGBTQ+ inclusive language in their non-discrimination policies.
The University of Alabama, the University of Alabama Birmingham and the University of Alabama Huntsville’s revisions to the policy include removing language including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. 
According to UA’s equal opportunity policy website, the change was made in late November. The news was first reported by The Crimson White, the University of Alabama’s undergraduate newspaper. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alex House, associate director of communications for the University of Alabama, said in an email Monday the policy will be applied the same way.
“Discrimination on the basis of ‘sex’ includes discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender status. Accordingly, the policy’s use of the term ‘sex’ encompasses those protections,” the statement said. “The University will continue to apply its policies consistent with applicable law and remains committed to providing a welcoming environment free from discrimination and harassment for everyone.”
Patricia Todd,  a former state representative who chairs Alabama Equality, an organization that advocates for LGBTQ+ rights, said in an interview Monday that UA removing explicit language that offered protections for the LGBTQ+ community was frustrating to see.
“I mean, the reality is, we are not the problem,” she said. “The LGBTQ community of Alabama just wants to live their life and not be subject to hate speech or marginalization by universities and the government. It’s very disappointing to see the University of Alabama System do that. But that’s sort of the era we are living in with this current president.”
The University of Alabama Birmingham also appears to have removed all diversity and inclusive language from its equal opportunity policy website. An archived version of the site from last April shows the policy overview box has been completely removed and language in the overview section regarding race, gender, sexual orientation and gender identity and expression were all removed. All topics except those relating to the LGBTQ+ community are still included in UAB’s equal opportunity policy.
Alicia Rohan, director of public relations for UAB, said in an email Monday afternoon “the reference to ‘all faculty and staff’ sufficiently covers equal opportunity on the Human Resources page.”
The University of Alabama Huntsville also removed LGBTQ+ inclusive language from its equal opportunity policy. An archived version of the site shows non-discrimination protections included those regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity and expression in mid-November.
A message seeking comment was left with UAH Monday afternoon.
No other public college or university in the state has removed explicit language including the LGBTQ+ community in non-discrimination protections. Todd said “time will tell” whether that changes.
“We have another two years of Trump being in office, and there’s no telling what he’s going to do in the next two years,” she said. “It concerns me greatly.”
Inclusive language is also being removed from other areas at other institutions. Auburn University recently removed diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) language from its Athletics Department mission statement after Libs of TikTok, a right-wing social media account that promotes anti-LGBTQ+ ideas and transphobia, attacked the language on social media last month.
Jennifer Adams, vice president of public affairs, communications and marketing for Auburn University, said in an email statement Monday the mission statement was updated because it didn’t reflect the new “guiding principles” set by the athletic department in 2022.
“In November 2022, the new athletics administration introduced a set of six guiding principles that were adopted for Auburn Athletics. These principles replaced the previous mission statements, which had been in use since at least 2013,” the statement said. “After it was discovered that the outdated mission statements remained on various athletics webpages, those pages were updated to reflect the guiding principles that have been in place since 2022.”
Todd said “the government should not be making those decisions.” 
“That should be a decision made by the athletic associations who run those athletic programs, not elected officials,” she said. “It’s obviously a hot issue, particularly with Republicans. But it’s like, how many trans people have you talked to? None.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC House looks to clear most of its plate this week
description: The North Carolina state House returns to work this week to take what may be its last votes before the November election.  House Republicans are set to give final consideration to two elections bills, one of them controversial.  House Bill 958, which makes changes to a range of voting practices, is on the House agenda […]
text:
The North Carolina Legislative Building (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)The North Carolina state House returns to work this week to take what may be its last votes before the November election. 
House Republicans are set to give final consideration to two elections bills, one of them controversial. 
House Bill 958, which makes changes to a range of voting practices, is on the House agenda for Tuesday. The Senate passed its version of the bill along party lines  last week, and the House will decide whether to accept the Senate’s changes.
Among other changes, the Senate added a provision that would reduce the early voting period in primaries, run-offs, and special elections from 17 days to 10 days.
House Bill 834, which focuses on ballot counting and obtaining missing voter signatures, is also scheduled for a House vote Tuesday. That bill passed the Senate unanimously last week.
Budget changes
The House is set to consider bills that make changes to the state budget. One of those bills, House Bill 268, is a hodgepodge of changes that includes a provision that kicks Secretary of State Elaine Marshall off of a state commission that oversees local government finances, and another that would force a governor’s Cabinet appointees out of their jobs if the Senate does not approve them during a two-year legislative session. 
The House will also consider a separate, smaller budget bill that includes an appropriation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy and approves an “America’s Semiquincentennial” license plate. 
Hemp
A bill that would ban intoxicating hemp products is perched in the House, with the Senate having passed it in early July. The bill is the product of negotiations between senators and House members.
The bill would have North Carolina law match a federal law taking effect in November that outlaws consumable products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC derived from hemp. 
The bill also outlaws possession of hemp-derived consumables by people younger than 21. 
Businesses that specialize in sale of hemp-derived consumable products say the proposed THC limit will be a death blow. They are trying to prevent House approval. 
‘Doing nothing was not an option’: NC Senate votes to crack down on hemp

Veto overrides
The House has put a bill banning encampments by homeless people on its Tuesday calendar, teeing up a vote to override Stein’s veto. 
House Bill 437 passed the House with a veto-proof majority in April. The bill would require local governments to crack down on people sleeping on sidewalks, storefronts, or rights of way. Local governments would be permitted to set up homeless camps on public property for up to a year when there is insufficient space in shelters. 
Another veto override of a bill allowing residents 18 and older to carry a concealed handgun without a permit or safety training has remained on the House’s schedule without a vote for months. The Senate, which has a veto-proof majority, cancelled Stein’s veto of that bill last year.  
Adjournment
The House is set to vote Wednesday on the adjournment resolution the Senate passed last week. It provides for brief monthly sessions into November.  
Senate leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, told reporters last week that he did not anticipate any more Senate votes until after the election.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Bombing Iran back to Stone Age is not a winning strategy. So why does Idaho’s delegation support it?
description: Donald Trump proclaimed on July 26 that he was going to “beat the f**king s**t out of” Iran. This was in response to an Iranian missile attack on a U.S. base in Jordan. Earlier, in his meandering April Fools’ Day speech, he had vowed to send Iran “back to the stone ages.” His incantations remind […]
text:
Emergency crews work at the site of a U.S.-Israeli strike on a residential building that also destroyed the adjacent Rafi-Nia Synagogue on April 7, 2026, in Tehran, Iran. The United States and Israel continued their joint attack on Iran that began on February 28. Iran retaliated by firing waves of missiles and drones at Israel, and targeting U.S. allies in the region. (Photo by Majid Saeedi/Getty Images)Donald Trump proclaimed on July 26 that he was going to “beat the f**king s**t out of” Iran. This was in response to an Iranian missile attack on a U.S. base in Jordan. Earlier, in his meandering April Fools’ Day speech, he had vowed to send Iran “back to the stone ages.” 
His incantations remind me of the famous 1965 words of Gen. Curtis LeMay, a former Air Force chief of staff. LeMay’s solution to North Vietnam’s aggression against South Vietnam was to “bomb them back in the Stone Age.” That faulty strategy did not work then, and it won’t work to “win” Trump’s war in Iran. 
The Vietnam War saw an estimated 7.6 million tons of explosive ordnance dropped across Indochina–1 million in North Vietnam, 4 million in South Vietnam, 2 million in Laos and ½ million in Cambodia. As an aerial artillery observer in South Vietnam, I managed to contribute a small tonnage. The U.S. did not achieve victory in that war despite the staggering amount of ordnance expended. It will not happen in Iran.
We should not forget that Iran survived eight years of a savage and grueling war with Iraq in the 1980s and came through basically intact. That war involved much more than aerial bombardment. It was primarily vicious ground combat that resulted in about 500,000 deaths. The Trump war is a piece of cake for Iran in comparison.
The gutless Republican-controlled Congress could step in and bring this insanity to a halt. After all, the U.S. Constitution gives Congress the power to start and stop wars. The lame excuses dished out by members of Idaho’s congressional delegation, all of whom solemnly pledged to support the Constitution, demonstrate the extent of the corruption that has allowed this wretched war to continue.
Sen. Jim Risch says a Senate vote against the war would send a message to Trump to “put your tail between your legs and run.” That message should be sent. The Iranians have the upper hand and they will not relinquish it before the midterm elections. In the meantime, Trump’s failure to bring the war to a halt will continue to inflict substantial damage on our economy and further degrade America’s standing in the world.
Risch has made the bald-faced assertion that Russia and China will not help Iran in the war. He must not be familiar with readily available information to the contrary. We all should know that both Russia and China have long-standing alliances with Iran. Russia is assisting Iran in targeting U.S. bases in the Middle East. Iran has received satellite imagery from China, as well as tactics learned by Russia in Ukraine.
It would only make sense that our two longest-standing and most malignant adversaries would take advantage of the Iran hostilities to damage the United States’ defense posture. Both are using Iran as a proxy to do just that. 
For its part, Iran is making gains by pretending to agree to certain limitations, giving Trump something to crow about, and then engaging in further hostilities. How better to obtain further concessions from a U.S. president who is desperate for an end to hostilities in order to raise his dismal approval ratings?
Both Russia and China have a strong interest in using the on-again, off-again hostilities as a means of degrading the U.S. military’s capabilities. We are throwing away our stockpile of sophisticated weaponry to prosecute a war that serves no strategic purpose for the United States, but which is a godsend to our most dangerous enemies. 
They need only encourage Iran to jack Trump around with continuing strikes and counterstrikes that deplete our inventories of Patriot and THAAD interceptor missiles. The THAADs cost about $13 million apiece while Patriots run about $4 million each. Russia must be thrilled that the U.S. no longer has stocks of Patriot air defense missiles available to sell to Ukraine.
The Iranians have developed tactics to deplete our supply of these air defense systems with an array of low cost drones and missiles. Our stocks of Tomahawk and ATACMS missiles have been seriously depleted. Replenishment of those stockpiles will take years, giving our strongest enemies a window of U.S. vulnerability to aggression.
Risch and the rest of our congressional delegation need to take seriously the degradation of America’s defense posture resulting from the continuing hostilities in Iran. The attendant domestic price hikes have devastated farmers and consumers in Idaho and across the country. 
It has happened because our cowardly delegation members refuse to honor the Constitution and their sacred oath of office.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Budget for Louisiana watchdog agency more than doubles with new emphasis on waste
description: Spending for the state government’s watchdog agency has more than doubled since Gov. Jeff Landry selected a new leader earlier this year.
text:
The Office of Inspector General’s budget went from $2.2 million to $5.5 million annually in the fiscal year that started July 1, a year-over-year increase of 131%. (Photo by Wesley Muller/LAI)Spending for the state government’s watchdog agency has more than doubled since Gov. Jeff Landry selected a new leader earlier this year. 

The Office of Inspector General’s budget went from $2.2 million to $5.5 million annually in the fiscal year that started July 1, a year-over-year increase of 131%, according to a legislative staff summary. 
Landry chose Angele Davis, previously a state budget czar for Gov. Bobby Jindal, as inspector general in January. She told lawmakers this spring she intends to use $3 million this year to hire outside contractors who can help her find ways to reduce state government spending. 
A similar amount of money was spent on consultants during the first year of Landry’s Fiscal Responsibility Program, launched at the end of 2024. That project was modeled after President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, and also set up to root out government waste. Landry has referred to his program as “LA DOGE.” 

Prior to becoming inspector general, Davis worked as a private contractor on Landry’s Fiscal Responsibility Program. She and the governor have repeatedly said that effort generated $1 billion of savings for the state, including $600 million in federal funding, $300 million in state funding and $100 million in other public financing. 
Neither the governor’s office nor Davis have detailed where the savings was achieved. For example, a comprehensive list of government contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars the governor’s staff said were reduced or eliminated has never been released. 

Those working on the Fiscal Responsibility Program also faced criticism for meeting in private and allegedly violating state transparency laws that required them to convene in public. After the backlash, the group partnered with the Louisiana Legislative Auditor, which doesn’t have to hold public meetings, and continued its work out of the public eye.

Last week, Landry signed an executive order to launch the Louisiana Taxpayer Protection Initiative, which is supposed to build on the work of the Fiscal Responsibility Project. Davis will lead the new effort after lawmakers made some tweaks to the inspector general law in May that expands the scope of her duties. 

“Louisiana taxpayers deserve transparency and assurance that their money is spent wisely,” Landry said in a video announcing the new project. 
The governor’s executive order on the initiative directs the inspector general to coordinate with federal partners to enhance fraud detection. The group is also supposed to find ways to leverage databases, artificial intelligence and other new forms of technology to detect government waste. 

Many state agencies that oversee public assistance programs are required to appoint a liaison to work with the inspector general on the effort. Those who must participate include the Louisiana Department of Health, Workforce Commission, Department of Education, Economic Development and Department of Children and Family Services. 

The Department of Public Safety and Corrections, which oversees the state prison system and Louisiana State Police, does not have to appoint a representative to the group, despite having a combined budget over $1 billion. 

Davis said in a text message Monday all state agencies will be subject to the initiative’s requests for information and the inspector general’s scrutiny, regardless of whether they have a liaison working with her. 

“No department is excluded from the Louisiana Taxpayer Protection Initiative,” she wrote.

title: Gov predicts Tennessee will be a finalist for nuclear campus
description: Gov. Bill Lee said Monday Tennessee has a “really good chance” at being one of two states in the running for a $50 billion nuclear energy campus but hedged on whether it would store nuclear waste. Speaking to the Nashville Rotary Club, Lee called it an “incredible opportunity” that the state should pursue because of […]
text:
Tennessee is one of five states in the running for a nuclear power campus. The state has a history of nuclear power research and production, including by three Tennessee Valley Authority nuclear facilities. One of those, Brown's Ferry, is picture here. (Photo: Tennessee Valley Authority)Gov. Bill Lee said Monday Tennessee has a “really good chance” at being one of two states in the running for a $50 billion nuclear energy campus but hedged on whether it would store nuclear waste.
Speaking to the Nashville Rotary Club, Lee called it an “incredible opportunity” that the state should pursue because of the importance of building new sources of energy, even saying the state has become the “global epicenter of the new nuclear renaissance.”
But while the U.S. Department of Energy is proposing a $50 billion investment with 25,000 jobs for a nuclear campus that will involve fuel production, uranium enrichment, reactor construction, nuclear production, fuel recycling and the nuclear waste storage, Lee said it’s unclear how those will be distributed among states in the running for the project.
The U.S. Department of Energy announced last week that Tennessee is one of five states being considered for a federal partnership to boost nuclear energy production.
Tennessee named finalist for federal partnership involving nuclear energy sites

Tennessee has been involved in nuclear energy and research for decades, playing a role in the development of an atomic bomb in the Manhattan Project at Oak Ridge during World War II. Lee formed a nuclear advisory council and put $70 million into an investment fund for nuclear projects.
Asked after the Rotary Club event whether the state would disclose potential sites if chosen, Lee told reporters he doesn’t know if the federal government is asking for a site yet. Lee, who is leaving office in January 2027, said the public will be included in an open process before decisions are made.
Pressed on the economic benefits of a nuclear campus versus the environmental risks of storing nuclear waste, Lee said the state has to make sure it can do both.
“You make certain that you protect the environment, protect the natural resources that we have,” while also bringing economic growth, he said.
Democratic Sen. Heidi Campbell of Nashville last week sent the governor a letter asking the state to disclose any location for new nuclear energy and waste sites as part of the potential partnership. Such a move would enable the legislature to review and comment before the state makes a decision.
Besides saying such a campus would be in the Oak Ridge area, the Lee administration has kept most details secret, Campbell said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas healthcare providers alarmed by potential end of state’s Medicaid expansion
description: The Trump administration’s decision not to renew Arkansas’ hybrid Medicaid expansion is alarming medical providers and experts who say the loss of insurance for thousands would be devastating and would damage a state healthcare system already facing serious strains. The disclosure Friday by Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ office has created uncertainty for a fi[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock.

(Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)The Trump administration’s decision not to renew Arkansas’ hybrid Medicaid expansion is alarming medical providers and experts who say the loss of insurance for thousands would be devastating and would damage a state healthcare system already facing serious strains.
The disclosure Friday by Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ office has created uncertainty for a first-in-the-nation program that supporters credit with cutting the number of uninsured and the costs hospitals pay to provide care for patients without coverage.
The decision also comes as hospitals around Arkansas have had to cut back services or partner with other providers to deal with financial hardships.
“Any threat to people not having a payment source is a threat to hospitals, especially in rural areas where margins are razor thin,” said Jodianne Tritt, executive vice president of the Arkansas Hospital Association. “Hospitals can’t absorb any more uncompensated care right now.”
Arkansas was the first southern state to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, under a model that uses Medicaid funds to purchase private insurance coverage for those eligible. More than 200,000 people are enrolled in the program, known as ARHOME, and the state’s waiver ends Dec. 31. It’s unclear what will happen to those receiving coverage after that date, though Sanders’ office has said it’s discussing a short-term extension with the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
Arkansas Explained: What’s happening to the state’s Medicaid expansion?

The decision not to renew the program comes less than a month after Centene, one of two insurers providing coverage through ARHOME, announced it would not participate in the program next year. 
State officials had already been preparing to roll out new work requirements for the program next year under the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a mandate expected to lead to thousands of people losing coverage.
CMS has not formally notified the state or commented publicly on its reasons for denying the renewal. Sam Dubke, a spokesperson for Sanders, said CMS determined Arkansas’ program doesn’t comply with the rules regarding budget neutrality, which requires ARHOME not cost the federal government more than would be projected without the program, under the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Joan Alker, executive director of Georgetown University’s Center for Children and Families, said the decision may signal how the Trump administration is handling programs like Arkansas’ expansion that were created under a request known as a section 1115 waiver.
Recent guidance from the administration restricted budget neutrality requirements for such waivers. 
“Certainly Arkansas has a unique model,” Alker said.  “However, this push towards limiting section 1115 waivers, even terminating them in some cases, is now very clear that that’s on the administration’s agenda and is part of this larger federal effort to cut Medicaid.”
Experts say the decision about the Medicaid expansion threatens to add to confusion for those using the program when combined with other changes, including the looming work requirements.
“I think anything that creates confusion and uncertainty will have an impact on how people interact with the program and coverage,” said Allison Orris, senior fellow and director of Medicaid policy for the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. 
Medicaid expansion in Arkansas and other states under the federal health overhaul has been linked to economic and health benefits, including a drop in the uninsured. 



Let us know what you think...


 


Department of Human Services spokesperson Gavin Lesnick did not say how long a possible temporary extension the state is seeking. In a statement, he said discussions with CMS were continuing. If the temporary extension is not granted, Lesnick said any changes to the expansion program would “center on service delivery, not eligibility.” 
Arkansas’ hybrid expansion has been the subject of fierce fights in the Legislature since it was adopted in 2013. Supporters have struggled to win the three-fourths majority needed in both chambers of the majority-Republican Legislature for its reauthorization. The program, however, easily won reauthorization earlier this year.
Sanders doesn’t plan to call a special session before the Legislature convenes next year, “but looking ahead to the next legislative session, will work with her partners in the legislature to build a sustainable model that maintains the same high quality of care and saves taxpayer dollars,” Dubke said.
The Legislature is scheduled to convene for its regular session in January. Medical groups said they were ready to be a part of the conversation on next steps forward.
“Any path forward must prioritize keeping patients connected to their care, reducing administrative barriers that delay treatment, and preserving access to the full spectrum of healthcare services — from primary care clinics to hospitals — in every community across the state,” said Carl Vogelpohl, president of the Arkansas Medical Society, which represents physicians in the state. 
Tritt and former state Medicaid Director Ray Hanley said the federal government’s decision leaves two options for continuing coverage for those on the program, but both face challenges.
One would be to move those on the program to traditional fee-for-service Medicaid, but it would reimburse less than what qualified health providers pay through the ARHOME program. 
The other would be to move them to a managed care system, though Hanley said contracting with a managed care organization for that would take at least 15 months.
Hanley said abandoning those receiving coverage altogether isn’t a feasible option.
“I think there is a bipartisan interest in not letting that happen,” Hanley said. “It would be political suicide.”
Advocate reporter Ainsley Platt contributed to this report

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Medicare for All and West Virginia
description: “Analyses show that administrative overhead, insurer profit margins, and PBM-related practices account for a significant share of premium spending. Roughly 16 cents of every premium dollar goes to profits and administrative costs, making overhead the second-largest category of premium spending.” — Rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va. I agree 100% with Rep. Carol Mille[...]
text:
A hospital “H” sign. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)“Analyses show that administrative overhead, insurer profit margins, and PBM-related practices account for a significant share of premium spending. Roughly 16 cents of every premium dollar goes to profits and administrative costs, making overhead the second-largest category of premium spending.” — Rep. Carol Miller, R-W.Va.
I agree 100% with Rep. Carol Miller. What I do not understand is why she and others in both the GOP and the Democratic Party do not endorse the proven way to do away with the overhead — single payer. Medicare has 2% overhead — the other 14% could go to giving the uninsured coverage instead of advertising and million dollar executive salaries.
We must not stick our heads in the sand and continue with a Dickensian free enterprise system; the uninsured sick be damned. Despite her rhetoric, Miller and other elected officials clearly do not want to talk about the elephant in the room — health insurance coverage trends. 
In 2010, prior to the passage of the Affordable Care Act  (Obamacare), 18% of the U.S. population was uninsured. By 2024, that number had dropped to 8%. But that still means that we have too many who are uninsured. 
For example, the uninsured rate for those 19 to 34 years old is 14%. Many of them are working at jobs without coverage. So, the private model insurance system is not only failing, but also failing at nonacceptable rate when it comes to covering the working poor.
In West Virginia, the situation is more stable than most red states. For example, Texas has 19% uninsured. However, in West Virginia the uninsured are still at 8% of the population, about the national average.
For those who are still insured, the situation is problematic. In West Virginia, premium contributions plus deductibles for basic family coverage amount to over 12% of a family’s total income.
Further, In West Virginia, premiums for those enrolled in full family coverage are above the national average. They are going up substantially due to the Trump era cuts in ACA subsidies.
The federal poverty level for a single American is $15,960 for 2026. Lowest cost plan premiums for someone 45 years old who made 401% of the federal poverty level — and therefore received the enhanced premium subsidy — have jumped from $170 monthly in 2025 to $675 now. The cost jump is even greater for someone 55 who made 400% of the FPL — from $18 to $1,041 now. The situation is even worse for a person aged 64 who made 400% of the FPL but was not yet eligible for Medicare, from $0 to $1400 in 2026.
Here is how this works out. Emily is a hard-working senior with a spotless employment record, but she works for a struggling small firm with no insurance coverage. She has an income of $64,000 in 2026, but is paying out $16,800 for a plan with minimal coverage — more than a fourth of her pre-tax pay.
And the situation gets worse every year. Larger companies are absorbing more of the premiums, but they are moving their operations out of the United States in part because of steadily rising health care costs. That means fewer jobs for Americans, especially blue-collar jobs in manufacturing. More and more employers who do stay are dumping the cost of premiums onto their employees and increasing deductibles.
The answer to our problem is simple technically — expand Medicare. A single-payer system will absolutely restrict the rise in costs and cover every citizen. Single payer or something similar is what all developed nations have enacted. Their per capita costs are much less and their mortality and morbidity rates are lower. 
We should expand Medicare incrementally, expanding traditional Medicare year by year, eventually making it cover all those over 55, like it does now for those over 65. In 2027, folks who are 64 would buy in. In 2028, people who are 63 would buy in, and so forth. It would be slow, but eventually everyone over 55 would be covered. 
Then, the results could be evaluated and it could be expanded to other groups. And, if the impact on providers is minimal, as I believe it would be, the phase-in could be revved up.
Elected officials of good faith on both sides of the aisles must come together and propose Medicare expansion as a bi-partisan compromise for the good of the nation. If Congress was dedicated to helping our country, rather than lobbyists funding their campaigns, passing this legislation would be simple.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Does Tennessee business growth matter if no one enjoys living here?
description: Tennessee’s election season is in full swing, and a cursory view of Republican candidates’ campaign ads would have one think they were watching Saturday Night Live skits. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, thought to be the frontrunner in the Republican gubernatorial primary, put out an ad laced with Asian stereotypes and racist dogwhistles, in which she […]
text:
Smoke billows from the Valero Energy plant in South Memphis, a neighborhood with industrial plants and one in which residents complain of pollution. A recent report from CNBC ranks Tennessee poorly for air quality, among other quality of life issues. (Photo: Karen Pulfer Focht/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s election season is in full swing, and a cursory view of Republican candidates’ campaign ads would have one think they were watching Saturday Night Live skits.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, thought to be the frontrunner in the Republican gubernatorial primary, put out an ad laced with Asian stereotypes and racist dogwhistles, in which she crushes fortune cookies to symbolize taking a hardline stance against China. I guess no one told Blackburn that fortune cookies were an American creation.
On the congressional side, former U.S. Rep. Van Hilleary and state Rep. Johnny Garrett are vying for the Republican nomination for the 6th Congressional District. They seem to think the best way to do that is by competing to see who can out-bigot the other in their anti-LGBTQ+ ads featuring drag queens. (And here we were told by Tennessee Republicans that the whole idea was not to show drag queens to the broad public, but I guess it’s OK if doing so scores political points?)
While Republican candidates are busy trying to out-cringe each other, Tennesseans face real issues requiring actual leadership and thoughtful policies, because the Volunteer State is collapsing on the very metrics that made living here enjoyable.
While two Republicans out-cringe each other with AI drag queen ads — unlike these real drag queens — Tennessee’s quality-of-life metrics fall in almost every category, including health care, crime rates and worker protections. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
CNBC’s “rude awakening” report is a dish best served cold
The Consumer News and Business Channel (CNBC), which has historically sung Tennessee’s praises for the state’s pro-business policies, has published damning report after damning report in recent years, marking Tennessee’s fall from 3rd to 9th place in “America’s Top States for Business.”
What happened? It’s not that Tennessee stopped trying to attract businesses. It’s that the state has failed to do anything else.
In its July 9 report, CNBC ranked Tennessee 50th in the nation for Quality of Life, based on metrics like:
Crime rates. Tennessee records 592 violent crimes per 100,000 people, 64.9% higher than the U.S. average. The state’s Republican leadership has taken an increasingly harsh stance on crime, passing bills on truth in sentencing, mandatory minimum sentences, bail restrictions and juvenile transfers to adult court, with nothing to show for it but increasingly policed and surveilled communities and a growing prison population.
Worker protections. Economic output only happens when workers are willing to sell their labor to business owners, and CNBC knows this. A 2025 report by Oxfam put Tennessee at 48th in the nation for workers. Republican leadership’s refusal to raise the $7.25 minimum wage or to legislate family leave, sick leave, heat safety standards, child labor protections or collective bargaining protections is making the business landscape worse for workers.
Infant mortality in Tennessee remains persistently higher than national average

Air quality. While the wealthy can buy, filter and hoard water, everyone must breathe the same air, which influences a state’s quality-of-life rankings. Republican legislators are not kind to our air, giving us regulatory rollbacks, an end to mandatory vehicle emissions testing, state preemption of natural gas bans, and lax oversight (if any oversight) on high-emission industrial and fossil fuel operations.
Healthcare and reproductive rights. Tennessee Republicans’ obsession with passing anti-abortion bills and reproductive healthcare restrictions has led to maternity deserts and worsened maternal mortality: Tennessee ranks 48th out of the 48 states that report maternal mortality. Tennessee also has the nation’s highest number of rural hospital closures per capita.
Inclusivity. CNBC gives Tennessee an “F” on matters of inclusivity. Quoting CNBC’s report, “Tennessee Republicans, led by Gov. Bill Lee, make no apologies for a rash of state laws targeting the LGBTQ+ community, including a so-called ‘bathroom law’ requiring transgender people to use the facilities designated for their sex at birth. The state also explicitly bars localities from adopting their own anti-discrimination ordinances. To underscore the point, Lee signed a resolution earlier this year designating June ‘Nuclear Family Month.’”
As June kicks off Pride celebrations, Tennessee designates it ‘nuclear family month’

Tennessee’s population data is a warning sign for the future
Tennessee’s most ardent defenders of our Republican policymakers will point to the state’s population growth and suggest it’s proof-positive of good policy. But even this bedrock argument is showing cracks.
Tennessee’s population is still growing, and the state still experiences positive net migration. But it’s worth noting the number of people moving to Tennessee is declining, and the number of Tennesseans leaving is growing.
According to IRS data, In 2020, 176,000 people left the state, 185,000 left in 2022, 193,000 in 2023 and 196,000 in 2024. Meanwhile, domestic migration into Tennessee peaked in 2021, and it’s been trending downward ever since.
Are we going to be a state for businesses? Or for people?
The iconic blue, smoke-like haze cresting the Great Smoky Mountains in east Tennessee was once composed entirely of natural emissions from trees and other flora, but now it’s mixed with noxious sulfate particles from the burning of fossil fuels and coal at nearby power plants.
Hundreds of sleepy Tennessee towns in at least 22 rural counties no longer have healthcare access due to hospital closures, a death knell for these communities, as few Americans are willing to live in a town, no matter how beautiful and utopian, if they cannot reach an emergency room or maternity ward in under an hour.
Tennesseans used to pride themselves on their ability to put in an honest day’s work and support a family on that labor, but monthly expenses have surged past wage growth. And because Tennessee’s regressive tax policies rely heavily on sales and excise taxes rather than income tax, working-class residents spend a much larger percentage of their earnings on consumer goods than top earners do.
From the environment to healthcare to the economy, this is not the Tennessee anyone signed up for, which is why a growing number are leaving each year, including many who voted for the current electeds who’ve made the state unlivable.
For those of us willing to stay, it’s time to vote for candidates who treat politics like a public service, not a comedy skit.
